Sports.title: The science behind Luke Littler's trophy-laden success
Sports.content:
Want to know the secret behind the success of darting phenom Luke Littler?

Littler has spearheaded darts' surge towards the mainstream since he broke on the scene with his debut run to the 2024 World Championship final as a 16-year-old.

Darts manufacturer Target Darts has supported the global superstar since the age of 12. In February 2024, the teenager signed a multi-year mega-deal reported to be worth up to £20 million - the most lucrative the sport has ever seen.

The science behind Littler's darts

Luke Littler uses 23g Target Luke Littler Gen 1 (G1) 90% tungsten darts featuring a straight barrel design.



Barrel and Grip Specifications



Material: 90% tungsten alloy with a black PVD coating.



Weight: 23 grams.Dimensions: 52 mm length and 6.5 mm width.



Grip Design: Dual pixel grip and deep ring cuts at the front/centre, with finer radial grooves at the rear.



Shafts and Flights Setup



Points: Extended custom points (around 40mm to 45mm Swiss/nano points) for tighter grouping.



Shafts & Flights: Target K-Flex integrated flight and intermediate shaft system, typically using No.6 shape flights.



Littler possesses a generational talent when it comes to playing darts and Sky Sports pundit Wayne Mardle has said "he's probably the most natural naturally gifted player I've ever seen in my life".

Since the moment the Warrington-born star first held a dart, he's become a record-breaker and history-maker.

James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says both the company and Littler are "aligned" in where they want to see the future of darts go.

Speaking at an event in which Target have set out a vision to inspire 100 million people to play darts by the end of the decade, he explained the process of how Littler sat down with chairman Garry Plummer, the design team, and engineers to build darts to perfect his game.

"I think some of the inspiration was drawn from Adrian Lewis' darts and the pixel grip, which is a unique grip that Target has and that worked its way into building up Luke's original G1," said Tattersall. "That was the barrel, but over the years Luke's tweaked it and challenged us to improve it. The point length has changed, the shaft and flight have changed to a K-Flex system before his first World Championships."

F-Flex is a one-piece flight and shaft innovation that screws into the back of the barrel.

Tattersall explained: "What it helps you do is when you're throwing darts together in such tight groupings like Luke does, the thing you want to avoid is that dart coming in and deflecting off the dart that's already in the board and the K-Flex helps reduce those deflections substantially.

"And longer points - it's like the balance of the dart and how it flies and how it lands through the air. I think another part of it is it keeps the barrel section of the dart further away from the treble and that creates more space in the board."

Talent vs Equipment?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the World Matchplay final between Luke Littler and Gerwyn Price

"His talent is all down to him," says Tattersall. "I think when you're talking about the equipment, we're talking about making Luke comfortable with all of that talent and giving him the right equipment that he's confident with to use and just to get those last few percentages, but Luke's an extraordinary player regardless."

With two world titles in three visits to Alexandra Palace, and 14 major titles to his name, Littler is well on his way to joining Phil Taylor as a legend of the sport.

The problem for his rivals is that he is still getting better after the Warrington star crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 to retain his Betfred World Matchplay title in Blackpool on Sunday.

Littler was in imperious form as he set a new record for the final with an average of 111.53, lifting his average for the tournament as a whole to 111.04 to break Phil Taylor's previous high mark of 106.31.

The win keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026 having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters.

The supporting cast behind Littler

Image: Littler is benefitting from a huge supporting cast

Littler's management have invested in sports psychologists, nutritionists, performance coaches, and biomechanics in order to get the most out of their talent, and the teenager has benefitted in every area to help support his game.

"Mentality is absolutely key. We want to protect the players. The stage is lonely up there, and darts is a gruelling sport," Tattersall said.

"It's a bit like a penalty shootout, but every single time you're throwing a dart. It's such a closed skill, and it's so repetitive. Your mindset's got to be really, really clear, and you get those big momentum swings, you think you're about to checkout the double, you miss by a millimetre, your opponent throws in a big 170 checkout, and that's a punch in the stomach. It's how do you recover from that for the next leg? That's sports psychology, and it's crucial in all sports. I don't know why it's a surprise that it should not be in darts."

'We want to learn about action - not create robots'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Littler smashed in six brilliant 100+ checkouts as he reclaimed the World Matchplay title in Blackpool

With biomechanics, the cameras observe how a player throws darts, with sports science data helping ways of working on the technique in order to improve.

Target have ideas but Tattersall insists implementing them will not turn the Luke Littlers of this world into robots.

"That's the last thing we want to do," he said. "What we want to do is discover and learn about the sport, and learn about that action, because why is it that there are different throwing techniques?

"If you look at something like golf, where you know suddenly you come along with the Vardon grip [or overlapping grip], and that becomes almost the only way to hold a golf club.

"I think the high jump has got that really famous example of how the sport, science, innovated, [Fosbury flop], you ended up with that kind of one technique point.

"I think there will always be different ways of throwing a dart, and there will be different ways of improving those different styles, and maybe that particular style is because you're tall, and maybe that particular style is because you've got longer arms, we don't know yet, but that's what we're going to find out, and then use that data accordingly."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Littler discusses the levels he's reaching at the moment and how it compares to the legendary Phil Taylor

Zoe Burton, Chief Transformation Officer at Target Darts, says Littler is already inspiring the next generation with his natural talent, although the company are slowly moving towards a performance technology system, which is currently being tested on a number of players.

"If you look at a young person and you think of their journey as they get into a sport, you need an inspiring player - that person who they look up to - and can almost aspire to be. Luke Littler provides that," said Buton.

"You need a natural talent, but that gets you so far. Then it's determination and I think psychology as well.

"What makes a star player become a great and world-class player is actually their ability to focus under pressure and make those doubles It's never going to be robotic."

Sports.title: 'Never had a season like this' - Russell 'p****d off' at latest Mercedes issue
Sports.content:
George Russell says he's "never" experienced a season with so much misfortune after an engine issue caused his disastrous start to the Hungarian Grand Prix.

Russell started Sunday's race in sixth, one place ahead of Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli, but his car went into anti-stall so he slowly crept off the line and dropped to the back on the long run down to Turn 1.

He quickly moved through the field to finish seventh but lost further ground in the title race to championship leader Antonelli, who is 50 points ahead of Lewis Hamilton and 59 points in front of Russell.

"Obviously the problems are happening, but the whole team feels it as well. They're as p****d off as I am with how it's unfolded," said Russell.

"We need to look at ourselves and ensure it's nothing we're doing wrong that is contributing to these errors. Oscar [Piastri] had his [gearbox] thing as well. It's not like we're the only one, but it does feel like it is happening substantially more to me than others.

"Hopefully it swings around. I don't wish any bad luck on anyone. But I've never had a season like this in my whole career, let alone my F1 career."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Oscar Piastri take the lead from Lando Norris as George Russell has a race start to forget at Hungaroring in Budapest

Russell explained that he was barely on the throttle pedal yet the engine was revving highly before the lights went out, which led to the "terrible start."

He told Sky Sports F1: "I was on the throttle waiting then all of a sudden the engine was going all over the place, it was revving really high and really low.

"Add it to the list of things that have happened in the first half of this year and pray things calm down in the second half."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix

Russell 'past the point of disappointment'

Both Mercedes drivers have suffered unreliability problems this season but Russell has been on the wrong end of things more recently.

He suffered a battery failure when fighting Antonelli for the lead at the Canadian Grand Prix, was one of five drivers to incorrectly be given a penalty for speeding in Monaco and claims to have been down on straight line speed compared to Antonelli, which culminated in a race-ending collision at the Belgian Grand Prix earlier this month.

Although he admits there are "things in my control I need to do better", Russell says "there are a lot of things out of your control".

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch all of George Russell’s unlucky moments so far this 2026 Formula 1 season

"I'm sort of past the point of disappointment now, because if I continue to be disappointed with everything that goes on, I'll just be disappointed every day of the week. So I've got to stay positive," he said.

"The pace was very strong. The team said I was as strong as anybody out there, which I haven't been there for probably three races, so I will take positives there.

"But yeah, it's just unbelievable the list of things that's happened this season."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell and Kimi Antonelli react to their respective seventh and third place finishes at the Hungarian Grand Prix

Russell was also forced to change his power unit ahead of Sunday's race after an engine crack in qualifying, meaning he may need to take a grid penalty later this year.

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff said: "In terms of engine penalties, I still very much hope we don't need to take it. We need to decide when that is, when we need to take one and which tracks."

Sports.title: Brundle's verdict on 'relentless' Norris, Piastri-Sainz incident and Malaysia return
Sports.content:
The Hungarian Grand Prix was an entertaining way to finish the first part of the 2026 F1 season before the summer break. The top four or five runners were often all visible in the same camera shot, and that included drivers from all four front running teams.

Lando Norris was on brilliant form and took both pole position and the victory, but not without a serious fight in both respects. It wasn't one of those days where a driver leads every lap from pole position and takes fastest lap. Oscar Piastri seized the lead in the second corner of the race, and Charles Leclerc in his Ferrari secured fastest lap but could only muster a fourth-place finish, and that would have been fifth had Lewis Hamilton in the sister Ferrari not attracted yet another penalty, this time for speeding in the pit-lane by 0.1kph.

It turns out Lewis did release the speed limiter a fraction early in order to beat Kimi Antonelli, who was on track, to the all-important safety car line which crosses the entire track and which decides who has the right to be in front, the driver exiting the pits, or the driver on track. It was declared that Antonelli was there a fraction earlier, and so Hamilton had to yield anyway. It was a pivotal moment for the final podium place and therefore the decision that speeding in the pitlane was a potentially competitive advantage was correct, however small the margin.

Relentless Norris and unfortunate Piastri

Norris was on the radio saying that he was faster than team-mate Piastri in the lead, without specifically asking to be let through. Then he asked to pit first, but the pit wall rightly denied that as team protocol is that the leading of the two drivers has first option on stopping.

It was beginning to look like Norris' slide wide in Turn 2 and handing the lead to Piastri would cost him a victory. McLaren pitted Piastri on Lap 16 to cover off the pit stops from Hamilton and Verstappen, and Norris next lap around on Lap 17.

But it was the second round of stops on this high tyre wear circuit that made the difference. Piastri pitted on Lap 33 again to cover Hamilton on fresh tyres, and then Norris had his chance to prove he was indeed faster by running hard and pitting on Lap 39, giving him a decent tyre life offset to his team-mate Piastri.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix

Through the latter stages of the race lapped drivers appeared to be slow or even reluctant to clear the way for the leaders coming through, and it turns out there was an issue with the blue light warning system. That does still leave mirrors and team radio though.

On that same Lap 39, Piastri was coming up to lap Carlos Sainz's Williams who was having his own battle with fellow countryman Fernando Alonso, and after running wide in the infamous Turn 2 which had given Piastri the lead on the opening lap, and which must have looked for all the world to Piastri that he'd seen him and was letting him through, just as Sainz swung heavily back to the racing line and clashed with the race leader.

Sainz had been informed by his Williams team but his position on the outside of a 180 degree turn meant he had no mirror sight of Piastri tight on the inside, and so his penalty was mitigated down to five seconds, which was zero comfort to a rightly angry Piastri.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oscar Piastri was livid after Carlos Sainz makes contact with him in Hungary

Piastri did well not to spin out but he lost crucial time and Norris would emerge from the pits into a lead he would not relinquish. In fact, he would relentlessly increase it despite a third stop under a Virtual Safety Car for fresher soft compound tyres on Lap 56 to recover, so painfully, Piastri's McLaren which had suffered transmission failure.

The young Australian hasn't been able to catch any kind of lucky break for the best part of a year now.

Verstappen fights off Ferraris

Max Verstappen spent much of the race complaining about aerodynamic degradation, poor handling, and inconsistent gear shifting with his Red Bull, but would finish in a fine second place after some impressive overtakes on Hamilton's Ferrari. Max thought Lewis was a bit tough on him in the braking zone, but he wasn't.

It was explained to me that if the Red Bull has any damage on the aero parts particularly underneath the car, on an aggressive kerb for example, this has a disproportionate affect on the overall downforce and so grip. Hence Max's aero degradation comment.

Ferrari had looked the team to beat throughout practice, and most folk in the paddock thought they were favourites even though Norris pipped them to pole. Hamilton had smartly saved a brand new set of soft tyres by clearing the first stage of qualifying on medium tyres. These would have been extremely handy from his front-row grid slot, but he attracted a three-place grid drop from a rather brutal but unintentional blocking of another driver who was on his final qualifying attempt. You'll not be surprised to read the blocked driver was Piastri.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Max Verstappen shocks Lewis Hamilton with a stunning overtake at the Hungarian Grand Prix

Leclerc fluffed his qualifying with a delete lap time for track limits, and had only managed to save a set of lightly used soft tyres to start the race with. You may remember that Ferrari humbled the entire pack from the start down to the first corner in the earlier races of the season, but such is the development curve in this business, even with a tyre advantage, Hamilton only made up one place on the opening lap and Leclerc, starting on the right hand and dirtier side of the grid, fell from the front row to fifth. And now they had to manage those soft tyres and following other cars, and so their race was immediately compromised.

Ferrari would try to help Hamilton with relatively early stops on Laps 13 and 30 for the speed of fresh tyres. But with Verstappen's combative prowess this paid no dividends. Ferrari pitted both drivers again under the Lap 56 Virtual Safety Car for fresher soft tyres but that only served to allow Antonelli to get ahead (as explained earlier), a position he would keep to the final podium spot.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton responds to his speeding penalty from the Hungarian Grand Prix

Mercedes curiously off the pace

Having dominated this season so far, Mercedes were curiously off the ultimate pace, and a three-place grid penalty for Antonelli for failing to sufficiently lift for yellow warning flags in qualifying when Verstappen spun in the final corner, meant that he had lined up seventh, one place behind team-mate George Russell who was also struggling for pace.

George had also collected some engine damage with a run over the kerbs in Turn 4 and would need a new power unit fitted for race day. Whether all this new kit was responsible for a truly awful start is not so far certain, but Toto Wolff seemed clear it was a car issue.

Everything on a racing car, and especially a Formula 1 car, is positioned as low as absolutely possible to lower the centre of gravity, and so helping the handling through corners, and this leaves components vulnerable.

Russell would drop all the way back to 21st and begin a long afternoon fighting back to seventh place, tantalisingly close to Isack Hadjar's Red Bull in sixth.

Antonelli would secure that podium to increase his championship lead to 50 points over Hamilton heading into the break, and 59 points over his team-mate Russell. That's very much the definition of 'damage limitation' from seventh on the grid in such a competitive field on a circuit notoriously difficult for overtaking.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell and Kimi Antonelli react to their respective seventh and third place finishes at the Hungarian Grand Prix

Liam Lawson would finish a fine eighth and Arvid Lindblad 10th for Racing Bulls to move them up into a fifth in the Constructors' Championship ahead of Alpine. What a happy and cohesive team that appears to be.

And Nico Hulkenberg scored two points for Audi in ninth. In my mind's eye, so far this season I think of Audi consistently around and inside the top ten on pace, but actually they are eighth of 11 teams in the championship, underlining that with an improvement in reliability they can be strong contenders in the relentless midfield battle in the second half.

Aston Martin made a decent jump in performance with a comprehensive aero upgrade, and apparently leapfrogging Cadillac and Williams, and threatening Haas, all at once, but they along with Honda still have a long way to go. Nonetheless it was finally encouraging for the Silverstone team.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fernando Alonso says Aston Martin’s new upgrades have delivered the improvements they expected, making the car easier to drive, but admits there is still more potential to unlock

Championship far from over

If McLaren have made a decent upgrade step which translates well to other circuits, this was the team's 14th Hungaroring victory, and with the top four are ever closer, this championship is far from over. There are still 291 points available assuming all the remaining races take place given the Middle East conflict.

On that subject, the Bahrain GP will now be run at the very popular Sepang circuit in Malaysia. This is the same impressive lateral thinking and flexibility F1 and its partners showed during the pandemic and I applaud it.

It sounds as if there will definitely be a European replacement race in late November or early December if Qatar and Abu Dhabi can't take place. We may need to fit some headlights and wipers for that race but the teams and drivers will handle it in their stride as usual.

I wish you all a happy summer break.

MB

Sports.title: Dubois splits from trainer McGuigan ahead of title defence
Sports.content:
Caroline Dubois has parted ways with trainer Shane McGuigan before she bids to defend her WBC and WBO lightweight titles against Amelia Moore in Birmingham on August 29, live on Sky Sports.

McGuigan, who has established himself as one of the world's best boxing trainers, began working with Dubois in 2021.

Together, the pair have enjoyed some great success, with McGuigan guiding Dubois to victories over Maira Moneo, Bo Mi Re Shin, and the 25-year-old's title-unifying victory against Terri Harper in April.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Caroline Dubois is also determined to fight rival Alycia Baumgardner sooner rather than later

Dubois and American Moore will fight at 135lbs over 10 two-minute rounds at the bp pulse LIVE Arena, with Mikaela Mayer and Chantelle Cameron set to headline the event, which is entirely composed of bouts between UK and USA female fighters.

The English fighter said earlier this month that she was "frustrated" by having to defend her titles, rather than unify the belts, after she had sought out a fight with IBF lightweight champion Elif Nur Turhan.

"From what I hear and from what my promotions are telling me and my team is telling me, they made her an offer and she [Turhan] asked for such an astronomical, ridiculous amount. It was absurd. It was crazy," Dubois said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alycia Baumgardner says she is chasing the biggest fights possible as she was asked if she would want to fight Caroline Dubois and Katie Taylor

"The amount that she asked for and it was, it wasn't even a laugh out of the room. It was just something… ignore that because it was just so ridiculous.

"She isn't about it. She thinks that she is something that she isn't and I'm really disappointed in her and how she's moving because it's all good to talk online. She asked for the most ridiculous number that you would, even if I told you, you would think I'm lying.

"So she just isn't about it. She's a joker and what you do with jokers, you just leave them alone.

"That's retirement money. That's, that's never-fight-again type of money."

Dubois believes the fight with Turhan will happen eventually and is also eyeing up a meeting with WBA lightweight title holder Stephanie Han.

Sports.title: Boulter knocked out of DC Open as Norrie ends losing streak
Sports.content:
Katie Boulter failed to build on a promising start as she suffered a 3-6 6-2 6-2 defeat to American Ashlyn Krueger in the first round of the Mubadala DC Open.

In Mexico, fellow Brit Cameron Norrie booked his place in the second round of the Mifel Tennis Open by Telcel Oppo with a 6-4 6-1 victory against world No 95 Aleksandar Kovacevic.

Boulter dominated the first set and went a break up in the seventh game as Krueger sent a backhand long.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Boulter and fellow tennis player Alex De Minaur got married earlier this month

The Brit, who was making her first appearance since a first-round Wimbledon exit, broke again two games later to clinch the opening set.

Krueger turned things around after making 16 unforced errors in the first set, to break Boulter twice in the second and level the contest.

The final set was a tense affair, with Krueger immediately going on the offensive, forcing Boulter to save two break points, but the Brit held service.

Boulter then hit back, taking a 2-0 lead, but could not sustain her momentum, with Krueger breaking her opponent three times over the next five games to seal victory.

Krueger will now take on four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka in the second round.

Norrie ends ATP Tour losing streak

Image: Cameron Norrie ended a six-match losing run on the ATP Tour in Mexico on Monday

Norrie ended a six-match streak without a win on the ATP Tour with a big victory against Kovacevic in Mexico.

Despite winning in straight sets, it wasn't all plain sailing for the Brit, who lost on service in the opening game.

He hit back immediately, levelling the set, but again struggled to hold serve, with Norrie saving two break points to fend off his opponent's advances.

The first set came down to the wire, with Kovacevic and Norrie trading breaks again in the eighth and ninth games, but it was the Brit who came out on top.

Norrie kicked into second gear in the second set, taking a 4-1 lead before seeing out the match in just over half an hour to book a second-round tie against either Aidan Mayo or Jamie Duckworth.

Sports.title: France turn to ‘legend’ Zinedine Zidane as head coach in long-awaited homecoming
Sports.content:
Zinedine Zidane has been appointed as France’s new head coach, replacing Didier Deschamps at the helm of the team he led to glory as arguably its greatest ever player.

The French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo announced Zidane’s appointment at the FFF headquarters in Paris on Tuesday, saying he has been given a four-year contract.

“This is an exceptional moment, exceptional because of the person sat next to me,” Diallo said. “Zinedine is one of the legends of French soccer and for many years he said one of his dreams was to take charge of the France team.”

The 54-year-old Zidane has not coached since leaving Real Madrid in 2021. “For me it’s a continuity, a dream,” he said. “I had some offers during the five years I was away to take charge of a club but I turned them all down for the France team. It was the only thing I wanted to do.”

Zidane called it “an immense joy” to take charge of the team he starred for. “I have so many emotions, I am ready for the challenge,” he said. “That’s what motivates me.”

Zidane praised Deschamps won the 2018 World Cup and stepped down after the recent World Cup, where Les Bleus lost in the semi-finals to Spain. “Today I have the opportunity to be in charge of this team and I will give everything so that this team can win,” Zidane said. “I would also like to congratulate DD for these remarkable years.”

Sports.title: How Premier League Futures programme is helping former academy prospects
Sports.content:
“Within six months of being the captain at West Ham and playing in the Youth Cup, I was delivery driving at Domino’s,” says Iyiola Adebayo.

Adebayo had joined at eight the academy that produced Rio Ferdinand, Joe Cole and Declan Rice and the defensive midfielder from Tilbury was tipped to follow in their footsteps when awarded a scholarship before anyone else in his age group. However, a dislocated shoulder set him back in the first year and despite making appearances for the under-21s and under 23s, he was released at 16.

“They thought maybe being in a new environment and being in a new club might allow me to push on and thrive because I had been there for so long,” he says. “It was a tough time, especially in terms of my identity. Because I’ve always been Iyiola that plays for West Ham.”

Desperate to find a club, but not fully recovered from injuries that plagued his final two years at West Ham, Adebayo went to several trials “probably at 50-60% of what I was capable of” and found it difficult to cope with the feeling of rejection.

“To have to go to parts of the country I’ve never been to before by myself, knowing I couldn’t fully show myself, it was definitely challenging mentally for me,” he says. “I remember having some conversations with my mum and my friends at the time about how I was struggling a bit mentally, and sometimes I didn’t want to be there, I wanted to go home. It was very difficult.”

Adebayo started working part‑time delivering pizzas to make ends meet when the former head of education at West Ham suggested attending the Premier League Futures programme. Adebayo was reluctant and had to be persuaded. “I was still dealing with my release. Sometimes when you’re in that phase you don’t want to do anything that reminds you of that situation,” he says.

The Futures programme started in 2017 as part of the requirement for academies to provide a minimum three‑year aftercare commitment for players released during the professional development phase (under‑17 to under‑21) and is an introduction into potential career pathways beyond the pitch. That includes two initiatives to support under-16 players without a contract and a 12-month programme for current, as well as former academy players, between the ages of 18 and 24.

For Adebayo, it has been life‑changing. He is in the final year of a sponsored football business and marketing degree at the University Campus of Football Business and also runs workshops to players in academies on mental health and lifestyle choices on behalf of Sporting Chance.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Iyiola Adebayo now runs workshops to players in academies that focus on mental health and lifestyle choices. Photograph: Premier League

He spotted the charity set up by the former Arsenal captain Tony Adams had a stand at the Premier League youth development conference he attended as part of the Futures programme.

“I went to speak to them when I was released because I felt quite a bit of anxiety around playing football and I did some counselling sessions with them. I remembered their logo and my experience with them,” he says.

“[The workshops] are about dealing with the pressures of being an academy player, whether that be peer pressure or the pressure to perform. Sometimes it’s about the messenger as well as the message. I’m not that far removed from the experiences they’re going through.”

The 23-year-old admits the Futures programme has opened his eyes to potential career paths. “I thought you’re either a coach, you’re a player, maybe you’re a kit man or a physio. But learning there’s hundreds of roles where you can make loads of money and have fulfilling careers, I think I was ready to hear it and ready to take the opportunity.”

According to Neil Saunders, the Premier League’s director of football, who studied at the University of Bath after being released by Watford as a teenager, there has been increasingly more emphasis on encouraging those not offered professional deals to move into higher education or to look for other jobs in the industry.

“A relatively small number make it through to the first team, but we want every single young person that comes through the academy to be able to look back on their time positively,” he says. “Many of the boys will have spent a significant number of years in academies and will become experts in performance analysis or in strength conditioning and coaching.

“While there are a finite number of jobs as a professional player, we want to make sure we’re equipping those young people with the opportunity to progress into roles beyond the pitch.”

Adebayo is planning his next step. “I’ve learned so much, because I’ve been made aware of so much and improved my skill set so much,” he says. “First, I probably want to work in player care and maybe after that I might want to go and work in the business or commercial side of sport. It’s made me very optimistic that I can still be involved in sport and football, but in many different ways.”

Sports.title: Mind the ever-growing gap: the Premier League keeps spending big
Sports.content:
The financial power of the Premier League is unmatched. The teams in England’s top division have collectively invested more than £1.4bn in new players already this summer (through disclosed fees alone), around £303m more than the 76 clubs from the Bundesliga, La Liga, Ligue 1 and Serie A combined.

These figures are the gross spend, so take no account of players sold to help balance the books. Factoring this in only increases the divide. The clubs of Ligue 1 and the Bundesliga are £203.4m and £72.2m in credit from their transfer dealings respectively. While La Liga (£163.1m) and Serie A (£124.1m) have spent more than they have earned, they are an ocean adrift of the Premier League’s net spend of £523.6m.

None of this is new; it has been the trend for many years. The worrying aspect for teams across the continent is that the gap between the Premier League and the rest may grow wider before the summer is out.

Despite their enormous outlay, top-flight English teams have spent about £230m less than Premier League clubs of 2025-26 had at this point last year. But only 25 deals were completed by the end of 1 July (which is when new contracts usually start, explaining why pre-arranged moves are often finalised then). It’s roughly half as many as the 47 that occurred by that date last summer. The expanded World Cup will probably have delayed some deals, creating a potential backlog of transfer spending that will soon hit the books.

Assessing clubs individually highlights why most might continue spending. Aston Villa, Brighton and Tottenham have already spent more in gross terms than in the entirety of the summer 2025 transfer window. Unai Emery has a net £109.6m burning a hole in his pocket following business which includes the departures of Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans. Brighton will need a larger squad as they have a Conference League campaign on the horizon while Tottenham are hoping to improve upon consecutive 17th-place finishes. Their trading may not be complete even though they’ve already outspent their efforts from last summer, with Spurs’ net spend of £149.7m the highest in Europe’s big five leagues.

Chelsea also have a higher net spend than last year, even before their reportedly agreed deal for Crystal Palace’s Maxence Lacroix goes through. Even if that transfer is not completed, would you bet against BlueCo throwing more money around, especially with a new manager to back? Danny Welbeck is the latest to emerge on the Stamford Bridge radar. Either way, Chelsea have already invested more in new talent than they had on this day last year. The same is true for Everton, Fulham, Manchester City and Newcastle, all of whom may have further incomings in the pipeline, too.

There are other clubs with work to do. The three promoted teams have only spent £8m more between them than Sunderland alone had at this point in 2025. Régis Le Bris added a total of 18 new players to his squad last summer, with fellow promoted sides Burnley (15) and Leeds (11) also hitting double figures for incomings. By these standards, Ipswich (with seven new players), Hull (four) and Coventry (three) must recruit further.

At the opposite end of the Premier League scale, Arsenal, Liverpool and Manchester United have collectively spent two-thirds of a billion less on new talent than they did last summer. The latest rumour mill gossip says the champions may make a move for Vinícius Júnior. If not the Brazilian then perhaps Bradley Barcola, though Liverpool are also said to be pursuing the Paris Saint-Germain winger. Neither player will be remotely cheap. United are believed to be targeting Ollie Watkins – he wouldn’t cost Vinícius or Barcola money, but neither would Villa sell to a rival at a reduced fee.

The Premier League also has clubs who have yet to make an outlay. It is unlikely Crystal Palace, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland end the summer without spending a transfer fee as is now the case. It would be remiss of Palace and Sunderland not to invest when they are in European competition this season. As for Forest, like Chelsea they have had an insatiable thirst for player turnover in recent times. With Elliot Anderson having left for an enormous fee, replacements will surely arrive soon.

It is remarkable to think the Premier League may not be halfway through its summer outlay when £1.4bn has already been used for recruitment. The top-flight English clubs collectively spent £3.1bn on players last summer, with over £600m in the final week of dealing alone. That figure may be blown away by the time the transfer window closes on 3 September.

Sports.title: Fifa president Gianni Infantino called to appear before Congress over Trump ties
Sports.content:
Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee, has launched an investigation into Fifa president Gianni Infantino, seeking documents that would detail the ties between soccer’s governing body and Donald Trump and his administration.

In a Sunday letter, Raskin wrote to Infantino and called for Fifa to provide any documents and communications related to gifts, payments or benefits provided to Trump and his associates, as well as the visitor logs for Fifa’s office space in Trump Tower, which it acquired last year. The committee also requested that Infantino sit for a transcribed interview.

Infantino’s relationship with Trump came under scrutiny in the lead-up to this summer’s World Cup. In December, at the World Cup draw in Washington, Trump was awarded a newly created “Fifa peace prize” at the Kennedy Center, where renovations were allegedly “rushed” on the administration’s orders to prepare for the event. Fifa opened its office in Trump Tower in midtown Manhattan last July.

Such scrutiny intensified during the World Cup. Trump made several calls to Infantino to lobby for a review of US striker Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before the Americans’ last-16 match against Belgium. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team and drew the ire of other teams and associations from around the world.

Alongside the leaders of Canada and Mexico, Trump joined Infantino for the World Cup trophy presentation after Spain beat Argentina in the final. The pair, who watched the final together in a glassed-in section of luxury seats, were met with boos from the New York New Jersey Stadium crowd when they took the field.

Raskin’s letter references the Department of Justice’s decision to “dismiss the indictments” of defendants in US government investigations into corruption in global soccer, including the 2015 prosecution of more than 20 high-level Fifa officials and sports-marketing executives.

“[Y]our election as Fifa president was supposed to mark a red-card break from a decades-long culture of corruption and scandals that dressed down world soccer’s reputation,” Raskin wrote to Infantino in the letter. “Instead, at the start of your tenure, you dismantled Fifa’s ethical guardrails and disabled the organization’s ethics committee by pushing out most of its members. This lack of transparency and oversight has since paved the way for you to ingratiate yourself with the Trump administration via tactics that a New York University law professor and one of your former ethics committeemen described as ‘legal bribery’.”

The letter also addresses Fifa’s World Cup ticketing policy, which is already the subject of investigations by several attorneys general in the United States. The use of dynamic pricing drew much criticism during the tournament, leading to massive surges and pricing out many fans from attending games.

“The most recent quid pro quo that Fifa and President Trump orchestrated is not a victimless crime. It hurts Americans. Fifa has taken its newfound favored status in the Trump administration as a sign that it may rip off its consumers, most notably, by employing illegal price-gouging and fraudulent sales tactics for the World Cup,” Raskin said in the letter.

The letter gives a deadline of 9 August to provide the requested documents and schedule the interview. Raskin does not have the power to compel Infantino to appear, given that Democrats do not hold the majority in the House, unless he garners Republican support.

Fifa’s interactions with the US government did not end with this summer’s World Cup. The US is expected to be the primary host of the Women’s World Cup in 2031, and the success of this year’s tournament has led many to speculate that the 2038 men’s World Cup could be hosted by the US. Fifa has been approached for comment.

Earlier on Monday, Infantino used a 15-part message on Instagram to denounce his critics, accusing them of spreading hate and false narratives. He touted the World Cup as a success.

More than 200 Fifa members have endorsed Infantino ahead of the presidential election in March, but some associations have stood in opposition. The Norwegian football federation is planning to submit a formal complaint to Fifa ethics investigations over Trump’s role in the reversal of Balogun’s ban.

Sports.title: Football transfer rumours: Manchester United to sign Juve’s Francisco Conceição?
Sports.content:
As sports fans everywhere eagerly await the resumption of cricket’s County Championship season, what better way to while away a few minutes than to contemplate the latest football transfer rumours?

Manchester United and Michael Carrick want to sign the 23-year-old Portugal winger Francisco Conceição from Juventus. The tricky former Porto player, who recently returned from the World Cup, is valued at around £43m (€50m). United are also said to be ahead of Chelsea in the race to snap up Alex Scott from Bournemouth.

Real Madrid, meanwhile, have increased their offer to RB Leipzig for Yan Diomande – who Leipzig had hoped to replace with Conceição – to around £98m. Reports in Germany say further talks are in order to get the deal for the 19-year-old Côte d’Ivoire international over the line.

Liverpool have emerged as favourites to sign the France international Bradley Barcola from Paris Saint-Germain, having reportedly held preliminary talks with the 23-year-old over a lucrative transfer.

Bruno Guimarães continues to be the subject of strong interest from the Premier League champions Arsenal. Newcastle, naturally, have insisted the Brazilian is not for sale, but personal terms have reportedly been agreed between the Gunners and Guimarães’s people, so a bid is surely imminent. Arsenal are also being linked with Vinícius Júnior, with Mikel Arteta apparently determined to sign the Madrid and Brazil forward. Speculation reached fever pitch on Tuesday when it was reported Vinícius Júnior will not train this week, further increasing uncertainty over his future. José Mourinho is keen to keep the winger.

Paris Saint-Germain have distanced themselves from a move for all-conquering Manchester City midfielder Rodri, but the Premier League club anticipate an offer from Real Madrid.

Seemingly having fought off Chelsea’s pursuit of Granit Xhaka, Sunderland are ready to boost their defensive options by signing the full-back Dayann Methalie from Toulouse.

Over in Spain, it has been reported that Sevilla are ready to sell Ruben Vargas for around £17m – Aston Villa, Newcastle and Brighton are among potential suitors in His Majesty’s Premier League.

Leeds are poised to confirm a £40m deal for James Trafford, who re-signed for Manchester City after a couple of seasons at Burnley, while Manchester United are keen to send Joshua Zirkzee on a season-long loan to Juventus, with an option for the Bianconeri to buy the 25-year-old.

Chelsea have held talks with the Brighton forward Danny Welbeck (35) and are also keen to sign Jordan Henderson (36). Welbeck knocked in 13 Premier League goals for the Seagulls last season and was fancied as a possible option for England at the World Cup, while Henderson made the cut, only to suffer a freak wrist injury. Chelsea are presumably drawing up eight-year contracts for both veterans.

In Germany, Borussia Dortmund have agreed to sign the midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas from Racing Genk in Belgium, for a fee that could rise to £32m.

And John Stones, a free agent after leaving Manchester City, has moved closer to completing his move to Inter as reported in these pages: a deal has been verbally agreed.

Sports.title: John Stones set for Inter move after shining for England at World Cup
Sports.content:
Inter are closing in on signing John Stones as a free transfer after the 32-year-old defender left Manchester City in June.

Inter and their rival Italian club Juventus were interested in Stones before the World Cup and the Nerazzurri are now in pole position to recruit him following his impressive form in England’s run to the semi-finals.

Stones made 13 appearances for City last season before being injured in December. Yet after being out for two months and staying injury-free, he was selected only five more times by City’s then manager Pep Guardiola.

At the World Cup, Stones started the opening game for Thomas Tuchel’s team against Croatia, was an unused substitute against Ghana and Panama, made substitute appearances in the knockout wins against the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Mexico, before starting the quarter-final victory against Norway and the 2-1 semi-final defeat against Argentina.

Towards the end of last season Stones spoke of his continuing ambition to play at the top level. “I still feel I have so much to give a club and I feel in a good moment physically,” he said. “There is a lot for me still to fight for in my career and a new challenge will be exciting. I’m keeping an open mind. I can take what I have learned here and maybe pass it on.”

While Inter are confident of signing Stones, the deal could yet collapse should a requisite Premier League club express an interest.

Arsenal’s William Saliba is out for an extended period with a back injury, meaning a defender is needed for cover in Mikel Arteta’s squad. Chelsea under Xabi Alonso are expected to play with three centre-backs so are in the market to sign at least one. Neither Arsenal nor Chelsea, though, are yet to make a move for Stones.

Sports.title: Chelsea explore surprise moves for Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson
Sports.content:
Chelsea are understood to be in talks over a move to sign Danny Welbeck from Brighton. The 35-year-old is a surprise candidate to bolster Xabi Alonso’s forward line after scoring 13 goals in 37 Premier League matches last season.

In a further unexpected move, there are also reports the club are in negotiations to bring in England midfielder Jordan Henderson from Brentford. The 36-year-old has a year left on his contract, but it is claimed the Bees would be willing to let him leave on a free transfer.

The former Liverpool captain made 34 appearances for Brentford last season and was a member of England’s World Cup squad. He broke his arm when he fell over advertising hoardings celebrating their win over Mexico.

Welbeck also has a year remaining on his deal and there is optimism a deal can be concluded as Brighton are understood to be willing to let the striker move for the right price.

Should a deal be reached it would increase the likelihood of departures from Stamford Bridge, with uncertainty surrounding the futures of Liam Delap and Nicolas Jackson. Delap is considered second-choice striker behind João Pedro, who impressed in his debut Chelsea campaign with 15 league goals, while Jackson spent last season on loan at Bayern Munich and has attracted interest from Aston Villa.

Delap had been expected to be given a second year to prove himself after an unsuccessful debut campaign following his £30m move from Ipswich a year ago, though this latest development would seem to cast doubt on his future.

Interest in Welbeck and Henderson reflects a revised Chelsea transfer policy as the club seek to recruit more established players under Alonso.

If the move happens, Welbeck would join a long line of players and staff to make the switch from Brighton to Chelsea in recent years, including the goalkeeper Robert Sánchez, midfielder Moises Caicedo and striker João Pedro.

Sports.title: ‘Born out of quality’: Webb vows to increase match officials from minority groups
Sports.content:
Howard Webb, England’s chief refereeing officer, has vowed to continue increasing the talent pool from under-represented communities in English football’s officiating pathway, rejecting the wider backlash against diversity initiatives.

Addressing that historic under-representation has prompted a new direction. In June, the newly named Professional Referees’ Body (Pro Ref), formerly called Professional Game Match Officials, announced that Select Group 1, 2 and its supplementary list had been merged into a new, single Professional Referee Group in the men’s professional game and will largely service the Premier League and the Championship from the start of the 2026-27 season. Pro Ref said it would create flexibility in appointments and help to recognise a wider variety of talented match officials as part of the organisation’s new direction.

At a conference held at the Emirates Stadium by Bamref – an advocacy group that helps to give voice to Black, Asian and mixed-heritage officials – Webb told the Guardian that Pro Ref’s diversity drive fosters healthy and important competition. “We’re doing it to increase the quality of the officials working at the higher end of the game,” he said, insisting the decisions behind it are “born out of quality, rather than any other aspect”.

View image in fullscreen Howard Webb, the chief refereeing officer at Pro Ref. Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The Guardian

In March, Reform UK’s Suella Braverman wrote to the Football Association demanding that it scrap its target for a quarter of England men’s coaching staff to come from minority ethnic backgrounds by 2028, calling the approach “utter woke nonsense”. The FA responded by defending the target as part of its wider commitment to reflecting the diversity of the game. Similar pressure has surfaced in US sport, where the NFL’s Rooney Rule is now facing a legal challenge from Florida’s attorney general. In the UK, employers can encourage applications and provide targeted training for under-represented groups.

Webb argued that the visibility of refereeing makes tokenism impossible. “If you are not good enough to officiate in the Premier League you will be found out really quickly. There’s no real hiding places,” he said. A more diverse talent pool, he said, is “much more likely to bring higher levels of quality, greater choice, greater competition, and ultimately raising standards for all”.

Farai Hallam is the latest example, following Uriah Rennie and Sam Allison as the third Black referee to officiate in the Premier League. In a defining moment, he waved away a penalty claim for Manchester City against Wolves in January, rejecting the video assistant referee’s advice.

Danielle Every, the Pro Ref chief operating officer, said the organisation has seen a shift in attitudes since it introduced structural changes. “I genuinely feel that there is more acceptance and understanding of why these interventions are important,” she said, pointing to data showing zero Black representation among Premier League officials in 2022.

View image in fullscreen Farai Hallam rejects Manchester City’s claims for a penalty despite a VAR review during January’s Premier League match at the Etihad Stadium. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

The stance comes as Pro Ref overhauls how it identifies talent. Webb described moving away from solely relying on the traditional observer system – in which officials were marked out of 10 after every match and ranked on a performance table – towards a coaching-led model built around a new “matchday performance developer” role. That model will be rolled out in League One and League Two as well as the women’s professional game. In the Premier League and Championship, the key match incidents panel, a primary layer of accountability, will remain. Referees at all levels expect their matches and performances to be subject to review by individual coaches.

The old system, Webb said, was “very rigid and restrictive”, and led to “some really good officials being left behind”. The change, he insisted, will help to surface talent from under-represented groups earlier than before.

Aji Ajibola, who co-founded Bamref in 2019, welcomed the progress on numbers but warned it counts for little without sustained backing once officials are inside the system. “We now have a duty of care to those that we’re bringing into officiating, to make them feel safe,” he said, describing plans for wraparound support covering mental health and wellbeing alongside coaching and mentoring.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“We’ve got expertise in our community, which then creates opportunities for us to get into other areas of the game,” he said, framing retention, not recruitment, as the next front in the campaign.

Tension between visible progress and lived experience was echoed by Akil Howson, inducted into the Bamref Hall of Fame at this year’s conference after becoming the first Black official in an FA Cup final. “Broken down the barrier finally after 158 years and now hopefully that door will never be shut again,” he said of the milestone.

Howson, who is entering his fourth season as a Premier League official, was blunt about how far the game still has to go. “I still go to some of my meetings and I’m the only Black person,” he said. “It’s getting better, but it’s frustrating because it’s not where it could really be.”

On his induction into the hall of fame, Howson pointed to what it signals for those coming through behind him. “It just goes to show how important visibility and representation is.”

Sports.title: Zinedine Zidane is announced as France's new manager on a four-year-deal - as football icon succeeds former team-mate Didier Deschamps
Sports.content:
Zinedine Zidane is announced as France's new manager on a four-year-deal - as football icon succeeds former team-mate Didier Deschamps

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Zinedine Zidane has been announced as France's new manager, with the long-expected announcement having finally been delivered.

The 54-year-old has signed a four-year deal with Les Bleus as he succeeds his former Juventus and France team-mate Didier Deschamps.

Deschamps left his 14-year tenure as France manager at the end of the World Cup, with his side losing 2-0 to eventual champions Spain in the semi-finals. They finished fourth after a 6-4 defeat by England in the third-place play-off.

Zidane's unveiling took place on Tuesday morning at the French Football Federation's (FFF) headquarters in Paris, alongside FFF president Philippe Diallo.

It is Zidane's first foray back into management since leaving Real Madrid in 2021, revealing he has rejected offers in the meantime as he waited for his 'dream' to become France boss.

'The French team was the only thing I wanted to do,' Zidane told reporters.

Zinedine Zidane has been announced as France's new manager on a four-year contract

'I've always looked at this team through the eyes of a future manager. I didn't take a club job for that reason. The only thing I wanted to do after Madrid was manage the French national team.

'I could have taken on a three-year role because Deschamps was there. He made that decision in January 2025, and the very next day I knew I wanted to be the next one. We met with the president and the deal was sealed.'

Deschamps oversaw 185 matches and 120 victories, guiding France to the 2018 World Cup title, the 2020-21 Nations League trophy, and the Euro 2016 and 2022 World Cup finals.

He and Zidane share a long association, having been team-mates in France's 1998 World Cup-winning side on home soil.

Zidane played a pivotal role in that triumph and won the Ballon d'Or that year. He made 108 appearances for the national side, scoring 31 goals and contributing 29 assists.

'You'll see my [team's] style soon,' Zidane said. 'I'm driven by the game. I was a No 10, and what drives me is scoring goals.

'I lived in Spain for 25 years, you know what that means. On the pitch, I was a leader. Now I'm becoming a leader through my experience.

'Winning in '98 is the best thing that's ever happened to me, winning with my team-mates. I spent those four or five years waiting for that day. I'm emotional; you can't see it, but I'm so excited. I'm happy.'

Speaking about Zidane's arrival, Diallo revealed that negotiations with the 1998 World Cup and Euro 2000 winner began in February 2025 after Deschamps said he would stand down after the 2026 World Cup.

'This is an exceptional moment, exceptional because of the person sat next to me,' Diallo said. 'Zinedine is one of the legends of French soccer and for many years he said one of his dreams was to take charge of the France team.'

'I would like to thank Didier Deschamps and his staff for their work. For 14 years he led the France team to the top.'

The length of the deal means Zidane will work through until at least the 2030 World Cup, incorporating two Nations Leagues (2026-27 and 2028-29) as well as Euro 2028 before the major showpiece.

His first match in the hotseat will be away to Türkiye in the Nations League on September 25. After that comes a trip to local rivals Belgium on September 28 with a clash against Italy on October 2 sparking his first game in charge on home soil.
