World.title: Egypt’s 242nd aid convoy heads to Gaza
World.content:
The 242nd humanitarian aid convoy, “Zaad El Ezza… From Egypt to Gaza,” began entering the Gaza Strip on Sunday, July 26, 2026, through the auxiliary gate of Rafah Land Port toward the Karam Abu Salem crossing, in preparation for delivering the assistance to Palestinians in the enclave.

An official source said the convoy’s trucks are carrying large quantities of humanitarian and food aid, including food supplies, relief packages, flour, fresh bread, legumes, canned food, medicines, personal hygiene items, tents, clothing and fuel products. The source noted that the trucks are being inspected by the Israeli authorities before being allowed into the Strip.

Israeli authorities closed the crossings linking Gaza to the outside world on March 2, 2025, following the expiration of the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire agreement and the failure to reach a deal to extend the truce. On March 18, 2025, Israel resumed military operations with intensive airstrikes and renewed ground incursions into areas from which its forces had previously withdrawn. It also blocked the entry of humanitarian aid, fuel and shelter supplies for displaced Palestinians who had lost their homes during the war, while refusing to allow heavy equipment needed for rubble removal and reconstruction into the enclave.

Aid deliveries resumed in May 2025 under a mechanism implemented by the Israeli authorities and a US security company, despite objections from the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), which said the mechanism did not comply with the established international framework for humanitarian assistance. The Israeli military later announced a 10-hour temporary humanitarian pause on Sunday, July 27, 2025, suspending military operations in parts of Gaza to facilitate the delivery of aid.

Mediators—Egypt, Qatar, and the United States—continued efforts to secure a comprehensive ceasefire agreement in Gaza and an exchange of prisoners and detainees. Those efforts culminated in an agreement reached in the early hours of October 9, 2025, on the first phase of a ceasefire plan proposed by US President Donald Trump during talks in Sharm El Sheikh, with Egyptian, American and Qatari mediation and Turkish support.

The second phase of the agreement entered into force on February 2, 2026, following the completion of the exchange of prisoners and detainees and the handover of the remains of the last Israeli detainee under the first phase. The agreement also allowed Palestinians to enter Gaza and enabled wounded and injured individuals to leave the Strip for treatment at Egyptian hospitals after the Palestinian side of the Rafah border crossing was reopened.

World.title: Egypt leads Africa in FDI inflows for fourth consecutive year
World.content:
Egypt ranked first in Africa for attracting foreign direct investment (FDI) for the fourth consecutive year, recording inflows of $15.5 billion, while also placing second among Arab countries, reflecting investors’ confidence in the Egyptian economy and the country’s economic reform program, Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid Saleh said.

Speaking on Monday, July 27, 2026, at the launch of the World Investment Report 2026, the minister said the report, issued by the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), highlights the shifts taking place in the global economy amid geopolitical tensions, growing national security considerations and changing international investment priorities.

He noted that global FDI flows increased by six percent, although investments were heavily concentrated in digital infrastructure and technology sectors. Total FDI inflows to developing countries reached around $900 billion, of which Africa attracted only about $70 billion. He called for international mechanisms to convert part of developing countries’ debt into investments that support growth and development.

Farid said the report showed that many countries have expanded reforms to improve their investment climates by simplifying procedures, adopting technology, and identifying priority sectors for investment, thereby strengthening their competitiveness amid global economic changes.

He added that the government has approved the establishment of a unified digital platform for setting up business entities, covering 468 economic activities and licensing procedures issued by 82 government bodies. The platform will enable investors to complete incorporation procedures and obtain licenses electronically in record time as part of the state’s efforts to reduce bureaucracy and improve the investment climate.

The minister also said the Ministry of Investment, in cooperation with the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, has identified 12 priority sectors for investment promotion, including manufacturing, renewable energy, information and communications technology, tourism, healthcare, agriculture, transport and logistics, financial services, textiles and the automotive industry. The initiative aims to attract more investment, deepen local manufacturing and enhance the competitiveness of the Egyptian economy.

Meanwhile, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty said the UNCTAD report reflects the profound shifts in the global investment landscape driven by geopolitical tensions and new industrial policies.

He stressed that despite international and regional crises, Egypt has succeeded in maintaining economic stability and strengthening investor confidence through its economic reform program and coordination with international financial institutions, enabling the country to retain its position as Africa’s top destination for foreign direct investment.

World.title: Egypt reaffirms support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed on Monday, July 27, 2026, Egypt’s unwavering support for Sudan’s unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national institutions during a phone call on Monday with Sudanese Foreign Minister Mohi al-Din Salem.

Abdelatty also stressed the importance of neighboring countries respecting Sudan’s sovereignty and security.

The two ministers underscored their shared commitment to further strengthening bilateral relations and expanding cooperation across various fields, in line with the strategic nature of ties between the two countries and in a way that serves their mutual interests and enhances the close coordination between them.

The Egyptian Foreign Minister emphasized the importance of upholding the principle of Sudanese ownership of the political process and supporting efforts to restore stability and end the conflict, paving the way for a comprehensive political settlement that preserves Sudan’s sovereignty and fulfills the aspirations of its people for security, stability, and development.

Abdelatty also affirmed Egypt’s readiness, along with Egyptian companies, to contribute to Sudan’s reconstruction once the war ends and security and peace are restored, citing the strategic partnership between the two countries and the extensive expertise of Egyptian firms in construction and post-conflict reconstruction.

For his part, Salem expressed Sudan’s appreciation for Egypt’s support at all levels and praised Cairo’s consistent position backing Sudan’s unity and stability.

He also reviewed the Sudanese government’s efforts to address the current challenges, stressing the importance of maintaining close consultation with Egypt during the coming period in a manner that serves the interests of both countries and peoples.

He added that Sudan looks forward to broad Egyptian participation in its future reconstruction programs.

World.title: Petroleum Minister, China’s CNCEC review strategic industrial projects in Egypt
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi discussed on Monday, July 27, 2026, with Deng Zhaojing, General Manager of China National Chemical Engineering Group (CNCEC), and his accompanying delegation ways to accelerate the implementation of several strategic projects being carried out by the Chinese group as the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractor.

The projects include the New Alamein soda ash plant and the Red Sea National Petrochemicals complex in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, as part of Egypt’s efforts to localize value-added industries and strengthen investment cooperation with China.

Badawi said Egyptian-Chinese relations are witnessing rapid growth across various fields, noting that the petroleum and mining sector is one of the main pillars of bilateral cooperation through strategic projects backed by the political leadership.

He said these projects contribute to deepening local manufacturing, reducing import dependence and creating new export opportunities.

The minister stressed the importance of expediting work on the soda ash project, describing it as strategically significant for localizing the production of a commodity that is currently imported. He also underscored the need to increase the project’s local content to maximize added value and support domestic industry.

He added that the Red Sea National Petrochemicals complex is among the largest strategic projects under preparation and will produce high-value petroleum and petrochemical products, capitalizing on Egypt’s strategic location and advanced infrastructure to strengthen its position as a regional hub for petroleum and petrochemical trade.

For his part, the CNCEC General Manager said that the close ties between Egypt and China provide a solid foundation for expanding joint projects. He noted that the group is implementing and investing in several key projects in Egypt, including the soda ash plant, the Red Sea petrochemicals complex, metallic silicon and bioethanol projects.

He added that CNCEC, which has operated in Egypt for nearly 20 years, regards the country as one of its key strategic markets. He reaffirmed the group’s commitment to the timetable for the soda ash project while working to accelerate implementation and increase reliance on local content in line with the Ministry of Petroleum’s vision.

Deng also invited Badawi to visit the group’s headquarters in Beijing to discuss future cooperation opportunities and explore new investment projects.

World.title: The Iran and Ukraine wars are colliding on the world’s biggest lake. Here’s what to know
World.content:
The Caspian Sea has become the latest region to be sucked into the growing conflict between Iran and its adversaries – not least because it’s a vital artery in the growing relationship between Iran and Russia.

Ukraine at the weekend said its drones had struck two Russian vessels carrying military cargoes in the Caspian, the world’s largest inland body of water. It asserted that both had left Iran for a Russian port.

In a post on X Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the targets included “ships that were involved in transporting military cargo from Iran, as well as a warship,” subsequently identified by Ukraine’s security service as a Russian missile boat.

Iran countered that one of its commercial vessels carrying a cargo of iron had been struck, killing one seafarer and injuring three others.

The ship, which it did not name, was sailing from the Russian port of Astrakhan to Anzali in Iran, which Iranian regional governor Hadi Hagh-Shenas described as “a safe and reliable corridor for commercial exchanges between the two ports.”

Tensions escalated further Monday when Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said, “Ukraine’s dangerous adventurism will certainly not go unanswered by us.” Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Chargé d’Affaires in Tehran was summoned to the foreign ministry over the incident.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei speaks at a weekly press conference in Tehran, Iran, on June 23. Xinhua/Shutterstock

Where is the Caspian Sea?

The recriminations reflect the growing importance of the Caspian, which is bordered by five countries, including Iran and Russia. With the blockade of Iranian ports in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, the Caspian has taken on new significance as a trade route.

The Caspian can help Iran towards “a diversified trade strategy, especially if Iran promotes trade with Russia, the Caucasus, Central Asia, China via rail, and, indirectly, Eastern Europe,” according to Bijan Khajehpour, managing partner of Vienna-based Eurasian Nexus Partners, a consulting firm.

It is “a strategic complement rather than a substitute for Iran’s existing maritime access through the southern waters,” Khajehpour told CNN.

Russian grain and steel are among the cargoes that cross the Caspian. Iran has developed several significant ports on the sea, among them Anzali. Oil and gas from Kazakhstan are transported from the Caspian to a hub on the Black Sea.

For Russia, the Caspian is an important conduit to central Asia and Iran – and a critical route in its expanding strategic partnership with Tehran, one that has a military component as well as Russia’s role in Iran’s civilian nuclear program and oil exploration in Iran.

“The recent blockade by the US (of Iranian ports) has underlined the strategic value of the Caspian Sea route” says Khajehpour. It is also less vulnerable to international sanctions because it is landlocked and largely controlled by Iran, Russia and neighboring states beyond Western naval reach.

Why is the sea so valuable to both Iran and Russia?

Russian Foreign Minister SergeI Lavrov, right, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, pose for a photo in Cholpon-Ata, Kyrgyzstan, on Friday. Russian Foreign Ministry Press Service/AP

The Caspian has become a passageway for the growing military links between Moscow and Tehran. Iran and Russia have a broad strategic agreement covering economic and military collaboration, although it is not a mutual defense pact.

Russia received its first batches of Iranian Shahed attack drones via the Caspian early in its war with Ukraine and has since produced new versions of the drones in plants on Russian soil.

The Caspian route linking Iran’s northern ports to the Russian port of Astrakhan has been targeted by Ukraine before. Last August a cargo ship – the Port Olya 4 – was destroyed while reportedly loaded with Shahed-136 drone components and Iranian munitions.

In 2024, CNN reported that a Russian cargo ship suspected of carrying Iranian ballistic missiles for Moscow’s war against Ukraine was seen at a Russian port on the Caspian Sea. The US Treasury department assessed that the Russian Ministry of Defense had “used the vessel Port Olya-3 to transport CRBMs (close-range ballistic missiles) from Iran to Russia.”

Then-US Secretary of State Antony Blinken said Washington believed the Russian military had received shipments of Iranian Fatah-360 ballistic missiles and would “likely use them within weeks in Ukraine against Ukrainians.”

At the same time, the US National Security Council warned of the deepening military cooperation between Iran and Russia. Spokesperson Sean Savett told CNN back then that “any transfer of Iranian ballistic missiles to Russia would represent a dramatic escalation in Iran’s support” for the Kremlin in its invasion of Ukraine.

Iran denied it was providing military assistance to Russia at that time.

What is Ukraine hoping to achieve from its strikes?

Ukraine’s drone attacks on vessels and energy infrastructure in the Caspian at the weekend are a demonstration of its growing long-range capabilities and its goal of damaging the industries that support Russia’s war effort.

It’s also a recognition that Iran – like North Korea – plays a significant role in supplying Russia with weapons.

And above all, it’s astute timing from the Ukrainians, with Zelensky traveling to Washington this week to meet with President Donald Trump. Besides the Caspian strikes, Zelensky has said that according to Ukrainian intelligence Russia has provided satellite data to Iran to carry out attacks on US facilities in the Middle East.

The message: we are on the same side.

World.title: Why this time around, Netanyahu’s meeting with Trump might not go to script
World.content:
For years, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s trips to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington followed a choreographed script: a red carpet, a warm handshake, and shared messages about the closeness of the Israel-US alliance.

But the relationship has markedly shifted since the two last met five months ago. The close cooperation and effusive praise from the start of the Iran war have given way to Trump’s expletive-laden outbursts directed at his most vocal international advocate.

This is Netanyahu’s seventh visit to the US since Trump returned to power — more than any other world leader. This time, though, he arrives in Washington as a leader facing reelection, trying to steady a relationship that has grown visibly strained.

Netanyahu has been working to secure an invitation to the White House for several weeks, according to a US official and an Israeli source, to discuss progress in the Iran war and warn Trump against diplomatic concessions.

Trump had been resistant to meeting, and some White House officials have been frustrated at what they regarded as Israeli attempts to secure a meeting through media leaks — to “will a meeting into existence,” the US official said. This week’s funeral of US Sen. Lindsey Graham provided an opportunity for a sit-down, even though it will be secondary to the larger event.

A senior US administration official said Trump has a “strong relationship” with Netanyahu and that Israel has “no greater friend” than the American president. “Americans and our allies around the world are already safer for the United States and Israel’s bold actions to deny the Iranian regime the ability to develop a nuclear weapon,” the official told CNN.

When the two leaders last met, in February, they laid the groundwork for what became a joint military campaign against Iran. The opening strikes of the war became a showcase of unprecedented military coordination, which Netanyahu and Trump both eagerly promoted and praised. But as the war dragged on, failing to achieve the overly optimistic goal of toppling the Iranian regime, the gap between them became clear: Netanyahu wanted to keep pressing – Trump wanted an exit.

In the lead-up to the war, Trump had been convinced by the prime minister and others that the conflict would be contained and last a matter of weeks. Several months later, his anger at the current situation — an uneasy and deadly stalemate — has led to expletive-filled private meetings and fury at the regime in Tehran for not folding in the way he once expected, according to a US official.

Netanyahu plans to present Trump with fresh intelligence on the state of Iran’s nuclear and military rebuilding, an Israeli source said, though he said Israel assesses “Trump has little interest in resuming a full fight, at least before America’s elections in November.”

The Israeli leader has avoided confronting Trump publicly over the sudden April ceasefire but his political allies slammed the agreement with Iran, and pro-Netanyahu media outlets openly targeted the deal’s architects: Vice President JD Vance, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Vance in turn accused members of Netanyahu’s cabinet of working to sabotage the Iran negotiations and sway American public opinion against the agreement, warning that Israel is alienating “the only powerful ally they have left.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with US President Donald Trump at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago club on December 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Florida. Joe Raedle/Getty Images

Trump is acutely aware of the political pressures Netanyahu faces ahead of Israel’s national election in October, according to officials, and knows his support for the prime minister could be critical. Aware of that leverage, Trump has selectively shown support, including last week when he said Netanyahu would not be arrested if he came to the United States after New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s initial refusal to roll back a campaign pledge to do so.

Trump has not blamed Netanyahu for the predicament, at least in public. But he has called him “crazy” and “difficult” for continuing a bombing campaign inside Lebanon that threatened a ceasefire. And he has excoriated him over the telephone for diverging from Trump’s war aims.

That divergence of aims extends beyond Iran.

As Trump pushed Netanyahu to stop fighting against Hezbollah, Lebanon became another point of friction. In one phone call in early-June reported by Axios, he told Netanyahu, “Everybody hates you now … everybody hates Israel because of this.”

Israel eventually agreed to a trilateral agreement with Lebanon one month ago but refuses to withdraw completely from southern Lebanon without Hezbollah’s disarmament first. Netanyahu told his security cabinet Sunday that the Trump administration wants to pull Israeli forces back from positions in Lebanon, as well as in Gaza and Syria, according to an Israeli source briefed on the meeting.

Netanyahu, the source told CNN, clarified that he intends to oppose the idea.

In addition to longstanding regional conflicts, two more issues emerged in recent weeks: Trump’s potential plans to sell advanced stealth F-35 fighter jets to Turkey and the US-Saudi civil nuclear agreement. Israeli officials worry the former could erode the country’s qualitative military edge while the latter could trigger a regional nuclear arms race. Trump has tied the Saudi deal publicly to normalization with Israel and expansion of the Abraham Accords, though Riyadh hasn’t confirmed or accepted any such link.

Asked on Monday about the possible fighter jet sales to Turkey and Netanyahu’s opposition to such a deal, Trump replied that “nobody” dictates the sales but him, calling Turkey a “tremendous ally.”

Ahead of his departure Monday, Netanyahu said he plans to discuss “all the issues on the agenda, first and foremost, Iran. Naturally, our goal is to safeguard our security and also to expand the circle of peace around us.”

The Israeli source said that Netanyahu will seek assurances that any arms sales to Turkey or nuclear cooperation with Saudi Arabia won’t compromise Israel’s military edge, along with progress on a new long-term US-Israel defense pact to replace the Obama-era memorandum that is set to expire.

“Netanyahu wants to move forward from the war to other things — such as a security agreement, perhaps normalization with Saudi Arabia — and to ensure that he is coordinated with Trump regarding things that he can use in the elections,” the source said. He believes that direct engagement with Trump can bypass disagreements within the administration, the source told CNN.

Netanyahu has dismissed the frictions as “tactical” disagreements, insisting the relationship is as close as ever. But an Israeli official said it took time to schedule the meeting with Trump, and that initially “he was blocked,” though it was unclear by whom. The meeting was only confirmed after Netanyahu announced he would attend Graham’s funeral.

The stakes for Netanyahu are as high as ever. According to most recent polls, he falls far short of the majority needed to secure another term in October’s election. Trump has long been one of his most valuable campaign assets, and demonstrating continued influence in Washington matters for Netanyahu, who still hopes to host him in Israel for a pre-election visit.

Notably, the meeting is not currently scheduled to include a public photo opportunity. Their meeting in February, however, was also kept off camera due to sensitive military planning before the war. The discretion this time could conceal the next campaign against Iran … or the tensions around the next ceasefire.

World.title: A weeks-old Gen-Z protest group managed to get India’s Modi to blink. What’s next?
World.content:
For more than a decade, India’s leader Narendra Modi has seemed politically unassailable, presiding over a government that has outmaneuvered opponents, dominated public discourse and squeezed the space for dissent in the world’s biggest democracy.

But last weekend, an online-fueled and youth-led protest movement just a few weeks old landed a blow none of the embattled mainstream political parties who oppose him have been able to: They forced his government to back down.

For days, tens of thousands of Gen Z protesters had flooded the streets of New Delhi, led by a satirical movement called the “Cockroach Janta Party”, to demand accountability for a university entrance exam leak they say robbed millions of students of a fair shot at their future. In their crosshairs was education minister and trusted Modi lieutenant Dharmendra Pradhan, on whose watch the leak had happened.

Pradhan’s resignation on Saturday was met with jubilation – and not a little surprise – at the Jantar Mandar, the eighteenth-century observatory in the capital that had become the colorful, buoyant base camp for the protest movement. Crowds took to the streets, dancing, singing and waving the national flag late into the night, celebrating what they saw as a victory for accountability and collective action.

It was a rare retreat for Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which has seen off multiple civil society protest movements since it rose to power in 2014, and a blow to the personal aura of Modi who has projected himself as India’s strongman leader.

Their success appears to have emboldened others to believe some form of change is possible.

“A week ago you couldn’t really give any feedback to the government,” said software engineer Akshit Tyagi, 22, from the protest site in the capital.

“Now everyone has come out… and there is a validation which is spreading, and people are realizing that they can actually demand things from the government.”

Three of India’s neighbors – Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bangladesh – have all witnessed tumultuous, youth-led political change in recent years.

Now, some in India are wondering whether the success of the so-called ‘Cockroaches’ could herald the beginning of something similar in a nation where widespread youth discontent simmers below the surface.

‘Didn’t anticipate this’

Supporters of India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) celebrate following the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, after days of protests demanding he step down over the alleged NEET examination paper leak scandal in New Delhi, India, on July 25, 2026. Elke Scholiers/Getty Images

Many of the young protesters at Jantar Mantar came of age during Modi’s hold on power, one defined by sweeping promises of national greatness, economic prosperity, and a renewed sense of nationalism. Those pledges defined their formative years, shaping expectations about their country’s trajectory and their place within it.

India remains one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies and during Modi’s three terms in office has invested heavily in infrastructure, technology and manufacturing. Yet many young Indians say that national success has not translated into opportunities for them.

The country boasts one of the world’s youngest populations, with over 360 million people between the ages of 15 and 29. However, a recent report revealed that nearly 40% of graduates aged 25 and under are unemployed.

When in May the government admitted that the exam papers for medical and dental courses had been leaked and that millions would have to re-sit nationwide, long held discontent exploded into widespread anger.

This was capitalized on by the CJP which originated as a satirical online movement created by Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate. It quickly became a vehicle for generational anxiety, and a platform to articulate grievances about employment, governance, and the lack of upward mobility.

“This indeed is a shock and setback for the BJP,” political scientist Rahul Verma, a fellow at New Delhi-based think-tank Centre for Policy Research said of the protests and Pradhan’s resignation. “They didn’t anticipate perhaps the kind of frustration or anxiety that is getting inbuilt in society.”

Over its twelve years in power, the BJP has weathered numerous protest movements – from public outrage over the sudden demonetization scheme that invalidated more than 80% of banknotes in the country, to widespread opposition against a contentious citizenship law, and months-long demonstrations by farmers protesting agricultural reforms.

Verma noted that these centered around policy or ideological disagreements, which allowed the government to rally its supporters with counter-narratives.

In contrast, he described the CJP’s protest as the “first movement driven by administrative failure,” and therefore much more difficult to contain.

Social media as a tool

A member of the Rapid Action Force (RAF) fires a tear gas canister towards protesters as supporters of India’s Cockroach Janta Party demonstrate on the opening day of the Indian parliament’s monsoon session, demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam paper leaks, in New Delhi, India, on July 20, 2026. Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

Officials were, at first, quick to dismiss them. In a televised interview last month, Pradhan even labeled the CJP the “B-team of terror groups.”

India’s mainstream television news channels devoted little attention to the movement, prompting students to document them on their own.

Protesters covered events in real time, filming Instagram reels, sharing videos and memes – often laced with dark humor and jibes at Modi – and posting updates from the protest site. Social media became a running chronicle of the movement, helping transform an exam grievance into a national conversation.

The flood of content drew more young people into the demonstrations and underscored the diminishing influence of traditional media in India among Gen Z. By the time those outlets finally began covering the protests extensively, the movement had already captured the public imagination.

Momentum soared further on July 20, when police used tear gas and sticks to break up a march to parliament by tens of thousands demanding Pradhan’s removal. Undeterred, the demonstrators maintained their stance, escalating their showdown with Modi’s government, and for the first time, some called for the removal of Modi himself.

Although Modi secured a third consecutive term in 2024, he did so with a reduced parliamentary majority, making discontent among any key voter blocs much harder to ignore.

The protesters were largely middle- and lower-middle-class youth and their parents, a demographic that has traditionally formed an important pillar of BJP support, according to Verma.

“Young and middle-class voters are significantly more likely to support the BJP, which made the protests especially problematic for the government,” he said.

Modi, known for cultivating an image of stoicism and control, appeared to shift tactics late last week, releasing two video messages on social media, selfie style, that addressed students directly – a noticeable attempt to engage on a platform where the movement itself thrived.

“Thank you friends,” he said in the second video, having changed to a new camera angle slightly further away from his face following widespread mockery of the first close-up version. “I appreciate the way you responded to my video and your positive suggestions.”

What’s next?

Protest site at Jantar Mantar deserted look after CJP withdrew its ongoing dissent movement in New Delhi, India, on July 26, 2026. Vipin Kumar/Hindustan Times/Getty Images

On Saturday, protest leaders said they would suspend demonstrations after the government assured them their other demands – including compensation for the families of students who had taken their own lives over the exam leak scandal – would be addressed. The main protest site in New Delhi has since been cleared.

The Cockroach Janta Party has achieved what few thought possible. But its longer-term legacy may depend on whether India’s Gen Z can transform that victory into a broader movement capable of sustaining pressure on issues that affect their future.

Modi remains broadly popular and his BJP a formidable vote-winning machine that just months ago notched up a big victory in state elections – including in key regions it previously had struggled to win.

The next general election is not until 2029.

“What this was… became a fight for the youth,” said protester Devansh Gupta, who works in advertising.

“All problems that the youth have are being put in front of the government, in I don’t know in how many years. I think this is one of the greatest things to happen to India in a very long time.”

In his final remarks before leaving the protest camp at the Jantar Mantar observatory, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke hinted that his party was not going away.

“This is not the end,” he said. “We will meet again soon.”

World.title: More than 63,000 people in central Spain have evacuated from path of fires
World.content:
Wildfires have forced at least 63,152 people to evacuate their homes in the central Spanish regions of Madrid, Toledo and Avila, Spain’s Interior Ministry said Monday.

The ministry has also temporarily suspended harvesting work with agricultural machinery in those three regions.

The fire in the province of Avila has burned more than 50,000 hectares (190 square miles), making it the largest fire in Spain’s history, the Minister for the Ecological Transition Sara Aagesen said.

In that province alone, more than 25,000 people have been evacuated and over 8,700 are confined to their homes.

World.title: 189 Elective Positions Won Unopposed
World.content:
With just over two weeks until Zambians cast their ballots on 13 August, this year’s general election has already produced a striking statistic: 189 elective positions have been settled without a single vote being cast, according to the Electoral Commission of Zambia.

The commission says the wave of uncontested seats stems chiefly from gaps in party organisation and candidate mobilisation, rather than any deliberate design. In each case, only one candidate successfully completed the nomination process for the post in question, which under Zambian electoral law means that candidate is automatically declared duly elected. No ballot paper is printed, and no contest takes place.

The scale of the phenomenon is notable. ECZ has confirmed that eight parliamentary constituencies, six mayoral and council chairperson positions, and 176 ward councillor seats fall into this category. ECZ commissioner McDonald Chipenzi said the commission would therefore skip printing ballots for those races altogether, trimming both printing volumes and overall election costs. Yet what looks like a simple administrative efficiency has opened up a much bigger conversation about the state of party readiness across the political spectrum.

The ruling United Party for National Development has been the chief beneficiary. Candidates including Jack Mwiimbu in Monze, Trevor Mwiinde in Choma South, Edgar Siakachoma in Kalomo South, Vumango Musumali in Zambezi West, Clement Andeleki in Kazungula North and Siakole Nchimunya in Sinazongwe will all walk into the National Assembly without having faced a rival candidate. None of their would-be challengers managed to file valid nomination papers before the deadline closed. A similar pattern played out at ward level, where several council seats were also decided without contest.

Political analyst Ngande Mwanajiti has urged caution against reading this simply as an overwhelming show of public confidence in the ruling party. In his assessment, the pattern says at least as much about internal party discipline as it does about voter sentiment. He argues that fielding a full slate of properly vetted, fully documented candidates requires groundwork that begins long before nomination day, not last-minute scrambling once the window opens.

“It should not take the ECZ to tell anybody that you have a problem with your political party,” Mwanajiti said, insisting that parties bear responsibility for sorting out candidate selection, compliance and internal structures well ahead of the electoral calendar.

There is also a tactical dimension to consider. Mwanajiti pointed out that once a seat is decided unopposed, the winning party effectively banks that constituency immediately, freeing up time, money and organisational energy to pour into other, more competitive races. Multiplied across 189 positions, that advantage becomes significant, and at a national level, he said, it currently sits squarely with UPND.

Much of the imbalance traces back to a turbulent nomination season for the opposition. The People’s Pact Initiative withdrew its backing of presidential candidate Fred M’membe amid an internal leadership crisis and a vote of no confidence. Citizens First’s Harry Kalaba lost both his running mate, Moses Mawere, and his Roan parliamentary candidate, Chishimba Kambwili, to Tonse Alliance. Independent candidate Given Katuta and Organised People’s Party’s Brian Mushimba were each abandoned by their own running mates. Patriots for Economic Progress leader Sean Tembo alleges his party’s registration records were tampered with entirely, forcing it out of contention.

Notably, such disruptions no longer threaten to derail the election calendar itself. The Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025 now allows elections to proceed on schedule even where a candidate resigns or is disqualified after nominations close, reserving fresh nominations strictly for cases where a candidate dies before polling day. Mwanajiti called this a welcome source of certainty, but stressed it shifts the burden squarely back onto parties to manage their own internal affairs responsibly.

“Preparations for one election begin almost immediately after the previous election ends,” he said.

The 189 unopposed positions stand as an early marker of how uneven party readiness could shape outcomes well before a single vote is tallied.

World.title: ConCourt asked to bar Kalaba, Mushimba from presidential race
World.content:
The Constitutional Court has been asked to disqualify Citizens First presidential candidate Harry Kalaba and Organised People’s Party presidential candidate Brian Mushimba from the 13 August general election, after both men lost their running mates within days of each other in July.

Youth Alliance Party president Mark Mwachilenga filed the petition on 21 July, arguing that the two candidates can no longer lawfully participate in the presidential race because their running mates withdrew after nominations had closed. The Electoral Commission of Zambia is cited as the first respondent, with Kalaba and Mushimba named as the second and third respondents in their personal and party-presidential capacities.

According to the petition, ECZ published a list of validly nominated presidential candidates and their running mates on 29 June. Kalaba’s running mate was Moses Mawere, while Mushimba’s was Andyford Banda. Mwachilenga states that Banda issued a press statement on 3 July announcing his withdrawal as Mushimba’s running mate, and Mawere followed on 10 July, announcing his own withdrawal as Kalaba’s running mate.

The petitioner argues that these withdrawals left both presidential candidates without running mates and, consequently, without prospective candidates for the office of Vice-President. He contends that despite the withdrawals, ECZ has continued to recognise Kalaba and Mushimba as validly nominated presidential candidates, a decision he describes as unconstitutional and illegal.

Mwachilenga argues that allowing the two candidates to remain on the ballot violates several provisions of the Constitution, including Articles 90, 100(1), 110(3), 110(4) and (5), and Article 266. He submits that the Constitution requires the offices of President and Vice-President to be contested together, with the vice-president serving as a running mate, and that both offices must be elected, sworn in and assume office simultaneously.

“The withdrawal of the running mates to the second and third respondents invariably means that the said presidential candidates are participating in a presidential election without a running mate, and potentially without a candidate for the position of Vice-President-elect,” the petition states.

Mwachilenga is seeking a declaration that Kalaba and Mushimba are disqualified from participating in the 13 August presidential election because they no longer have running mates as required by the Constitution. He is also asking the court to order ECZ to proceed with the election using only qualified candidates, and to declare that the continued participation of the two respondents without running mates is unconstitutional and illegal.

As an alternative remedy, Mwachilenga is asking the court to allow Kalaba and Mushimba to select and appoint new running mates before polling day, rather than face outright disqualification. He states in his filing that he is a Zambian citizen, a registered voter, and president of the Youth Alliance Party, which is currently in the process of registration under Zambian law.

The petition lands against the backdrop of a recently amended constitutional framework. Under the country’s previous rules, the withdrawal of a presidential running mate after nominations had the potential to create legal uncertainty and disrupt the election calendar, with resignations of running mates capable of triggering a postponement of elections.

The Constitution of Zambia (Amendment) Act No. 13 of 2025 revised the procedures for handling changes involving candidates after nominations close. The amendments provide clearer guidelines allowing elections to proceed as scheduled where a candidate resigns or is disqualified after nominations, while reserving fresh nominations only for cases where a party-sponsored candidate dies before election day. It remains unclear how this amended framework will bear on the ConCourt’s determination of the petition, since the matter concerns the status of running mates rather than the presidential candidates themselves.

Neither Kalaba nor Mushimba had issued a public response to the petition at the time of publication. ECZ has also not issued a statement addressing the specific claims raised in the filing.

The case adds to a broader pattern of running mate turbulence that has emerged during this year’s nomination period. Independent presidential candidate Given Katuta was similarly left without a running mate after John Nyirenda withdrew, while the People’s Pact Initiative separately withdrew its endorsement of Socialist Party leader Fred M’membe following an internal leadership dispute.

With the Constitutional Court yet to set a hearing date, the outcome of the petition could materially affect the shape of the presidential ballot paper with just over two weeks remaining before Zambians go to the polls.
