World.title: Polanski’s Greens brace for the ‘Burnham bounce’
World.content:
An opinion poll by More in Common published Monday put Labour on top for the first time since March 2025, with its surge coming at the expense of the Greens, who recorded their lowest share of the vote since October last year when Polanski became leader. A separate YouGov poll also released Monday showed no change from last week, though it noted the party is down eight points from a February peak.

Polanski insists he is the “opposite of worried about Andy Burnham,” predicting Labour MPs’ “last roll of the dice” in switching leader won’t improve things.

But a senior Green Party local politician, granted anonymity to speak frankly, acknowledged: “It’s going to be difficult, there is going to be a Burnham bounce,” warning the party needs to “sharpen those key lines that give us differentiation.”

The party is already attacking Burnham for employing corporate lobbyists like his chief of staff James Purnell, and claiming the new prime minister’s rhetoric on Gaza, public ownership and homelessness is hollow, and does not represent a change from Starmer.

It is also on a drive to find more polished spokespeople to hit the airwaves.

Drawing the battle lines

One area where the Greens see a dividing line with Burnham is over Gaza.

World.title: Spain’s biggest blaze risks scorching conservatives ahead of key election year
World.content:
At a national level, the PP is still topping the polls and is on track to take power in 2027, profiting from the web of corruption scandals ensnaring Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's ruling Socialist Party.

But the fires threaten to expose vulnerabilities. The conservatives are not only being criticized for failing to invest in firefighters, but also risk looking out of step with the severity of the challenge posed by climate change, in part thanks to regional alliances with the far-right Vox party that are steering the PP toward increasingly anti-ecological positions.

Madrid Regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso, a conservative heavyweight, has felt the sting of public anger over her political priorities. On Sunday, she said she'd come under fire from constituents accusing her of prioritizing investment in fighting bulls — a vote winner with a right-wing base — rather than firefighters.

From left: Madrid Regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso, Villamanta Mayor Mariano Núñez Muñoz, King Felipe VI, Queen Letizia and Lt. Gen. Francisco Javier Marcos. They are pictured visiting wildfire evacuees on July 26, 2026. | Javier Soriano/AFP via Getty Images

"In two or three municipalities, they were talking about bullfighters," a palpably irritated Ayuso complained. “What do bullfighters have to do with all this?”

The populist Madrid president accused her political opponents of stirring up grievances to “divide” her constituents, adding that the bullfighting sector had been especially impacted by the wildfires. “We must remember that they are the first ones who have lost livestock and land,” she added.

But political opponents like Manuela Bergerot, spokesperson for the left-wing Más Madrid party, argued that once the fires are extinguished, it would be time to probe "the precarious situation of firefighters, cuts in prevention and climate change denial."

World.title: Political chaos turns spotlight on Romania’s MAGA champion
World.content:
The views of Simion, a former football hooligan who relishes a fight with the establishment, matter: His party, the Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR), has a huge lead in opinion polls and may soon get a chance to put its case to voters if a snap election is called.

He savaged the EU’s green deal, economic and defense policies, and said Romania did not want to return to a time when larger states dominated it. “We have been occupied by these kind of dictators like we have in Russia and we had in U.S.S.R., and dictatorial tendencies from Germany,” he said. “We want to be part of Europe formed of free, sovereign nations.”

Romania has been locked in crisis without a fully functioning government since May, when AUR joined forces with the social democrats to bring down the country’s liberal-led ruling coalition.

Heir to Orbán

On the EU’s eastern flank, bordering Ukraine, Romania plays a critical role in Europe’s security, providing logistical support for the war and housing a major NATO base and a U.S. missile defense shield site.

Simion, who has described himself as “Eurorealist, not Euroskeptic,” has long been a contender for power. If he ever wins, he would potentially be a more disruptive figure for European mainstream politics than Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán. Last year in his campaign for the presidency, he consciously copied U.S. President Donald Trump and has proposed halting aid to Ukraine, triggering alarm among centrist politicians in Brussels.

Simion said in the interview that the constitutional solution to Romanian parties’ failure to agree a new coalition was to hold a snap general election, something that has never happened in the country of 19 million people since the fall of communism in 1989.

World.title: Heat, drought, fire: Europe needs to restore wetlands, rivers and landscapes
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

Europe is experiencing climate whiplash. As a record-breaking heatwave has recently swept across the continent, wildfires are spreading, health systems are under growing pressure and critical infrastructure is proving increasingly vulnerable.

 

Heat, drought, fire and floods are no longer isolated events. They are increasingly arriving in rapid succession, exposing landscapes and infrastructure that are no longer fit for the climate we now live in.

Europe needs Landscapes that absorbe, store and release water slowly

Climate change is warming Europe. But decades of draining wetlands, straightening rivers, sealing soils and degrading natural landscapes have left Europe far more vulnerable to its impacts. Landscapes that once absorbed, stored and slowly released water are increasingly unable to buffer climate extremes amplifying extreme heat, prolonging droughts and making floods more destructive.

As these extremes intensify, the European Commission is drafting its new European Framework for Climate Resilience – including new binding legislation intended to shape how Europe prepares for escalating climate shocks in the decades ahead. This is a critical opportunity to shift climate adaptation from responding to disasters towards large-scale action reducing climate risks at their source.

The danger is that the emerging framework risks becoming another exercise in adaptation bureaucracy: more plans and more assessments – without defining what meaningful climate resilience should actually require or achieve.

Prevention with nature-based solutions

Europeans already understand this. In response to the European Commission's recent public consultation, one message stood out clearly: invest more in prevention, with nature-based solutions becoming the first line of defence against escalating climate risks.

Meanwhile, degraded landscapes continue to amplify the very risks adaptation policy is supposed to reduce. Europe’s landscapes are engineered for a climate that no longer exists: drained, sealed, straightened and degraded over decades.

Wetlands, floodplains, peatlands, healthy soils and forests – the systems that naturally store water, recharge aquifers, reduce heat and buffer extremes – have been systematically removed from the landscape. The result is a continent where water moves too fast when it rains, disappears too quickly when it does not, and leaves societies exposed to increasingly volatile cycles of flood, drought, fire, and sea level rise.

Restoring the sponge function of landscapes

This is no longer an environmental issue alone. Stable water cycles are foundational to Europe’s economic resilience, public health and safety and long-term competitiveness – and natural water infrastructure is a critical part of that security system.

Restoring the sponge function of landscapes protects cities from floods, stabilises water supplies during drought, reduces wildfire risk, supports food production, cools urban areas and helps keep critical infrastructure functioning during climate extremes.

The evidence for a different approach is no longer the problem. Recent research from Germany’s KliMaWerk programme found that large-scale water retention and landscape restoration measures are significantly more effective and resilient over time than isolated technical solutions alone – and that the real barrier to overcome is governance.

The real test for the Commission's upcoming legislation will be whether it merely recognises systemic climate risks or gives member states the tools and incentives to reduce them at their source.

Flexibility to define targets and measures

One option would be to require member states to assess where natural water retention measures could reduce flood, drought and wildfire risks as a mandatory component of adaptation planning (drawing inspiration from Scotland’s Flood Act). Another would be to require national or regional “sponge targets”, inspired by the Flemish Blue Deal, to increase landscape water retention capacity and reduce hydrological volatility, building on existing instruments.

This would not impose one-size-fits-all measures from Brussels. Member states would retain flexibility to define targets and measures suited to their own hydrological realities. But they would no longer be able to ignore the role degraded landscapes play in amplifying climate risks.

Such an approach would also help shift Europe from endless disaster recovery towards prevention, as Europe cannot insure, compensate and rebuild its way out of accelerating hydrological instability.

Reducing climate risks at their source

This debate can no longer remain confined to environmental NGOs. Water companies, farmers, insurers, businesses and regional authorities all have a direct stake in restoring landscape resilience, because the economic costs of instability in Europe’s water cycle are now simply too large to ignore. Europe’s climate risks are systemic: our response to this escalating crisis must now become systemic too.

Europe has an opportunity to redefine climate adaptation. By placing the restoration of landscapes and healthy water systems at the heart of climate legislation, the new European Framework for Climate Resilience can help shift Europe from managing climate disasters to reducing climate risks at their source—strengthening economic resilience, public safety and long-term competitiveness.

World.title: Europe set to miss 2030 hepatitis elimination targets, health agency warns
World.content:
Despite progress over the last few years in preventing hepatitis B and C, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) warns the region is off track to meet the 2030 elimination targets.

 

“No one should die from a disease that is preventable, diagnosable and treatable, yet millions of Europeans are living with chronic hepatitis B or C infections – often without knowing it – which can lead to severe long-term consequences such as liver failure or liver cancer,” said Bruno Ciancio, Head of Unit for Directly Transmitted and Vaccine-Preventable Diseases at ECDC.

Hepatitis B and C are transmitted through infected blood or bodily fluids and are among the leading causes of chronic liver disease.

While acute hepatitis B infections have been falling steadily since 2006, driven by long-standing vaccination and prevention efforts, an estimated five million people in Europe are still living with chronic hepatitis B or C, and around 60,000 die every year from liver disease linked to these infections, according to the ECDC.

Among people younger than 25 years, the proportion of acute hepatitis B cases fell from 11% in 2015 to 8% in 2024, reflecting the impact of childhood vaccination programmes and other prevention measures.

Routine screening for hepatitis B in pregnancy is also well established across all 30 European Union and European Economic Area countries, helping to bring down transmission of the virus from mother to child to below 2%, the ECDC said.

Ciancio noted that effective control solutions are already in place. Those include vaccination to prevent hepatitis B, harm reduction and infection control initiatives to reduce transmission, testing to identify infections early, and treatments that can cure hepatitis C and control hepatitis B.

Gaps across Europe

However, experts have identified gaps in routine childhood vaccination. Only a minority of countries have reached the World Health Organization (WHO) target of fully vaccinating 95% of children against hepatitis B, with others even reporting a decline in coverage in recent years.

Harm reduction measures — such as opioid agonist treatment and the provision of sterile needles and syringes — are effective in limiting transmission of hepatitis C. Still, coverage remains inadequate, and only seven countries meet the WHO target for distributing sterile injection equipment to people who inject drugs.

“Our collective challenge is to ensure that these life-saving interventions are accessible to everyone who needs them,” Ciancio said.

Sexual transmission remains a major route of hepatitis B transmission. For hepatitis C, most cases are linked to injecting drug use and sex between men.

Yet, the ECDC noted that specific prevention efforts targeting sexual transmission of hepatitis across different populations have not been systematically monitored across countries.

World.title: The timing of war and peace is not yours to decide, Iran tells US
World.content:
Iran said it would not allow the US to determine when the two countries go to war or make peace, as four consecutive nights without new exchanges of fire raised hopes that Qatar and Pakistan-led mediation could revive the collapsed interim agreement.

 

"We will not allow the United States to determine the timing of war and peace," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said at his weekly press briefing on Monday.

He said any decision on future talks would be based solely on Iran's national interests and that Tehran would continue defending itself "for as long as necessary".

Speaking to Austria's ORF television on Sunday, Baghaei acknowledged that Tehran and Washington were still exchanging messages but said US military actions had destroyed the conditions for meaningful negotiations, with Iran's immediate priority being the protection of its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump told reporters that Iran had requested talks "through intermediaries and directly," claiming Tehran was willing to negotiate because of the military pressure it had faced.

"We are holding deep talks with Iran," he said. "If they fail, we will return to a wide-scale military operation."

He said he had responded positively to mediators' requests to give diplomacy another chance but would not allow talks to drag on indefinitely. "I have plenty of time," he said, while insisting Iran had "taken a beating" during the past two weeks.

Strait of Hormuz remains key pressure point

Despite renewed diplomatic efforts, the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz remains unresolved.

Baghaei said talks with Oman over the administration of the strategic waterway were continuing but stressed they were strictly bilateral and unrelated to the US.

"The Strait of Hormuz remains closed," he said.

Deputy parliament speaker Haji Babaii said any arrangement with Oman over the waterway must not clash with Iran’s sovereignty and that Washington should not be involved in the issue.

He insisted that Iran would not retreat from its position on the strait, saying decisions over Hormuz would ultimately be determined by Iran’s leadership and people.

The Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil and gas passed before Iran effectively closed it following the start of the war on 28 February, remains the central sticking point in any settlement.

Iran's position is that it holds sovereign authority over the waterway and may designate approved transit routes, a claim the US, Gulf states and most of the international community reject under UNCLOS, the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. Tehran has signed but never ratified the convention.

Small boats line the shore as cargo ships and other commercial vessels appear anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, Monday, July 27, 2026. (Razieh Poudat/IS AP Photo

Iran's IRGC said it intercepted six vessels attempting to transit through routes not approved by Iranian authorities, forcing them to turn back after warning shots.

Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters also accused the US of imposing what it described as an illegal naval blockade by threatening Iranian commercial vessels and oil tankers operating inside Iran's territorial waters.

For its part, US Central Command (CENTCOM) said it had redirected 17 commercial vessels, disabled two others and boarded two ships to enforce compliance with maritime restrictions.

Oil markets reacted positively to the absence of new military strikes, with Brent crude prices falling after reaching two-month highs last week.

Economic pressure continues to mount

The temporary military pause has not eased conditions inside Iran. Tehran remains confronted with electricity shortages, fuel imbalances, inflation and declining purchasing power.

In a recent exclusive report, Euronews Persian documented how rising prices are forcing many Iranians to cut back even on essential food purchases.

Leila, a 42-year-old translator living with her mother in western Tehran, said many families can no longer afford fruit despite Iran being one of the region's largest producers.

"The reality is that many families' incomes have not kept pace with inflation," she said. "After paying for rent, bread, rice, meat and dairy products, we are forced to reduce purchases of things like fruit, even though they are important."

Another interviewee, retired Tehran resident Mohammad Bagher, said his family's fruit consumption had fallen by roughly 70% compared with previous years despite receiving a relatively high pension.

Meanwhile, Iran-backed Houthi forces have intensified attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, with recent strikes targeting facilities around Jizan and Yanbu, while Saudi Arabia has launched retaliatory air strikes across Yemen.

Commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — which carries around 12% of global maritime trade — has slowed significantly as insurers reassess security risks.

The escalation comes despite a separate US-Houthi understanding reached in May 2025, under which the group had agreed to pause attacks on US-linked vessels. The arrangement has not prevented the Houthis from attacking Saudi and other Gulf targets.

Trump said the US was not currently involved in operations against the Houthis but warned Washington could intervene if the group became "a problem".

World.title: Last-minute holidays boom among British travellers as next-day bookings jump 26%
World.content:
As heatwaves, airfare prices and geopolitical tensions continue to bring a sense of uncertainty to summer travel plans, some Britons are embracing last-minute holiday bookings – often just a day or two before their trip.

 

According to new data from online travel agent loveholidays, British travellers are eyeing “spur-of-the-moment escapes” this summer, with bookings for next-day holidays increasing by 26% year-on-year.

Bookings made within two days of departure have also risen by 19%, the data revealed, while holidays booked within three days of travel are up 15% compared to last year.

Despite the short notice booking trend, the choice of holiday destinations remain “tried and tested”, said loveholidays.

Mallorca, Tenerife, Antalya, Costa Blanca and Ibiza are the five most popular choices for next-day departures, with each offering “reliable sunshine, short flight times and frequent flights from UK airports”.

Another priority is convenience, with all inclusive holidays accounting for 41% of bookings departing the following day, as Brits look for “hassle-free breaks that require little planning once they've arrived”.

"The traditional booking window is evolving, and the idea that you should have your summer holiday booked months in advance is becoming less of a rule than it once was,” said Al Murray, Chief Marketing and Supply Officer at loveholidays.

“More holidaymakers are swapping months of planning for spontaneous getaways, indicating a willingness to make quick decisions when the right combination of price, availability and time off comes together.

“Interestingly, that spontaneity of booking doesn’t translate into riskier choices. Holidaymakers are still gravitating towards familiar favourites, suggesting Brits are becoming more impulsive about when they book, but not necessarily where.”

World.title: What do the numbers tell us about Europe's heatwave?
World.content:
Western Europe experienced its hottest June on record this years as prolonged periods of extreme heat pushed temperatures to unprecedented levels across multiple countries.

 

The impacts extended beyond discomfort, putting pressure on healthcare systems and damaging crops.

These four figures help indicate the scale of the heatwave across the region.

20.74: The average temperature

Western Europe recorded its hottest June since records began, with an average temperature of 20.74 degrees, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change service.

This average temperature was 3.06 degrees above the June average between 1991 and 2020, surpassing a previous record set in June 2025.

Across Europe as a whole, June was the second-warmest on record, with England and France recording their warmest June ever. For Germany, the month was its second warmest on record and set a new all-time national maximum temperature.

The thermometer of a drugstore shows the temperature of 38 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) as temperatures reach record highs, in Rome, Wednesday, June 24, 2026. AP Photo

10,000: Excess heat deaths

More than 10,000 excess deaths were recorded in the late-June heatwave, according to data from EuroMOMO, the European Mortality Monitor.

More than 9,000 of these deaths were among those aged 65 and over, with France alone recording at least 5,764 excess deaths.

France's national public health agency said that the deaths amounted to 36% more than anticipated and the highest mortality rate recorded since the 2003 heatwave.

The high death toll has intensified scrutiny over France's preparedness for extreme heat after sweeping reforms in 2003, which critics have argued have not gone far enough to shield the population from the worst impacts of extreme heat.

In late June, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a government crisis meeting to assess how the country could prepare for future heatwaves.

€2 billion: Projected hit to grain harvest

An analysis by the independent non-profit The Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) estimated that the June heatwave could reduce the value of Europe's grain harvest by around €2 billion.

France and Hungary accounted for almost three-quarters of estimated losses, with the French grain harvest revised down by 4.1 million tonnes, worth around €891 million, after extreme heat hit wheat and maize crops during their early development.

Hungary also suffered, losing an estimated 2.4 million tonnes of grain valued at €444 million.

Tom Lancaster, analyst at the ECIU, said that the heatwave came at a "terrible time for European cereals farmers, hitting crop development and reducing yields across the continent."

"This will hit farmers in the pockets, reducing their income and undermining European food security at the same time," he said.

The ECIU says that the losses are likely to make Europe more dependent on imports and could push up global commodity prices, depending on harvests in the Southern Hemisphere later this year.

3: Number of heatwaves in as many months

Scientists have warned that the June heatwave was not an isolated event.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service documented major heatwaves across Western in May, June and early July, with record sea surface temperatures helping to fuel extreme conditions.

A new heatwave is expected to hit Europe this week, sparking fire warnings in parts of southwestern France and northern Spain according to the European Forest Fire Information System. The UK and Portugal are also expecting to see temperatures climb.

The latest spell of high temperatures has helped spark wildfires across France and Spain, particularly in the regions outside the Spanish capital of Madrid, where officials warn the fires are the worst the region has ever suffered.

According to their European State of the Climate 2025 report, Europe is the world's fastest-warming continent, with temperatures rising at around twice the global average.

It warned heatwaves are expected to become more frequent, more intense and occur later and earlier in the year as the climate continues to warm.

World.title: White House's Rick and Morty AI parody featuring Donald Trump sparks huge backlash
World.content:
An AI-generated video parodying the hit show Rick and Morty was posted on the White House’s official social media channel and has sparked backlash, with many pointing out its insensitivity to the current climate.

 

The now-viral clip is based on the opening sequence of the popular animated science-fiction sitcom created by Dan Harmon and Justin Roiland.

It sees Donald Trump and J.D. Vance piloting a flying saucer as they are chased by a winged demon, showing a space alien being arrested by border czar Tom Homan, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer removing his face to reveal he is a robot.

The parody video posted by the White House Screenshot The White House/X

The clip ends with a glowing "MAGA" title.

Screenshot of the viral clip Screenshot The White House/X

The short clip is consistent with many posts by the White House and Trump, who attempt to harness trending memes, shows and movies to drive their brand.

Trump has heavily relied on AI-generated visuals and pop culture pilfering antics to ridicule his political adversaries and marginalised groups – something Kurt Sengul, a researcher at Macquarie University in Australia, ferred to as “memetic warfare” when speaking to Euronews Culture.

However, the timing of this recent video's release has led critics, including former congresswoman and former Trump ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, to slam the video as "tone-deaf", "unserious" and "pathetic" - especially at time when the US is at war with Iran and prices continue to rise.

“People can’t afford gas, groceries, rent, and healthcare and this is the weird embarrassing crap the official White House account is putting out,” wrote Marjorie Taylor Greene.

One social media user wrote: “I know it’s all become background noise but the official White House account posting an AI Rick and Morty parody just really feels like new lows in having no shame, abjectly pathetic and pure uncut Reddit at the same time - not to buy into norms but there used to be some dignity.”

Many are calling for the creators of Rick and Morty to sue, while commentator Harry Sisson added: “WTF…We just want health care and not whatever the hell this is.”

The bizarre post from the White House coincides with Dan Harmon admitting that aspects of Trump and his predecessor Barack Obama have inspired his new Rick and Morty spin-off cartoon, titled President Curtis.

The series follows President Andre Curtis from Rick and Morty, showing how he and his staff respond to interdimensional and paranormal crises.

Harmon told The Hollywood Reporter: “Curtis has a naïveté that you could overlap with Trump, who is like, ‘I’m an outsider, and I consider this job simple, and I don’t care about the bureaucracy of it.’ On the Obama side, it’s the charmer and the guy who gets organic joy in being liked – that whole rock star aspect of Obama.”

Harmon's new show, President Curtis, premiered on Adult Swim on 26 July.

World.title: Japan: Strong earthquake shakes Kumamoto, injuries reported
World.content:
Dozens of people were hospitalized after the earthquake hit Southern Japan. According to media reports, multiple houses collapsed, with some people trapped inside the damaged buildings.

A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto Prefecture on Japan's southern island of Kyushu on Tuesday afternoon, triggering emergency warnings and prompting authorities to assess the extent of the damage.

At least 50 people were hospitalized after the earthquake, according to NHK. The broadcaster also reported that 12 houses collapsed, with four people trapped inside.

NHK said "Many people" were trapped inside a shopping mall damaged by the quake. Earlier, local police also reported what sounded like an explosion at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, though there was no immediate information on damage or casualties.

Authorities assess damage as tsunami threat eases

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also said initial reports indicated multiple injuries, damage to civilian infrastructure, and fires in several affected areas.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said.

"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed," she added.

Although the earthquake caused widespread disruption and temporarily raised fears of a tsunami, officials later confirmed that the threat had subsided and that Japan's coastline was no longer in danger.

"This earthquake occurred inland, and no tsunami activity has been observed so far," a spokesperson for the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said. "For this reason, we hope to lift the tsunami advisory at a relatively early stage, depending on future sea level conditions."

The earthquake struck at 4:27 p.m. local time and registered the highest possible level of seven on Japan's Shindo intensity scale, which measures ground shaking Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

Power and nuclear facilities remain safe

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority reported that no abnormalities were detected at three nearby nuclear power plants, providing reassurance in a country still sensitive to nuclear safety concerns following the 2011 Fukushima disaster.

However, the earthquake disrupted electricity supplies across the region. According to Kyushu Electric Power, approximately 45,000 households and facilities in Kumamoto temporarily lost power following the tremor.

Several major industrial facilities are located near the earthquake zone, including operations belonging to Sony and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker. Sony stated that it was evaluating conditions at its facilities, while TSMC did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Japan's long history of major earthquakes

Kumamoto is no stranger to devastating seismic events.

In 2016, the region was struck by two major earthquakes, first a magnitude 6.5 quake and then a magnitude 7.3 tremor two days later. The disaster claimed 273 lives, injured more than 2,800 people. Thousands of buildings were either damaged or destroyed, making it one of Japan's most destructive recent earthquake disasters.

More recently, a magnitude 7.2 earthquake struck northern Japan on June 25, causing little damage and no fatalities. Earlier this year, on April 20, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in northern Japan injured at least ten people and shook high-rise buildings as far away as Tokyo, prompting authorities to issue a temporary advisory warning of an increased risk of even stronger earthquakes. That advisory was lifted a week later.

One of the world's most earthquake-prone nations

Japan sits along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire," one of the most active seismic zones on Earth where four major tectonic plates meet.

Home to approximately 125 million people, the country experiences hundreds of earthquakes every year and accounts for roughly 18% of the world's seismic activity.

While most tremors are relatively minor, Japan remains haunted by memories of the catastrophic magnitude 9.0 earthquake and tsunami that struck the country's northeast coast in March 2011. The disaster killed or left missing around 18,500 people and triggered the Fukushima nuclear crisis.

Tuesday's earthquake demonstrated the country's preparedness systems, emergency response capabilities, and monitoring of critical infrastructure. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi office also posted a safety guideline on X, assuring that their safety remains their top priority.

As authorities continue to assess the impact of the Kumamoto quake, residents are being urged to stay alert for potential aftershocks and follow official safety guidance.

World.title: As US-Iran war rages, who's risking the Strait of Hormuz?
World.content:
Though Iran continues to attack vessels as leverage in its war with the United States, data show that several shippers continue to transit the waterway.

The Strait of Hormuz has become one of the world's most dangerous waterways since March, when Iran began attacking shipping vessels as a pressure tactic in its ceasefire talks with the United States. Still, though a significant proportion of the global oil trade bottlenecks at the strait, shipping traffic never completely halted.

With the United States and Iran issuing conflicting statements as to whether the Strait of Hormuz is open, DW analyzed public data sources to track how shipping traffic has changed during the course of the war and which vessels are still taking the risk of transiting the maritime choke point, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.

Shipping through Strait of Hormuz disrupted

As Iran's strikes on and interception of vessels in the Strait of Hormuz continue, mines have also been reported in the prewar shipping lanes.

The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), a project of the US-led Combined Maritime Forces, assesses the threat to shippers as "severe," its second-highest warning level. However, according to one of JMIC's latest advisory notes , issued after attacks resumed on July 6 and 7, "commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remained at reduced levels, with vessels transiting via both the southern Omani corridor and the northern Iranian-controlled route."

JMIC added that shippers remained cautious of transiting the strait amid the attacks on vessels in recent weeks.

DW's analysis of data from the open-source platform Global Fishing Watch showed that, nevertheless, several shipping companies have navigated their vessels through the Strait of Hormuz throughout the war. Though the platform's primary purpose is to monitor fishing efforts, it also collects data on all other vessels using satellite imagery and relying on signals transmitted by ships' automatic identification systems (AIS).

As ships can switch off their AIS transponders — and have reportedly repeatedly chosen to while transiting the Strait of Hormuz — the number of vessels is likely higher than shown.

Based on AIS signals, a combined total of at least 84 ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz in two periods of the conflict: from the start of the war on February 28 until the announcement of a ceasefire on April 7 and following the renewed attacks on July 6 and 7. This aligns with reports of the United States saying it gave passage to about 70 ships and adding that not all of them transmitted signals.

For comparison: In the same periods of 2025, more than 900 ships crossed the strait.

Of these 84 ships, 34 moved from east to west into the Persian Gulf and 50 crossed the strait in the opposite direction, moving out of the gulf.

In which countries are ships that transit the Strait of Hormuz registered?

As part of the AIS signal, ships transmit which flag they are sailing under, but this information is entered manually aboard the vessels. In only a few cases investigated for this story did the flag reflect the actual country of origin of the registered owner or the ship manager of a vessel. This information can still be looked up manually in different databases using the ship's international ID number and its name.

Only nine Iranian- and two Pakistani-owned ships transited under their respective national flags. All of the other 73 ships hoisted a flag different from the vessel owner's country.

Analysis of this data shows that a wide variety of companies operating in the region continue to cross the Strait of Hormuz.

At the top of the list is the United Arab Emirates, which neighbors the strait. The UAE's Abu Dhabi Crude Oil Pipeline (ADCOP) runs overland parallel to the waterway in the south. 13 cargo ships registered in the United Arab Emirates transited the strait during the shutdown, as well as two liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) tankers and three support vessels.

Most of the UAE-based ship owners in the dataset appear to have only one to five vessels in their fleet. One of the UAE-registered vessels that was detected passing into the Persian Gulf on July 11 is managed by Lubeck Shipping LLC, a company associated with an Iranian oil tycoon that has been sanctioned by the United States .

Also sanctioned by the United States is Salina Ship Management PvT Ltd. , a company from the Indian state of Maharashtra that US officials accuse of helping Iran move petrol. The company manages one of the four Indian oil and LPG tankers that Global Fishing Watch recorded entering the strait.

India, like many Asian countries, is heavily reliant on the Strait of Hormuz for energy supply. China, Pakistan and Vietnam, too, had oil and LPG tankers in the Persian Gulf that they moved out of the Strait of Hormuz before a ceasefire was announced on April 7.

All seven vessels owned and managed by companies from Greece, the world's biggest shipping power, were freighters, typically carrying unpackaged dried goods such as iron, coal and grains.

Why risk transiting the Strait of Hormuz?

The primary motive for continuing to move oil and other goods via the Strait of Hormuz despite the threat of attacks by Iran is financial — "simply because the reward seems higher than the risk," said Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler, a business intelligence company headquartered in Belgium that specializes in analyzing global commodity flows.

"The key point is that producers of oil (or gas, aluminum, and other products) within the Strait of Hormuz essentially have only two options," economist David Wech wrote in an email. Wech monitors the flow of energy commodities such as oil and refined products for the British company Vortexa.

"Option 1: to halt production and earn no money at all — or even incur losses due to operating expenditures," Wech wrote. "And option 2: accept the risk of transiting the strait and thereby earn 90% or more of their normal revenue. With an oil price of currently more than $80 per barrel, we're talking about billions of USD."

With hostilities hot again as of July, the Brent Crude oil price is on yet another upward trend, perhaps one of the most perceivable global effects of the war and the near shutdown of the Strait of Hormuz.

What are alternatives to Strait of Hormuz?

In prewar times, roughly 25% of the global maritime oil trade passed through the Strait of Hormuz. Alternative routes have limited capacity to compensate for the loss of oil flow through the strait, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Two pipelines are currently used to bypass the Strait of Hormuz: the UAE's ADCOP and another in Saudi Arabia.

The ADCOP in the United Arab Emirates would allow ships to land and load in the northeastern port of Fujairah and transport oil out of the Persian Gulf without transiting the Strait of Hormuz.

The Abqaiq-Yanbu crude oil pipeline system (East-West Crude Pipeline or Petroline) in Saudi Arabia has some capacity left, the IEA reported in February. Publicly available shipping data for Yanbu show an increase in oil-related ship traffic from May through June, compared with previous years.

"Combined, Yanbu and Fujairah have been able to reroute over 4 million barrels a day of crude from having to pass through the Strait of Hormuz," Smith said. "This has been able to act as a release valve to keep barrels flowing to key customers in Asia — but only offsetting 4 of the total 15 million barrels per day that typically passes through the strait."

The alternative routes have their own risks. Reports are increasing of piracy and attacks on ships by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow choke point between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. "Bab al-Mandeb has the potential to add further supply woes to a global supply picture that is already severely constrained," Smith said.

So, the release valve to the Strait of Hormuz might soon become a maritime choke point of its own.

Edited by Milan Gagnon and Andreas Becker.

World.title: Germany news: SPD seeks LGBTQ+ protections in constitution
World.content:
07/28/2026 July 28, 2026 Online holiday bookings hit German record

Bookings for holiday accommodation in Germany through major online platforms have reached a record high.

Travellers booked 68.3 million overnight stays through Airbnb, Booking.com and Expedia in 2025, up 13% from 2024 and more than 83% from 2019, the Federal Statistical Office said.

Domestic demand drove the increase, with German guests accounting for 48.5 million nights, up more than 15%. Foreign visitors booked 19.8 million nights, led by travellers from the Netherlands, Poland and the US.

Around 94% of stays were in properties with fewer than 10 beds, which are not covered by Germany's monthly tourism statistics.

Bavaria recorded the most overnight stays, with 10.6 million. Travel patterns varied considerably between Germany's states.

Around 90% of guests in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Schleswig-Holstein came from within Germany, while city-states and western regions attracted a larger share of international visitors.

Foreign guests accounted for more than two-thirds of bookings in Berlin, at 67.7%.

Their share was also above average in North Rhine-Westphalia, at 42.3%, and Baden-Württemberg, at 40.8%.

World.title: India news: Activists decry AI surveillance at CJP protests

07/28/2026 July 28, 2026 Bihar, Assam to withdraw cases against protesters

Hours after the CJP issued a statement over a breach of their demand to withdraw police cases against protesters — the ruling BJP’s Bihar and Assam governments said that all such charges will be dropped and protesters detained before 6 pm on July 26 will be released.

The party's West Bengal government, however, has not given any such assurances.

Union ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh had assured the the party that no action would be taken against peaceful protesters, news agency PTI reported.

In a press release issued by the Home and Political Department the Assam government said five cases had been registered in Assam in connection with the protests, leading to the arrest of 13 people.

"No adverse legal action will be initiated by any of the Police authorities within the State against those persons who have been involved in these protests," the press release said.

The statement said that the process of withdrawing the registered cases, irrespective of the stage of proceedings within Assam, will be initiated promptly as per law.

According to the police, altogether 694 people had been detained for participating in the protests in Bihar.

The Bihar government also announced that it will withdraw all cases lodged against protesters over the NEET paper leak and release those jailed under various charges.

World.title: Zelenskyy to meet Trump as Ukraine seeks stronger air defense
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is in the United States to press for stronger military cooperation, as Kyiv and Moscow intensify long-range strikes amid stalled peace efforts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived in the United States ahead of talks with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, saying Kyiv's top priority was securing stronger air defense and strategic cooperation as Russia intensified attacks.

"Our number-one priority is anti-ballistic defense and strategic cooperation with America. Peace needs to be brought closer," Zelenskyy said in a post on X after arriving in the US.

The two leaders are due to meet at the White House before attending a tribute to Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Ukraine, who passed away earlier this month.

US-Ukraine ties improving

The long-strained relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have improved in recent weeks.

Since returning to office in January last year, Trump largely stopped direct US arms shipments to Ukraine, instead allowing European allies to buy American weapons and supply them to Kyiv.

However, Washington remains a key ally, providing intelligence and access to the Starlink satellite network used by Ukrainian frontline troops to communicate.

In a sign of improving ties, Trump, in a meeting with Zelenskyy in Turkey earlier this month, pledged to help Ukraine produce Patriot air defense systems, saying Kyiv would be able to produce them "pretty quickly."

This has been a long-running request from Kyiv in order to counter Russian missile attacks.

Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes

The Trump-Zelenskyy meeting comes as more than four years have passed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war, both sides have stepped up long-range strikes.

Russia said on Tuesday that more than 390 Ukrainian drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, damaging residential buildings.

Russian state media also reported that Russian forces struck two vessels, including a ship in the Black Sea that Moscow claimed was transporting military supplies for Ukraine, according to Reuters.

World.title: Heat wave threatens to worsen France, Spain wildfires
World.content:
A fresh spell of extreme heat, driven by climate change, is expected to intensify some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades, stretching firefighting resources.

A forecast of an incoming heat wave across France and Spain this week is threatening to hamper firefighting efforts as some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades rage on.

France's weather service forecast temperatures of up to 40 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) from Tuesday, while Spain's AEMET warned of a new heat wave from Wednesday till the end of the week, with highs of 42 degree Celsius in the northeast and 39 degrees Celsius in central regions.

Authorities said soaring temperatures, dry winds and low humidity would push wildfire danger to "extreme" levels, even as forests turned tinder-dry by successive heat waves this year.

The return of searing temperatures, from Tuesday in France and from Wednesday in Spain, threaten to complicate fire-fighting efforts [FILE: July 23, 2026] Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP

Thousands of firefighters and water-dropping aircraft raced to contain the blazes before temperatures rise further.

Experts linked the scale of the fires to increasingly frequent and intense heat waves driven by climate change, as hotter and drier conditions are making wildfires more destructive.

Macron warns of 'hard' times

In France, President Emmanuel Macron said one fire in the Landes region had been contained, but a much larger wildfire near Bordeaux continued to burn after scorching about 42,000 hectares, forcing around 220,000 people to evacuate and destroying hundreds of homes.

"The weeks ahead will be hard. We must hold firm," Macron said.

Overnight on Tuesday, firefighters prevented a massive wildfire along the Atlantic coast west of Bordeaux from spreading, authorities said.

According to officials, 93 firefighters have been injured since the operation began.

Aid from Germany arrived in the region on Monday in the form of two transport helicopters and an A400M transport aircraft carrying equipment.

In Spain, wildfires west of Madrid and in other regions have forced about 60,000 people to flee.

With the coming heat wave threatening to fuel further spread of the wildfires, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska firefighters in Spain made progress after a "positive night" against wildfires to the west of Madrid.

"It has been a reasonably positive night, thanks to the tremendous effort of all the public emergency services," Grande-Marlaska said. "We are in critical hours."

France and Spain are battling the worst wildfires in living memory, which have ripped through hundreds of hectares of woodland, destroying properties and forcing evacuations Image: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance





Some 150,000 hectares of land have burned in Spain and 115,000 hectares in France since the start of this year.

At a campsite near Navaluenga, west of the capital, ravaged by Spain's worst wildfire on record, the site co-owner Maria Angeles Canete said her family lost everything.

"We had this campsite, we had another one, and we've lost it all. We have nothing," she told the AFP news agency.

EU firefighting resources stretched thin

The European Union deployed additional firefighting aircraft to France, while EU commissioner Hadja Lahbib warned that resources are under growing strain as extreme fire conditions spread across southern and central Europe.

"Extreme conditions are looming for Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, in addition to France, the Iberian Peninsula... where the situation is expected to worsen, including in Portugal starting today," Lahbib said.

In Italy, a wildfire in the southern Puglia region forced the evacuation of hundreds of tourists from beaches and campgrounds, authorities said.

07/28/2026 July 28, 2026 Iran executes two men in relation to January protests

The Iranian judiciary announced on Tuesday that two men convicted of acts of violence during anti-government protests in January had been hanged.

"The death sentences of Abolfazl Sepahi and Amir-Hossein Safari were carried out this morning," the judiciary's Mizan Online portal said.

It said the pair had been found guilty of "attacking police officers with machetes and knives, tying them to road signs, pulling them on the ground, dousing them with gasoline, and setting them on fire."

Other charges, according to Mizan, included "moharebeh [waging war against God] by drawing weapons and creating fear and terror" and "corruption on earth for committing acts that severely disrupted public order and security in the country."

The Mehr news agency reported that the executions took place in "a square in the city of Malekshahr" in the central Isfahan province, in the presence of members of the public.

Two other men were hanged on similar charges in Isfahan province on July 19.

In December 2025, a protest movement initially sparked by the high cost of living in Iran rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.

Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, attributing the violence to "terrorist acts" which they claimed were orchestrated by the United States and Israel, while rights groups based abroad maintain that security forces fired on protesters.

According to Amnesty International, Iran conducts the second most judicial executions of any country, after China.

World.title: US singer D4vd to stand trial in killing of 14-year-old girl
World.content:
D4vd is accused of murdering 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez in 2025. Prosecutors allege that he dismembered her body and drove around with her decomposing remains in his car.

Content warning: This article discusses child sexual abuse and murder.

A US judge ruled on Monday that there is enough evidence for singer D4vd to stand trial over the killing and dismembering of a 14-year-old girl with whom he had an illegal sexual relationship.

After prosecutors presented evidence over a five-day hearing, Los Angeles Judge Charlaine Olmedo ruled that the 21-year-old singer, whose real name is David Burke, would stand trial.

He faces multiple charges including murder, continuous sexual abuse of a child under the age of 14, and unlawful mutilation of human remains. He has pleaded not guilty.

Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan Hochman said outside court that prosecutors are still deciding whether to seek the death penalty.

What are the allegations against D4vd?

In September 2025, the dismembered, decomposing body of 14-year-old year old Celeste Rivas Hernandez was found in the back of a Tesla that was registered in Burke's name.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke first met Rivas Hernandez when she was 11, and began sexually abusing her when she was 13 and he was 18.

Los Angeles police detective Corey Farrell told the court under questioning that the parents of both Burke and Rivas Hernandez knew about their relationship and that her parents had given consent for her to travel to London with him for a week.

The detective also read text messages to the court in which Rivas Hernandez said she had fallen pregnant and had an abortion.

Around 24 hours before she was murdered, Rivas Hernandez sent Burke a series of expletive-laden text messages. Prosecutors said the text messages showed she was jealous of another woman and threatened to expose their illegal relationship.

Celeste Rivas Hernandez was 14 when she was murdered Image: Damian Dovarganes/AP Photo/picture alliance

The singer then allegedly paid for an Uber to bring Rivas Hernandez to his home where prosecutors said he stabbed her to death upon entering.

Prosecutors alleged that Burke then proceeded to immediately cover up the killing. Burke sent Rivas Hernandez multiple text messages asking where she was and expressing concern — messages which prosecutors say were sent as cover after he murdered her.

Meanwhile, prosecutors also pointed to Burke's online order receipts under a fictitious name, which showed he purchased chainsaws, a shovel and an inflatable pool.

He allegedly used the items to dismember her body in his garage, where DNA matching the victim was found on blood stains, according to prosecutors.

He also purchased a portable "burn box" incinerator that turned out to be too small to destroy her body, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors presented evidence over five days [FILE: April 20, 2026] Image: Ted Soqui/AP Photo/picture alliance

Burke then allegedly drove around for weeks with Rivas Hernandez's dismembered body in his trunk before the seemingly abandoned Tesla was ultimately towed to an impound lot in Hollywood.

Prosecutors reject accident claims

Prosecutor Beth Silverman told the court that "there's nothing in this case that sounds like an accident."

Burke's lawyer meanwhile said "there was no evidence of deliberate intention to kill."

Burke, performing as D4vd, gained a massive following on social media like TikTok and Soundcloud with his breakthrough track "Romantic Homicide" in 2022.

In April 2025, he played at the Coachella music festival and released his first album "Withered," two days after authorities say Rivas Hernandez was killed.

Edited by: Rana Taha
