World.title: Quiero comprar un piso que está alquilado y ocuparlo de inmediato, ¿cómo me aseguro de que el inquilino se irá?
World.content:
Los lectores envían sus preguntas al consultorio de vivienda de EL PAÍS en colaboración con Legálitas

Pregunta. Tengo intención de adquirir un piso que actualmente está alquilado. El inquilino dice que está dispuesto a marcharse en cuanto se venda, pero tiene contrato vigente por tres años más. Mi intención sería ocupar el piso inmediatamente tras la compra. ¿Cómo debo actuar? Aunque no tengo razones para desconfiar del inquilino tampoco me gustaría tener problemas. ¿Debería formalizarse de alguna manera la salida del inquilino antes de hacer cualquier pago? F. Atorrasagasti

Respuesta. Antes de adquirir una vivienda que se encuentra alquilada, es importante tener en cuenta las siguientes circunstancias y derechos reconocidos por la Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos:

La compraventa no extingue el contrato de arrendamiento: la venta de la vivienda no supone la finalización del contrato de alquiler, por lo que el comprador se subroga en la posición del anterior arrendador, asumiendo todos los derechos y obligaciones derivados del contrato vigente, incluidos la renta pactada, la duración del arrendamiento y el resto de sus condiciones.

Derecho de adquisición preferente del inquilino: la ley reconoce al arrendatario un derecho de adquisición preferente, también conocido como derecho de “tanteo y retracto”, en caso de venta de la vivienda. Por ello, salvo que en el contrato de arrendamiento conste la renuncia expresa a este derecho, el inquilino podrá adquirir el inmueble en las mismas condiciones ofrecidas a un tercero comprador.

Por este motivo, lo más recomendable es realizar cualquier desembolso una vez que la vivienda haya sido entregada libre de ocupantes y el arrendatario haya abandonado el inmueble.

No obstante, si ello no fuera posible, y una vez comprobada la existencia de una renuncia válida al derecho de adquisición preferente, resulta aconsejable formalizar un acuerdo por escrito entre el propietario y el inquilino. En dicho acuerdo, el arrendatario debería comprometerse a abandonar la vivienda en una fecha determinada, preferiblemente antes de la firma de la escritura de compraventa o, como máximo, el mismo día de su otorgamiento.

Asimismo, sería conveniente incluir una cláusula adicional que establezca una penalización por cada día de retraso en la salida de la vivienda y entrega de la posesión, como posible indemnización de los daños y perjuicios.

Para una mayor garantía, este acuerdo debería suscribirse con anterioridad o en el mismo momento de la firma del contrato de arras, fijando una fecha concreta de salida del inmueble anterior a la formalización de la compraventa ante notario e incluyendo el derecho a recuperar las arras en caso de incumplimiento por parte del inquilino de su compromiso, recuperando cuando menos la cantidad entregada a cuenta y sin perjuicio de la reclamación de daños y perjuicios al inquilino.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: A San Andrés de Teixido, por el Camiño Vello
World.content:
Una ruta a pie por la salvaje Costa Ártabra, en el extremo septentrional de España, buscando el segundo santuario más visitado de Galicia, que se alza desde tiempos remotos al pie de los acantilados más altos de Europa

Dicen que “a Santo André de Teixido vai de morto quen non foi de vivo”. ¿Y eso es malo? Respondamos gallegamente: depende. Si para ir allí, uno se reencarna en una babosa y se arrastra a cámara lenta por un camino abarrotado de peregrinos, corriendo el serio peligro de acabar espachurrado bajo una suela Vibram, no es bueno. En cambio, si se reencarna en una bolboreta, en una mariposa macaón o en una blanca esbelta ­–por citar dos especies habituales en el extremo norte de la Península–, y se va parando en cada flor a libar y copular, no está mal.

Probablemente Dios y san Pedro no pensaron en esta posibilidad cuando hallaron a san Andrés triste y solo en su santuario coruñés, pues no recibía ni la milésima parte de visitas que el de Santiago, y le prometieron que a su templo vendrían todos los mortales y que aquel que no lo hiciera en vida, lo haría reencarnado en un animal. O no lo pensaron bien o no sabían de mariposas.

Más información 13 razones por las que queremos viajar

Tras los pasos del Padre Sarmiento

Al santuario de San Andrés de Teixido, como al de Santiago, llevan todos los caminos. Hay casi tantos como peregrinos, que son legión –unos 70.000 al año– desde que se enteraron de que Dios y san Pedro habían prometido lo que prometieron a san Andrés. Todos valen, pero el original, el primero del que hay noticia fidedigna, es el que siguió el ilustrado Padre Sarmiento en 1755. Este escritor y erudito benedictino, que había pasado su niñez y parte de su juventud en Pontevedra, se interesó como ningún otro en su tiempo por todo lo gallego, en especial por la lengua y la geografía, a tal punto que iba anotando en un cuaderno los nombres exactos de los lugares por los que andaba. Gracias a eso, hoy puede seguirse sin dificultad el camino que hizo. Bueno, y gracias también a la Diputación de A Coruña, que lo señalizó en 2001 con monolitos de granito en los que un pescado rojo indica la dirección correcta. Para más facilidad, en Wikiloc están la descripción, el mapa y el track de este camino de 39 kilómetros, que suele hacerse dividiéndolo en dos etapas de unas seis horas de duración cada una.

El santuario de San Andrés de Teixido, destino final del histórico Camiño Vello y uno de los principales centros de peregrinación de Galicia. Andrés Campos

El Camiño Vello, que así se llama –aunque también podría llamarse Bello, con be, porque lo es– arranca en el monasterio de San Martiño de Xuvia, en la parroquia de O Couto, en Narón, junto a la ría de Ferrol. Bordeando ésta se sube hasta el molino de mareas de As Aceas –de mediados del siglo XVIII, que llegó a ser una de las mayores fábricas de harina de Galicia­­­–, donde el camino se desvía tierra adentro para ir en busca del Pazo Libunca, un palacete modernista de 1922 cuyo primer dueño y constructor, el indiano Francisco Montenegro, dicen que se encendía los puros con billetes de mil pesetas. Ahora es un hotel muy majo pero carillo, donde se necesitan al menos 24 de aquellos billetes –unos 145 euros– para dormir una noche de verano. Pasando después por la necrópolis prehistórica del Monte dos Nenos y por el Marco de Portonovo de Valverde –pedrusco milenario donde confluyen los términos de Narón, Valdoviño y San Sadurniño– se llega, ya casi al final de la primera etapa, a la ermita de Liñeiro, más conocida como la Capela da Fame, la Capilla del Hambre, nombre popular que suena fuerte y claro, como las tripas del peregrino después de caminar 22 kilómetros.

Las caldupeiras de Porto do Cabo

En Porto do Cabo –pueblo chico pero de hermosos y extensos dominios, divididos entre los municipios de Valdoviño, Cedeira y Cerdido–, se acaba la primera etapa del Camiño Vello y también la fame, el hambre que cualquiera arrastra tras andar seis horas por el monte. Aquí, alrededor del puente medieval, se ponían antaño las caldupeiras, mujeres que por poco dinero –un patacón de cobre– daban a los peregrinos una cunca rebosante, no de aguachirle, sino de guiso sustancioso: un caldo gallego, vaya. Y aquí se siguen poniendo, con pañoletas, mandiles, zuecos de cuero y ollas humeantes, las mujeres de la Asociación Veciñal Porto de Cabo, cuando se celebra la romería más importante a San Andrés de Teixido, el primer fin de semana de septiembre.

Vecinas de Porto do Cabo caracterizadas como caldupeiras durante la romería de San Andrés de Teixido, una tradición que recuerda a las mujeres que alimentaban a los peregrinos. Andrés Campos

Una de estas caldupeiras, Antonia Martínez, y su marido y presidente de la asociación vecinal, José Picallo, son los propietarios de Casa do Morcego, bautizada así en recuerdo de los muchos murciélagos que la habitaban antes de ser transformada en un hotelito rural encantador, el mejor de la ruta. Murciélagos ahora se ven pocos. En cambio, hay bolboretas a patadas: mariposas de los muros, vanesas pintadas, mantos oscuros, colias, níspolas… El huerto está lleno de ellas y también de verduras que acaban en la cocina de la casa y en las tripas cada vez más silenciosas del caminante.

Casa do Morcego es un lugar que envicia, donde uno se estaría, no una noche, sino una semana explorando los contornos de la mano de Antonia Martínez y José Picallo. En el mismo Porto do Cabo se conservan la histórica hospedería Casa da Bastona y el puente medieval sobre el río das Mestas, el cual desagua en la ría de Cedeira cerca de un lugar donde se acaba la poca fame que el caminante pueda aún tener: Taberna do Puntal. Tampoco se come mal en el restaurante O Castro, con vistas a la playa de Pantín, la catedral gallega del surf. Ni en Badulaque, en el puerto de Cedeira, a tiro de caña de la lonja. Más frescos, los rapes y las almejas no pueden llegar. Luego lo suyo es dar un largo paseo digestivo viendo el casco viejo de Cedeira, el castro Sarridal, el Castelo da Concepción y el atardecer desde el mirador de San Antonio de Corveiro.

Bichos y bestas de la Serra da Capelada

Tras desayunar y sellar el pasaporte de peregrino en Casa do Morcego, comienza la segunda etapa del Camiño Vello subiendo por espesos y fragantes montes de eucaliptos para, a los cinco kilómetros –una hora y media a paso regular– pararse a desayunar otra vez en Panadería Prados (981 48 24 58), en A Venta, en la parroquia cedeiresa de San Román de Montoxo. En este horno de leña, además de un pan irresistible –lo habitual en Galicia–, hacen ricas cocadas, bollas de manzana, bizcochadas y empanadas de raya. Conviene llevar una mochila XXL porque todo, dentro del cuerpo, no cabe.

La ermita de San Roque de Reboredo marca la entrada a la Serra da Capelada en la segunda etapa del Camiño Vello. Andrés Campos

Siguiente parada, en la capilla de San Roque de Reboredo, ermita del siglo XVII que señala la entrada a la Serra da Capelada. Quienes peregrinan a Teixido han de mirar siempre bien dónde pisan, por si alguien que no fue allá en vida está haciendo el camino transmutado en insecto, anfibio o reptil, pero aquí deben extremar las precauciones porque el prado de la ermita está plagado de ranas galaicas y de luciones, lagartos ápodos, sin patas, también conocidos como culebrillas de cristal. A los que pasen sin despanzurrar ninguno, san Andrés se lo agradecerá. Y san Roque, patrón de los peregrinos y amigo de los animales, no digamos. Esta era una de las muchas capelas habitadas por ermitaños que dieron nombre a la Serra da Capelada, orónimo que el Padre Sarmiento explicó en 1755, cuando peregrinó anotando todo en su cuaderno de viaje.

A partir de aquí, el paisaje se vuelve más agreste. Se puebla de bestas, los caballejos semisalvajes que cada primavera rapan y marcan con festiva algazara los ganaderos de la comarca. Y se puebla también de amilladoiros, montones de piedras en los que el peregrino previsor arroja la que ha transportado en la mochila desde su lugar de origen para que el día del Juicio Final demuestre que ha estado aquí en vida y no tenga que volver desde el más allá, convertido en un bicho. Eso, si es que es capaz de encontrarla, sepultada como está bajo hogazas de pan, dulces varios y empanadas de raya.

Un artesano elabora y vende sanandresiños, los tradicionales amuletos de pan asociados a la romería de San Andrés de Teixido. Andrés Campos

En el mirador Chao do Monte, a un kilómetro justo del final, se obtiene la primera vista del santuario de San Andrés de Teixido. Si el caminante no supiera que está en la esquina más norteña de Galicia, diría que aquella iglesia de allá abajo y aquellas casitas de piedra casi negra con llagas blancas, rodeadas de acantilados y de verdores tan intensos que hacen daño a la retina, son un pueblecito de la isla canaria de La Gomera. Y si no supiera que san Andrés no pisó nunca España y que terminó atado a una cruz en forma de aspa en la ciudad griega de Patras, diría lo que dice la leyenda: que aquella peña oronda que aflora del mar al pie del blanco caserío, cual navío panza arriba, es la barca de piedra en la que vino a Galicia, emulando a Santiago, y con la que naufragó al llegar, demostrando que estos acantilados no son un buen lugar para atracar.

“A San Andrés van dos y vuelven tres”

Una vez en San Andrés de Teixido, la tradición manda acercarse a los puestos de productos típicos –exvotos, licores, herba de namorar, rosquillas, juncos del bien parir, pines con forma de percebe…– para comprar los sanandresiños, amuletos hechos con masa de pan sin fermentar, endurecidos al horno y pintados de vivos colores, que tienen diferentes formas, adecuadas al uso que se les va a dar: la flor, para conseguir el amor; la mano, para formular un deseo; la sardina que pescó san Andrés, para conjurar las envidias… Son muy bonitos y prometedores, pero para comer no valen. Para eso, están los percebes y todo lo que sirven, sin florituras, en la Taberna Hermanos Bouza.

Lo segundo que hay que hacer en San Andrés de Teixido es entrar en la iglesia, erigida sobre la roca viva, y pedir la bendición del titular, a cuyos pies suele haber gran variedad de ofrendas: fotos de carné, extremidades de cera, barquitos de madera… Por haber, hay hasta ataúdes de personas que, gracias al santo, no llegaron a necesitarlo. Y lo tercero, dirigirse a la fuente de los Tres Caños, de los cuales tres hay que beber para que se cumpla un deseo. Si se arroja una miga de pan y flota, también es buena señal. Y si se tiene una verruga y se lava con esta agua, puede que se caiga o puede que no. En el peor de los casos, se tendrá una verruga lustrosa. Las que tienen una piel preciosa, verde brillante con reticulado en negro y ocelos axiales azules, son las lagartijas serranas (Iberolacerta monticola) que pululan en el merendero aledaño.

Una lagartija serrana junto a la fuente de los Tres Caños, donde la tradición invita a beber tres sorbos para pedir un deseo. Andrés Campos

Antiguamente, también era tradición bajar hasta la rompiente en busca de la hierba de enamorar, hacer un ramito con ella y depositarla en el santuario como ofrenda. Ahora, que hay más conciencia ambiental, se recomienda comprar la que venden en los tenderetes, procedente de cultivos. A la Armeria pubigera se le atribuyen propiedades enamoradoras –una pizca en el bolsillo del otro obra el milagro–, afrodisiacas y empreñadoras. Y no falla, según lo que dicen: “A San Andrés van dos y vuelven tres”.

Acantilados gigantes y playas salvajes

En San Andrés de Teixido termina el Camiño Vello, pero el viaje a pie se puede alargar una jornada más –tres en total– bordeando los acantilados situados al noreste del santuario, que hay quienes dicen que son los más altos de Europa continental, aunque otros, más cautos, añaden que están a la par con los de Irlanda y Noruega. En el filo más elevado, a 620 metros sobre el océano, descuella la Vixía de Herbeira, un puesto de vigilancia costera del siglo XVIII desde el que los barcos enemigos debían de verse, si es que se veían, como microbios. El mar sí se ve, pero tan lejos que no se oye. Aquí, incluso en verano, sopla un viento recio, fresco, de jersey obligado. En ir y volver desde San Andrés de Teixido se tarda cuatro horas, siguiendo esta ruta de Wikiloc.

La playa de Fornos, en el municipio coruñés de Cariño, destaca por sus aguas transparentes y su entorno prácticamente virgen. Andrés Campos

El cabo Ortegal, ya en el vecino concejo de Cariño, es el segundo más norteño de la Península después del de Estaca de Bares. Y el más afilado, con el sitio justo para la carretera y un faro como de juguete. Le acompañan tres temibles islotes, Os Aguillóns, como si él solo no diera ya bastante miedo. Los que saben de percebes dicen que aquí se cogen los mejores de Galicia. Y los que saben de rocas, que estas son las más antiguas de la península Ibérica, de hace 1.156 millones de años. De la Vixía de Herbeira al cabo Ortegal hay 11,5 kilómetros de camino, unas tres horas sin parar apenas.

A la Vixía de Herbeira y al cabo Ortegal también se puede ir en coche, si es que uno no tiene las fuerzas o las ganas suficientes para prolongar a pie el Camiño Vello. Pero a donde solo se puede ir andando es la playa de Teixidelo. Escondida al pie de los tremendos acantilados de la Serra da Capelada, es la única playa del mundo de arena negra no volcánica. Su misterioso color es producto de la erosión de rocas ricas en peridotita y olivino. Para descubrirla, se ha de caminar desde el mirador de Teixidelo, muy cerca de San Andrés de Teixido, siguiendo una ruta de circular breve pero muy abrupta y empinada, de seis kilómetros y casi tres horas de duración, solo para senderistas expertos. Los que no lo sean se moverán mucho mejor por estos vertiginosos vericuetos de la Serra da Capelada acompañados por los guías de Portal Norte.

Otras playas salvajes alucinantes, con acceso más sencillo, son las que rodean la península de Figueiroa, en el vecino concejo de Cariño. A un lado de la península está la de Fornos, de 400 metros de largo por 60 de anchura, cuyas aguas verdes nada tienen que envidiar a las del Caribe. Salvo la temperatura, lógicamente. Al otro, la de Figueiras, más pequeña –260x15 metros– y recogida, frecuentada por las mariscadoras que siembran y luego recogen, rodilla en tierra, su cosecha berberechil. Y en medio, la más seductora, la de Os Cabalos o de A Postiña –350x30 metros–, solo accesible a pie desde las otras dos cuando la marea baja. Las fuertes corrientes de la ría y las violentas mareas hacen casi imposible bañarse en ella. Si nos gusta bajar a la playa cinco minutos, a deshora y sin gente, es perfecta.

World.title: Rosa Vañó (Castillo de Canena): “Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego con las que he trabajado”
World.content:
Economista de formación, dejó su exitosa carrera de directiva en Coca-Cola para desarrollar, junto a su hermano Francisco, la explotación olivarera que había creado su padre en Jaén. Además, conoce muy bien el mundo de las discográficas ya que trabajó para Warner Music y Universal

Es la gran dama del aceite español. Rosa Vañó (Madrid, 63 años), economista de formación, abandonó una exitosa carrera como directiva de Coca-Cola, donde se dedicaba al desarrollo de nuevas líneas de negocio, lanzamientos y reposicionamiento de productos, para dedicarse, junto a su hermano Francisco, al sueño que inició su padre, Luis Vañó: impulsar Castillo de Canena, una explotación olivarera con almazara situada en Canena (Jaén), propiedad de su familia y reconocida con numerosos premios nacionales e internacionales. Anteriormente trabajó en las discográficas Warner Music y Universal, “donde aprendí a gestionar egos y a entender que hay que contar con los medios de comunicación como embajadores y transmisores de la creatividad y el valor añadido de los músicos”. Ejerce también como tesorera de la Real Academia de Gastronomía.

Pregunta. Con este bagaje, decide desarrollar su propio negocio.

Respuesta. Sí, porque teníamos la enorme suerte de tener campo, almazara y también el castillo. Se puede empezar de cero, pero de distintas formas. Es un recorrido profesional que te va formando y quitando miedos. La ignorancia es muy valiente y te hace creer que puedes hacer las cosas mejor, de forma diferente y de manera especial. Todo esto cuesta mucho trabajo. Primero, porque no es fácil hacerlo y porque hay mucha gente que lo hace igual o mejor que tú. Al final, la fórmula no es otra que trabajo, pero bien entendido.

P. ¿Qué significa esto?

R. El trabajo no son horas, es calidad y flexibilidad. Los peores resultados los he tenido cuando he trabajado 14 horas al día. He sido menos resolutiva y creativa. Me parece importante la conectividad para mi conciliación como madre, como hija y como profesional. Son las tres prioridades de mi vida. El teléfono me permite tener mi sitio de trabajo en cualquier lugar.

P. Comentaba que sabe manejar los egos. ¿Se ha encontrado con muchos?

R. Madonna es una de las personas más complicadas y con más ego que he conocido y con la que he trabajado en mi vida. Me tocó trabajar con ella en promoción y en gira. Por el contrario, con Phil Collins o los hermanos Young [Malcolm y Angus], de AC/DC, me he divertido mucho. Son personas que han dejado el ego a un lado. Y no tiene nada que ver con que sean hombres o mujeres. Por ejemplo, Prince era un hombre que tenía inseguridades, pero con una gestión muy peculiar de su ego. Porque el ego no es solo el de tipo Madonna, en el que tienes que interpretar su gestión, sino también cómo se siente, cómo es su timidez y cómo tienes que relacionarte con él. Seal tampoco era una persona fácil. Fue mi primer artista y era complicado de manejar.

P. ¿Qué se hace en esos casos?

R. Callar, entender y destensar la situación, aunque no tengas la culpa. Hay que intentar destensar y tratar de ser empático y resolutivo. El ego es más complejo que creerse superior, por eso hay que entender cómo es la personalidad de cada uno. Ha sido una gran escuela de vida.

P. Salir a vender aceite por el mundo habrá sido mucho más fácil, ¿no?

R. La primera vez que salí a vender aceite fue en España. Entré en un restaurante, que no voy a decir cuál, por la puerta principal. Me preguntaron a qué iba y les dije que a vender aceite. Me dijeron que eso era por la puerta de proveedores, que estaba por detrás, donde estaban los cubos de basura y los cascos de botellas. Entré por ahí. Hoy, si no me dicen lo contrario, siempre entro por la puerta de proveedores. Entiendo que, si el cocinero me tiene que recibir en su cocina para probar el aceite, esa es la puerta. Hay que entender cada situación.

P. ¿Ha hecho mucha calle?

R. Al principio hay que hacer mucha calle. Ahora también, pero tenemos más gente que te ayuda. Estoy en un momento de mi vida en el que tengo que mirarlo todo con mucha positividad. Lo mejor es hoy y tengo que estar preparada para el día de mañana. Debe haber un relevo. Hay decisiones que ya no me toca tomar a mí, sino al equipo, a mi sobrino y a mi hijo [ambos se llaman Luis y llevan el apellido Vañó]. Me pueden pedir opinión, pero no puedo empecinarme en que la decisión es mía porque hay gente alrededor que tiene que liderar. Odiaría ser la típica persona que es la primera que llega a la oficina y la última que se va. O la que va todos los días, con 80 años, a ver qué pasa.

P. ¿A qué dedica el resto del tiempo cuando no trabaja?

R. Voy a ir por orden de frivolidad. Me gusta jugar al golf; hago pilates tres días a la semana, que me divierte mucho, y camino. Soy una gran aficionada a viajar, pero con causa. Mi afición siempre ha sido la antropología, la arqueología y el arte antiguo. Me ha interesado saber cuándo el hombre deja de ser animal y adquiere un toque divino o humano. Me gusta viajar con contenido, por ejemplo, para ver el románico del norte de España, el misterio de las catedrales, conocer culturas antiguas... Es algo que no he hecho en los últimos años todo lo que me habría gustado y me gustaría retomarlo. Coger un barco y recorrer las esclusas francesas, pararte en los vignerons y vas viendo el paisaje, me gusta. Me voy a dedicar a viajar más. También he descuidado mucho mi afición a las exposiciones. Antes iba prácticamente todos los meses a ver dos exposiciones en Madrid y, si tenía que irme fuera, también lo hacía. Pero ahora, por mi situación personal, he descuidado un poco esa faceta. Me encantaba ir con toda la familia a ver una exposición y luego irnos a comer. Me parece gratificante. Adoro leer.

P. ¿Cuál es su género preferido?

R. Leo mucha historia, pero como formo parte de varias tertulias literarias me hacen leer todo tipo de libros. Uno de los más recientes ha sido Historia de una escalera. También acabo de leer varias obras de Hermann Hesse para una tertulia. Me esfuerzo por leer cosas diferentes de las que suelo leer durante el insomnio.

P. ¿Qué lee en esas noches en vela?

R. Leo a Agatha Christie y a sir Arthur Conan Doyle. Quiero lecturas ligeras para quedarme dormida. La ópera me ha encantado toda la vida. He estado en distintos teatros, como el Bolshói o La Scala de Milán. Verdi y Puccini me encantan porque mi madre me los ponía de pequeña. Voy a cuatro o cinco óperas al año. También me encanta la música barroca. No me pierdo los ciclos de Händel en el Auditorio Nacional de Música de Madrid.

P. ¿Qué restaurantes frecuenta?

R. Tanto de producto y muy clásicos como sorprendentes y de vanguardia. Me gustan los dos extremos. Estuve hace poco en Desde 1911 y trabaja con un gran producto. También me gustan las verduras de Saddle o el ganso de Navidad, que tomo con mis hijos. Los atunes guisados de El Campero me encantan. No me gustan los crudos. Estuve hace poco en Tetsu y me pareció espectacular y divertido. De Jaén me gustan Juan Carlos García, de Vandelvira, y Pedro Sánchez, de Bagá; también Dani Carnero, del restaurante Kaleja en Málaga. Son maravillosos. Y José Álvarez, en la costa de Almería, con su proyecto de tomates.

P. ¿Su desayuno preferido?

R. Una tostada de pan bien caliente, restregada con ajo, aceite de oliva virgen extra y sal. El ajo es maravilloso de todas las maneras. No soy muy cafetera, tomo uno al día. Me gusta su olor, pero no tanto el sabor.

P. ¿Le gusta darse caprichos?

R. No, salvo gastronómicos. Comprarme ropa siempre tiene que ser algo organizado. Hace años, una compañera de trabajo me dijo que salía con la misma ropa en todas las fotografías. Nunca se lo agradeceré lo suficiente porque no había caído en ello. Soy muy estructurada con lo que me pongo, pero ir de compras me aburre. También me aburren las obras en casa y comprar cosas para decorarla.

P. ¿Tiene algún viaje pendiente?

R. Cuando era pequeña leí los libros de Jack London y sus viajes a los mares del Sur. Por eso me atrae la Polinesia, aunque luego quizá sea un coñazo y tenga que llevarme 200 libros, preguntándome qué hago yo en un palafito. Me gustaría conocerla. También me gustaría ver una aurora boreal. La Antártida me resulta muy atractiva. Y me apetecería hacer un viaje en barco entre Moscú y San Petersburgo.

P. ¿Algún remedio para el insomnio?

R. La edad no perdona. He probado todo lo que no es químico y, a veces, funciona y otras no. Ya convivo con él, incluso cuando estoy de vacaciones en Granada, frente al mar Mediterráneo, al que tanto quiero. Lo que no me gusta es pensar por la noche porque es muy mala compañera. También escucho pódcasts ligeros y de true crime; eso me evade y evita que me invadan los malos pensamientos, porque soy una persona muy positiva y estable.

World.title: Dutch government is neglecting Bonaire climate change ruling
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The government is not taking measures to address its legal obligations to protect the former Dutch colony of Bonaire from the ravages of climate change, according to an investigation by NOS.

A court in The Hague ruled in January the government had acted in a discriminatory manner towards Bonaire by excluding the Caribbean island from its climate plans.

Although the cabinet has appealed, ministers are still obliged to comply with the terms of the judgment, including providing an assessment of how much greenhouse gas that the Netherlands believes it can still emit without exceeding the Paris climate goals.

That report was due today and, according to the NOS, the government has not submitted it.

“Failing to provide insight into that scope is simply negligent,” climate lawyer Laura Burgers of the University of Amsterdam told NOS.

In response to questions from the broadcaster, climate minister Stientje van Veldhoven-van der Meer said that the cabinet will provide more information on Budget Day – 15 September – regarding how the Bonaire ruling will be implemented.

Eight people from the Caribbean island of Bonaire joined forces with environmental organisation Greenpeace to sue the Dutch government for failing to protect them against climate change.

World.title: Vandals attack homes as row over asylum seekers turns violent
World.content:
A bitter war has broken out in two Brabant villages over plans to accommodate 50 refugees in the area, with supporters having their homes vandalised by anti-immigration campaigners.

Slogans using words such as teef (bitch) and hoer (whore) were scrawled on the walls and windows of homes in Bokhoven and Engelen, near Den Bosch, where the council’s plans have been the focus of heated protests and riots.

One couple, who gave their names as Rob and Ingrid, told Omroep Brabant they were not outright supporters of the plan, but had called for an open debate about the implications.

“We understand that people in De Vutter [the location of the proposed shelter] have real concerns,” Rob said.

He accused opponents of the scheme of trying to shut down the discussion through intimidation and violence. “A few months ago Ingrid called in our village newspaper for us to stand together as a village and organise things properly,” he said.

“That open approach has meant that the media and others have put us on the side of the actual supporters and our name has been circulated by extreme opponents.”

Spreading law

The municipality announced in April it wanted to house 50 boys and girls aged between 15 and 18 on an industrial site in the area, to meet its obligations under the so-called “spreading law” that requires councils to share the responsibility for accommodating asylum seekers.

Demonstrations that were held outside community meetings turned to riots as stones were thrown and fireworks were let off.

Police in riot gear with dogs cleared away a group of 100 protesters, some of whom tried to block the A59 motorway, and arrested two people during two nights of violence.

In May the council announced it was postponing the decision so it could hold more community information sessions. Two days later an explosion damaged the building where the refugees were due to be held.

Rob said it was clear from camera footage that the attacks on his home had been carried out by a group of youths.

“Once the police have caught the youths, we would like to have a conversation with them,” he said. “They probably have no idea how it affects you emotionally when you go through this.”

Syrians attacked

In a separate incident, police in Geesteren said a family of asylum seekers from Syria had been targeted several times by vandals and had their car set on fire after moving in to the village earlier this year.

The family, whose children are aged six, three and one, were allocated the house after being granted settled status, four years after they first arrived in the Netherlands.

Windows in the property have been smashed three times since March and on Sunday night their car was set ablaze. Police are treating the incident as arson, but say locals are too anxious to come forward with information.

Community silence

“The anxiety means people don’t dare to talk to us,” local police spokeswoman Chantal Westerhoff told NOS. “What I mean by that is that we have no tips at present or indications of who caused this.”

The mayor of Tubbergen, Anko Postma, whose municipality includes Geesteren, said extra protection was being arranged for the family.

“This must have a big impact on a family just as they are trying to build a new life here,” he said. “We are in contact with them and are looking at what support they need.”

The father, Al Arab, told NOS he was considering leaving the village because he was worried his family were becoming a burden. “Maybe it’s better if we go. Our dear neighbours are getting scared,” he said.

World.title: Four Dutch tourists found after speedboat goes missing in Malawi
World.content:
Four Dutch tourists who were reported missing when a speedboat failed to return from a trip on Lake Malawi have been found safe.

Malawian authorities put out an alert after the Tanzanian-registered boat failed to arrive at the expected time at Nkhata Bay on Sunday.

Three crew members, two from Malawi and one from Tanzania, were also on board, but there had been no contact from the vessel since it left Mbamba Bay, on the Tanzanian side of the lake, between 10am and 11am.

The Dutch foreign affairs ministry said the visitors were safely on land and had been given medical assistance, but did not give any further details of their condition, citing privacy concerns.

“Thanks to the search operation by the local authorities, in co-operation with the embassy, this worrying situation has thankfully been concluded.”

The speedboat belonged to a Tanzanian businessman, who alerted the authorities when he was unable to contact the crew and visitors on board, local news site the Nyasa Times reported.

Boats crossing the lake are required to register their arrival time with the port master 24 hours in advance, but this protocol was not followed. Local fishermen, boat operators and lakeshore communities were all urged to look out for the missing vessel during the search operation.

World.title: Prince Bernhard cashes out of real estate to go into AI

Prince Bernhard has sold his entire business portfolio, including his stake in the Zandvoort motor racing circuit, and will now focus on AI.

The first cousin of king Willem-Alexander told Dutch press agency ANP that he was selling his interest in Media Park in Hilversum, IT company Levi9, and his extensive real estate portfolio to his business partners.

“The world is changing faster than ever. New technologies, artificial intelligence, and major societal changes are creating opportunities that we could hardly have imagined ten years ago,” he said.

The 56-year-old did not disclose the amount of the sale, but business magazine Quote has estimated his net worth at around €160 million.

Bernhard’s large real estate holdings – 98 buildings according to Quote – have earned him the nickname pandjesprins, or the property prince.

In 2017, an investigation by Amsterdam newspaper Het Parool found that Bernhard’s companies engaged in practices that violated Amsterdam’s housing regulations.

Earlier this year, Bernhard announced he and his wife, Princess Annette, were separating after 25 years of marriage.

The prince bought the Zandvoort circuit 10 years ago with the aim of bringing Formula 1 back to the Netherlands. F1 racing returned to Zandvoort in 2021 after a 36-year absence, after the scheduled 2020 race was cancelled because of the coronavirus pandemic.

The final edition of the Dutch Grand Prix will be held later this year. Organisers announced in 2024 that they wouldn’t continue beyond the current contract because the costs were too high.

World.title: Manhunt launched after Dutch man found strangled in German hotel
World.content:
German police are urgently trying to trace the travel companion of a Dutch tourist who was found strangled in a hotel room close to the border.

The 35-year-old victim was discovered by staff on Sunday at Hotel Rheinpark in Rees, a German town about 30km south of Doetinchem.

A postmortem examination confirmed that the man had been strangled. He checked in to the hotel with another man on Saturday evening, but only the victim’s details were recorded in the guest register.

A murder inquiry was launched and forensic researchers spent several hours examining the room after the body was found at around noon, after the two guests failed to check out on time.

German media said the pair arrived on Saturday in a Dutch-registered car from the Enschede area.

Police are treating the man who checked in to the hotel room with the victim as the main suspect and have launched an urgent appeal to find him. They are also studying camera footage and trying to trace the two men’s route through phone data.

World.title: Sinking foundations could trigger €54bn housing repair bill
World.content:
More than 400,000 buildings in the Netherlands have problems with their foundations or are likely to develop them in the next 10 years, a government watchdog has warned.

Buildings are sinking for a combination of reasons, including falling groundwater levels, bacterial erosion, drought, structural faults and the impact of construction work. Earthquakes caused by gas drilling in Groningen have also destabilised houses in the northern province.

In around 120,000 cases the buildings are in urgent need of repair, the council for the environment and infrastructure (Rli) concluded in a report. If nothing is done the cost of repairing the damage could add up to €54 billion.

The problems have been made worse by the impact of climate change, Mandy Korff, foundations expert at the TU Delft university told Nu.nl. “If the groundwater level drops, whether through human activity or climate change, the ground level sinks and houses without foundation piles sink with it.”

Housing shortage

The Rli has called for new housing developments to be built on land that is solid enough to bear the load, but that will make it even more challenging to meet the government’s target of 100,000 new homes a year, which is one of the cabinet’s main priorities.

“Shortage of space is connected to the choices we make about accessibility, agriculture and where we need to build houses based on where people want to live,” Korff said.

Since April surveyors have been obliged to include details of the state of the foundations in homebuyers’ reports. Tamara Evers of SVn, a non-profit organisation that arranges loans for sustainable housing repairs, said the move was a step in the right direction, but foundation problems were not always visible.

She also questioned if homeowners should bear the responslbility for the repairws alone. “Some can afford to repair their homes, others can’t, and the question is whether if is fair to leave it to the individual homeowner when you consider all the different underlying causes.”

World.title: Two youths come forward over assault during Nijmegen Vierdaagse
World.content:
Two teenage boys have handed themselves in to police after a security guard was assaulted during last week’s four-day Vierdaagse walking festival in Nijmegen.

The guard suffered serious injuries when he was punched and kicked at a bicycle parking lot in Nijmegen’s Stationsplein during the night of Tuesday to Wednesday, police said.

Police said at least four people were involved in the assault and released photographs of the suspects with their faces blurred. They warned that their faces would be revealed if they did not come forward within a week.

The photographs of the two youths who came forward have since been taken offline.

No details were disclosed about what might have led to the attack.

It is one of several incidents to take place during this year’s Vierdaagse, the annual walking festival around the Gelderland city.

An 18-year-old man from Rotterdam was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of assaulting another man at the weekend.

Fatal shooting

On Saturday evening four teenagers and a 19-year-old youth were arrested for allegedly assaulting a girl on Molenstraat, while police also had to deal with a fight that broke out at a pavement café in Bloemerstraat in which tables and chairs were thrown.

On Tuesday night an 18-year-old man, also from Rotterdam, was fatally shot on Graafsweg, close to the festivities. He died of his injuries in hospital despite the efforts of paramedics and an air ambulance crew to resuscitate him.

Another 18-year-old man was arrested in connection with the shooting, which police said was not directly linked to the Vierdaagse events.

The city council stepped up security around the festival in response to the incidents by restricting the number of visitors and authorising police to carry out preventive stop-and-search checks.

World.title: What books to take for your summer holiday
World.content:
Are you getting ready for your summer holidays and trying to decide which book to take to read on the beach? We’ve got some suggestions for you.

Summer House with a Swimming Pool

Not to be too on the nose, but the book by famed Dutch writer Herman Koch is the perfect book for your beach bag. It brings together all of Koch’s best: unlikeable characters, an unreliable narrator, a page-turning plot and the complicated relationships between parents and children. Plus, it’s literally set during a summer holiday.

A disturbing summer holiday: Summer House With A Swimming Pool

Death on a Tiny Scale

The book follows the bumbling Tony Solano, a technical writer in London, as he travels abroad to close down the office he’s inherited from an unknown party. He hires a temporary assistant to help with the administration, as the Brit doesn’t speak a word of Dutch and is now faced with a lease, case files and an inadvertently adopted a cat. If you liked it, a second in the series has already been published and author Julie Broussely, a Brit who relocated to the Netherlands, is underway with the third.

Death on a Tiny Scale: a fun mystery with some small problems

The Ghost Ship

Want some romance with your pina colada? The Ghost Ship starts in the gallows, ends in the gallows and in between has swashbuckling lady pirates, forbidden romance and 16th century Amsterdam. Author Kate Mosse, widely known for her archaeological fiction novel Labyrinth, is the author of more than 10 historical fiction books.

Pirates, romance and a history lesson: The Ghost Ship

Bearer of Bad News

Going to the mountains instead of to the beach? Follow the adventures of mediocre hairdresser Lucy Rey just stumbled across the perfect wanted ad that will free her from a job she hates and a cheating boyfriend, or is there more to this post that has turned up on her social media feed? The book follows Rey from a miserable life in Las Vegas on an unexpected journey to the Italian mountains, where she’s been offered a job that seems too good to be true and turns out to be much more complicated and personal than she ever expected.

Bearer of Bad News: a quirky and funny read

The Goldfinch

If you are going to insist on something that will impress those passing by your cabana, The Goldfinch is the way to go. Donna Tartt, of The Secret History fame, partially sets her third novel in the Netherlands and the titular painting is a Dutch classic that (in real life) hangs in the Mauritshuis. The book follows 13-year old Theo Dekker as he survives a terrorist attack, steals the priceless art work and ends up in a hotel room in Amsterdam more than a decade later.

The Goldfinch: A hefty classic that is worth its weight in gold

The Diary Keepers

If you are one of those people who wants to learn something while you’re on holiday, author Nina Siegal dived into more than 2,000 personal diaries kept by the Dutch during World War II, combining excerpts to create a compelling day-by-day narrative of the Holocaust in the Netherlands. The book splices together a vivid account, sometimes presenting differing views of the same event, of a near-daily record of the war.

The Diary Keepers: eyewitness accounts of World War II

A decision to place a World War Two-era village under monument protection has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! UNESCO has added the modernist city centre of the Polish port city of Gdynia to its World Heritage List, recognising its interwar urban planning and architecture. The designation, approved during the World Heritage Committee’s 48th session in Busan, South Korea, is Poland’s 18th World Heritage site and comes as Gdynia marks the centenary of gaining city rights. In its justification, UNESCO referred to “an urban organism that harnesses a building-block-based planning approach to develop a characteristic, compact complex of modernist architecture, with robust individual architectural expressions”. Gdynia’s city centre “illustrates a critical break with historicism in the progression of turning the village of Gdynia into a new major sea gateway of the first Polish Republic between the First and Second World Wars”, it added. Granted city status in 1926, Gdynia was rapidly developed by the newly independent Polish state from a small fishing village into a major Baltic seaport, growing to more than 100,000 residents in under 20 years and providing Poland with a modern maritime gateway. It is now Poland’s 13th largest city by population, with just under 210,000 residents, and the third largest by area when including its maritime territory. Nowy tydzień zaczynamy od dobrych wieści! Komitet Światowego Dziedzictwa UNESCO oficjalnie uznał modernistyczne centrum Gdyni za dobro o wyjątkowym znaczeniu dla całego świata. Nie ma lepszego momentu niż 100-lecie Gdyni na to wyjątkowe wyróżnienie!https://t.co/L3WZZCJCAz — Gdynia (@MiastoGdynia) July 27, 2026 Oktawia Gorzeńska, Gdynia’s deputy mayor, who represented the city in Busan, celebrated the decision of the committee as “a wonderful gift for our anniversary and a tribute to the vision and determination of the people who created one of Europe’s great modernist cities”. The city’s mayor, Aleksandra Kosiorek, added that the decision “confirms that the vision which launched the history of modern Gdynia over a century ago has retained its power and universal significance.” Gdynia’s central district of Śródmieście was built largely between 1926 and 1939. Its rapid development at the time drew international attention, with a National Geographic reporter writing that “Poland dreams of building her New York”. Unlike Warsaw and nearby Gdańsk, it escaped extensive destruction during World War Two, preserving much of its original street layout and interwar architecture. According to the city authorities, UNESCO experts have recognised the Gdynia’s centre as one of the world’s most outstanding examples of early modernism in urban planning. The nomination also highlighted Gdynia’s distinctive model of modernist urban planning, setting it apart from contemporaneous developments such as Germany’s Bauhaus, Berlin’s housing estates, Kaunas in Lithuania and Tel Aviv. Gdynia’s modernist architecture is characterised by white façades and maritime-inspired details, including round windows and building forms resembling ship hulls. Gdańsk in Poland has been named a global City of Literature by @UNESCO. It is now one of only 63 such cities in the world, and the third in Poland to obtain the distinction https://t.co/QdMxlT65V4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2025 Notable examples include the so-called “bank building”, a modernist tenement block, and the Museum of Emigration, housed in the former Maritime Station, which from the 1930s until 1979 was a transit building from which thousands of Polish emigrants left for their new homelands. According to the city, the road to recognition took over 20 years, beginning in 2007, when the historic urban layout was entered into the regional register of monuments. It was designated a Monument of History in 2015, and Poland submitted the site to UNESCO’s Tentative List in 2019. Two sites in Poland were included in the inaugural World Heritage List in 1978: the Historic Centre of Kraków and the nearby Wieliczka and Bochnia Royal Salt Mines. Gdynia’s inscription is the 18th for Poland overall and the first for a Polish modernist urban complex. The most recent Polish additions before Gdynia were the Krzemionki Prehistoric Striped Flint Mining Region in 2019 and, in 2021, the beech forests in the Bieszczady Mountains. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s “shocking decision” not to sign into law the government’s planned windfall tax on excess profits by fuel companies amid a sharp surge in fuel prices caused by the war in Iran. While Nawrocki did not veto the bill, he exercised his right to refuse to sign it and instead send it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment, a process that can take years. The president argued that the retroactive nature of the tax “raises serious constitutional concerns”. Nowy podatek nie obniża cen paliwa. Ma przede wszystkim dostarczyć pieniędzy do budżetu. Nie mogę zaakceptować sytuacji, w której próbę łatania finansów państwa przedstawia się obywatelom jako ochronę ich interesów, podczas gdy skutkiem będzie kolejna fala podwyżek – Prezydent… pic.twitter.com/LqI7Cojdrr — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 In mid-June, the government approved a 60% tax on excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€927 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among others, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. The bill was approved by parliament on 3 July. It received support from Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, but was opposed by the right-wing and far-right opposition. According to a regulatory impact assessment, state energy giant Orlen is expected to account for about 60% of the tax base for the windfall tax, with the remaining 40% generated by other market participants. Poland’s government has approved a windfall tax on fuel companies' excess profits after the surge in energy prices due to the war in Iran. It expects the measure, which still requires parliamentary and presidential approval, to raise 4bn zloty (€940m) https://t.co/DpXa8VJDjf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 The legislation then passed to Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year. However, this time he instead exercised his right to refer the bill to the TK without either signing or vetoing it. In a speech announcing his decision on Friday, Nawrocki said that the proposed measures “raise serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that tax would be retroactive: it would go into force in August but would apply to revenue earned from the beginning of March. “In a democratic state governed by the rule of law, citizens and businesses must know what regulations apply at the time decisions are made,” said Nawrocki. “The state cannot change the rules a few months later and send a bill for actions taken in accordance with applicable law.” The president also argued that, ultimately, the costs of the tax would be passed on to consumers, who have already been paying much higher fuel costs since the government’s protective measures expired at the end of June. “Unfortunately, it appears that the government first lowered fuel prices for propaganda purposes, and now has decided to impose a hefty bill on Poles,” declared Nawrocki. Once a bill is sent to the TK for assessment, there is generally no time limit on how long the tribunal can take to consider it. In practice, this means that some cases can can remain unresolved for years. If the TK does find a bill to be constitutional, the president must sign it into law. Currently, a majority of judges on the TK, including its chief justice, were appointed by and are regarded as aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland until 2023 and which supported Nawrocki’s presidential candidacy last year. The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision not to approve the windfall tax was condemned by government figures, including finance minister Andrzej Domański, who accused the president of “once again striking against Poland’s public finances”. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increased tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. “Instead of standing on the side of Poles, he sided with fuel corporations reaping huge profits from the current situation on the fuel market,” wrote Domański on social media. Tusk, meanwhile, wrote that the president had “blocked a bill that would have allowed taxing the gigantic profits of fuel conglomerates, making it possible to fund cheaper fuel at our stations”. He told consumers to “remember this [when you are] at the fuel pumps”. In response, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, called Tusk an “economic dilettante” for thinking that imposing a tax would somehow lower costs rather than cause prices to rise. He instead called on the government to again lower VAT and excise duty on fuels. Od dawna wiadomo, że obecny premier jest gospodarczym dyletantem. Teraz próbuje przekonać Polaków, że nałożenie nowego podatku na paliwa sprawi, iż ceny na stacjach spadną. Zamiast nakładać kolejne podatki, proszę obniżyć VAT i akcyzę, tak jak robił to rząd Prawa i… https://t.co/3xvav6Dieu — Paweł Szefernaker 🇵🇱 (@szefernaker) July 25, 2026 The dispute over the tax comes as Poland faces an increasingly difficult fiscal situation. It had the second-largest budget deficit in the European Union last year, at 7.3% of GDP. That was far higher than the 5.5% the Polish government had pledged in 2024 when it was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Data released last week by Eurostat showed that, in the first quarter of 2026, Poland had the EU’s third-largest annual increase in debt-to-GDP ratio, at 4.5 percentage points. In March, credit rating agency Fitch, which last year switched Poland’s credit outlook to negative, warned that the “political gridlock” between the president and the government will continue to hinder policymaking, including tackling “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz (pictured above on the right), a prominent figure in the underground resistance that fought against the Soviet-installed communist authorities in the years after World War Two. Dziemieszkiewicz, who was killed by the communist security services in 1951 and dumped in an unmarked mass grave, was identified through a combination of historical detective work and genetic testing, including exhuming the remains of his deceased mother and sister to obtain DNA samples. “Once again, we can say that the communist authorities did not win. Heroes prevail,” declared Krzysztof Szwagrzyk, deputy head of the IPN. “Even in the most difficult situations, we must seek the truth, find those of whom no trace was supposed to remain, and restore their names.” While World War Two officially came to an end in 1945, tens of thousands of Poles, known as the “cursed soldiers” (żolnierze wyklęci), continued to fight against the Soviets and the communist regime they installed in Poland. While most had laid down arms by 1947, some continued fighting well beyond then, including Dziemieszkiewicz, who operated under the nom de guerre “Rój” (meaning “swarm”). Dziemieszkiewicz, who was 20 years old when the war ended, came from a family that had been part of Poland’s wartime resistance. His anti-communist views were hardened when his elder brother, Roman, was killed by Red Army soldiers in 1945. After being conscripted that year into the Soviet-backed Polish People’s Army, Dziemieszkiewicz defected and joined the underground resistance forces, where he rose to command a unit tasked with eliminating regime officials and members of the communist Polish Workers Party (PPR). Dziemieszkiewicz’s group killed around two dozen members of the communist security services and more than 20 informants, according to the IPN. In 1950, the communist authorities intensified efforts to dismantle Dziemieszkiewicz’s unit, using threats and blackmail to recruit hundreds of agents and informants in an effort to locate the resistance fighters. Eventually, one such informant gave up Dziemieszkiewicz’s location in exchange for a promise to release her parents from captivity. Dziemieszkiewicz found himself surrounded by several hundred soldiers and was killed while trying to escape. After his body had been identified by his family, Dziemieszkiewicz was buried in a section of Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw where the remains of those killed by the communist security services were placed en masse in unmarked graves. Exhumations by the IPN, which was established after the fall of communism to investigate communist and Nazi crimes in Poland, have located over 200 complete bodies at that site as well as several thousand bone fragments. During that work, one set of remains was found buried with an eagle symbol and remnants of a black cloth. IPN researchers realised that the item was similar to a beret that appeared in posthumous photographs of Dziemieszkiewicz’s body taken by the communist security services. That prompted them to carry out genetic testing on the remains and compare them to samples taken from Dziemieszkiewicz’s mother and sister, who were buried in a cemetery in the town of Maków Mazowiecki. “We have found ‘Rój’, commander of one of the longest-fighting units of the independence underground,” declared the IPN on Friday, announcing the confirmation of his identity. They described Dziemieszkiewicz as “legend in life and a symbol of the fight against communist oppression”. The identification was announced today during a press conference at @PrzystanekH. The identification is the result of many years of work carried out by the IPN. It was preceded by extensive archival and investigative research, the analysis of forensic evidence, archaeological… https://t.co/Rcf4wemJFc pic.twitter.com/XgMUAgSQc6 — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) July 24, 2026 At a conference announcing the findings, the IPN noted that Dziemieszkiewicz’s remains had been located right next to those of another prominent anti-communist resistance fighter, Zygmunt Szendzielarz, who fought under the nom de guerre “Łupaszko”. “It is an incredible situation that two great and distinguished soldiers of the Polish underground lie next to each other in this part of the Powązki Cemetery,” said Szwagrzyk. However, Szendzielarz, who was executed by the communist authorities in 1951, has a contested legacy, given evidence that his unit was involved in the massacre of dozens of Lithuanian civilians. Some other “cursed soldiers” have faced similar accusations of war crimes. While it was often IPN historians who uncovered evidence of such actions, the institution has more recently begun to honour those figures, particularly under the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice government between 2015 and 2023. Opposition MPs walked out of parliament yesterday as the chamber commemorated an underground officer who fought against Nazi-German occupation and the imposition of communism in Poland, but has also been accused of a war crime against civilians https://t.co/MIY7krOxTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 9, 2022 Dziemieszkiewicz himself, however, like most of the cursed soldiers, has not faced such accusations. In 2007, President Lech Kaczyński posthumously awarded Dziemieszkiewicz the Commander’s Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta, one of Poland’s highest honours. In 2020, his image was featured on a commemorative silver coin issued by the National Bank of Poland. Through a combination of brutal repression and offering amnesties, the communist authorities managed to end most resistance efforts by 1947. However, the last “cursed soldier” to die in combat, Józef Franczak, was killed in 1963, 18 years after the end of the war. World.title: Three quarters of Poles support cooperation with Ukraine against Russia despite historical dispute
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A new study shows that, while most Poles were angered by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s recent decision to name a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, they still overwhelmingly support cooperation with Ukraine and believe that Russia benefits from the dispute. The study, carried out by Polish state research agency CBOS, also finds that a large majority of Poles believe good relations with Ukraine will only be possible once historical issues are resolved. The polling was carried out this month in response to the ongoing diplomatic crisis that began in May, when Zelensky named a military unit after the “heroes of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA)”. The UPA is widely revered in Ukraine for its role in fighting against Moscow-backed Soviet rule. However, in Poland it is associated with the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians – mostly women and children – were slaughtered during World War Two, often with great brutality. Zelensky’s decision sparked anger in Poland, where the massacres are regarded as a genocide (though Ukraine strongly rejects that label). In June, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, Poland’s highest honour, which he had received in 2023. In its new survey, CBOS found that 59% of Poles support Nawrocki’s decision, while only 28% oppose it. However, they were divided over the consequences, with 41% saying it would bring Poland more losses than benefits and the exact same proportion saying the benefits would outweigh the costs. More broadly, 84% said the Polish state should react when another country glorifies historical figures responsible for crimes against Poles. However, when asked if Ukrainians have the right to honour their own historical heroes, even if those figures left a negative mark on Polish history, 44% agreed and 42% disagreed. At the same time, over three quarters of respondents (77%) said that good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past, but a similar proportion (73%) also believe that politicians on both sides “fuel conflicts between Poles and Ukrainians for their own political gain”. Poland has cautiously welcomed President @ZelenskyyUa's announcement of a five-point plan to alleviate the diplomatic crisis triggered by his earlier decision to name a military unit after a group that led massacres of Poles during WWII https://t.co/M3GXD9vtAr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 18, 2026 Yet the survey also showed that, for Poles, historical disputes have not displaced security concerns, and in particular the view that, for Poland and Ukraine, Russia is a shared enemy. Some 75% of respondents agreed with the statement that “Poland and Ukraine should, above all, cooperate in the face of the threat from Russia, rather than focus on the issues that divide them”. The most frequently cited priorities in relations with Kyiv were security cooperation (61%), building good neighbourly relations (46%), commemorating victims of the Volhynia massacres (43%), strengthening Poland’s regional leadership (41%), and ensuring Polish companies participate in Ukraine’s reconstruction (40%). Just over half of Poles (52%) agree that “Poland and Ukraine have more common aims and interests than conflicting ones”, while 32% disagreed. A huge majority (80%) agreed that “Russia benefits from the Polish-Ukrainian dispute”. W ocenie społecznej zdecydowanym priorytetem w relacjach z Ukrainą powinna być współpraca na rzecz bezpieczeństwa – wskazało ją 61% badanych.📊 ➡️Więcej w komunikacie #CBOS "Wokół polsko-ukraińskiego sporu o imponderabilia i nie tylko":https://t.co/pIvYbu8gyz#Ukraina #relacje pic.twitter.com/LOpmAKNnXn — CBOS (@CBOS_Info) July 23, 2026 Based on the answers in the survey, CBOS identified three broad groups of respondents classified by their views of the dispute. The largest, described as “moralists”, accounted for 46% and placed greater emphasis on historical grievances. Among this group, 99% supported Nawrocki’s decision and said good Polish-Ukrainian relations could not be built without addressing the past. “Pragmatists”, who made up 34% of respondents, placed greater emphasis on future cooperation. Some 96% said Poland and Ukraine should cooperate against the Russian threat rather than focus on historical disputes. The smallest group, labelled by CBOS as “withdrawn”, represented 20% of respondents who were more likely to lack a clear view on Polish-Ukrainian relations. Long-simmering tensions between Poland and Ukraine over WWII massacres have finally boiled over, prompting a diplomatic crisis.@danieltilles1 looks at how we got here and what it may mean for the two countries and Europe more broadly https://t.co/a8tiYJJHRr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 22, 2026 Recent weeks have seen moves from Ukraine towards finding a diplomatic solution to the crisis. In early July, foreign minister Andrii Sybiha visited Warsaw to propose an “anti-crisis package” of measures. Last week, Zelensky himself outlined a five-point plan to alleviate the dispute, including opening up Ukrainian historical archives and permitting more exhumations of victims of the massacres, most of whom remain buried in mass graves in Ukraine. The Polish authorities have cautiously welcomed Zelensky’s announcement, though also emphasise that they are waiting to see concrete action. Meanwhile, there is no indication that Zelensky will change his decision to name a unit after the heroes of the UPA. World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
