We cannot do what we do without your support. Keeping dogs and cats chained up at home will be banned in Poland from next year, after President Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill prohibiting the practice. His decision ends a long-running dispute over the issue, after Nawrocki last year vetoed a previous proposal to ban chaining because it also included what he argued were excessive and unrealistic additional measures on minimum kennel sizes for dogs. Zawetowana w listopadzie 2025 r. ustawa łańcuchowa była źle przygotowana i przeregulowana, ponieważ nakładała na obywateli obowiązki, których wielu nie byłoby w stanie spełnić. Dzisiaj otrzymujemy ustawę lepszą, z pozytywnym głosem takich podmiotów jak rolniczy samorząd.… pic.twitter.com/h7kIAI77KR — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 The new law bans owners from tethering dogs and cats at home. Animals must be kept either inside the house, in a fenced garden or, if that is not possible, in a kennel “large enough for the animal to move freely and satisfy its natural needs”. Dogs kept in kennels must be provided with daily exercise outside of it. Dogs and cats can still be put on leashes in certain situations, such as when they are being walked, but also during transport, while participating in shows, performances or training, if they are at vets or groomers, or if they represent a danger to humans or other animals. Those who are found to have violated the new law can be fined between 1,000 and 100,000 zloty (€232-23,166). If they are deemed to have acted with “extreme cruelty”, they can also face a prison sentence of up to five years, reports the Forsal news service. Now that the bill has been signed by Nawrocki, it will be published in the official Journal of Laws (Dziennik Ustaw), after which it goes into force 12 months later. The new measures represent a successful second attempt to introduce a leashing ban. A previous bill was approved by parliament last September. However, in December, Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition, announced that he was vetoing it. The president argued that, “although the intention – protecting animals – is just and noble, the law itself was poorly drafted”. In particular, he said that elements introducing minimum sizes for dog kennels were unrealistic and would “harm farmers, breeders and ordinary rural households”. After an attempt by parliament to overturn the veto failed, legislators went back to the drawing board and, following discussions with the president’s chancellery and animal rights groups, drafted a compromise bill that was approved by parliament earlier this month. The bill received support from the current ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, as well as most MPs from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. The far-right Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) voted against it. Thousands of people have protested in Warsaw against President @NawrockiKn's veto of a law that would have banned the chaining up of dogs Parliament will vote on Wednesday on whether to overturn Nawrocki's veto, which would require a three-fifths majority https://t.co/0GRup2sppb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 15, 2025 “We now have a better law, with positive feedback from entities such as the agricultural chamber,” said Nawrocki today. “It demonstrates that the pressure of the presidential veto makes sense. My previous decision to refuse to sign this bill forced the government and parliament to work harder.” However, although Nawrocki said the new law would no longer entail “rigid and costly requirements” for kennels, his office noted in a separate statement that the legislation requires the agriculture minister to issue a regulation establishing “minimum kennel area, taking into account the dog’s size”. It remains unclear if and how that would differ from the requirements Nawrocki previously vetoed. The presidential chancellery also noted that the law itself already outlines that kennels must be made of “wood or wood-like material with thermal insulation”, must be insulated from the ground, and must have openings on at least two sides to allow light and air to enter. A dog who throws a ball to passers-by from a balcony above one of Poland’s most famous streets and waits for them to throw it back has become a star. World.title: Nearly One in Five Prague Farmers’ Market Vendors Fail Veterinary Inspections
World.content:
Nearly one in five vendors inspected at Prague’s farmers’ markets during the first half of 2026 were found to have breached food safety or labeling regulations, according to the State Veterinary Administration (SVS).

Between January and June, veterinary inspectors checked 53 vendors across Prague and identified violations in 10 cases, representing almost 19 percent of all inspections.

Nationwide, inspectors carried out 165 inspections, with irregularities detected in 27 cases, or roughly 16 percent.

Officials said the most common problems in Prague involved improper storage temperatures for food of animal origin, incorrect or incomplete product labeling, and inadequate protection of food from contamination during sale.

Inspectors also highlighted several cases they considered particularly serious. In one instance, a vendor was found producing meat products without the legally required authorization while packaging them with the identification mark of a production facility that no longer exists. Authorities said such practices can mislead consumers about where products originate.



The SVS warned that food safety risks increase during the summer months, especially at outdoor markets where high temperatures make it more difficult to maintain proper cooling conditions.

Across the Czech Republic, labeling violations were the most frequently recorded offense this year, accounting for 26 cases. Problems related to hygiene and production practices—including incorrect storage temperatures and insufficient protection against contamination—followed with 22 cases.

Inspectors also documented 18 violations involving improper handling of food products and 12 cases where the origin of goods was unclear or could not be verified.

The SVS noted that a single inspection may uncover multiple breaches. While inspectors found violations in 27 inspections nationwide, the total number of individual offenses reached 82.

Inspection results remained largely unchanged compared with the same period last year. During the first six months of 2025, inspectors also carried out 165 inspections, finding violations in 16 percent of them. The main difference was that hygiene-related shortcomings topped the list last year, while labeling issues have become the most common problem in 2026.

Looking at the full year, the SVS carried out 380 market inspections across the Czech Republic in 2025, compared with 372 inspections in 2024. The proportion of inspections uncovering violations rose slightly from 17 percent to 18 percent.

World.title: Not an Official Visit: Petr Pavel Attends Hungarian GP as F1 Photographer
World.content:
The president of the Czech Republic, Petr Pavel, has made his way to the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday – but was not an official visit.

Ever wondered what world leaders do in their free time? For Czech Republic president Petr Pavel, the answer is sports photography – and he’s particularly passionate about motorsport.

This weekend, he was attending the Hungarian GP with a full photography kit – and an official FIA accreditation. He arrived at the Hungaroring for Saturday’s sessions and was already taking pictures, accompanied by Czech F1 photographer Jiri Krenek.



This wasn’t the first time he was seen at a major motorsport event as a hobby photographer. Most recently, Pavel travelled to France in June to attend the Le Mans 24 Hours, once again equipped with full camera gear.

In fact, the former NATO Military Chairman has attended several races on both two and four wheels over the years.

Within the Czech Republic, Pavel covered the MotoGP and World Superbike events at Brno, while he has travelled as far as the US and Saudi Arabia to photograph NASCAR and the Dakar Rally respectively.

Last year, he also raised nearly 30,000 euros for a charity dedicated to children, single parents and the elderly by auctioning a photo album.

While it is unusual for politicians to attend races purely for leisure, several leaders regularly appear at major motorsport events in their own countries.

Last year, then British Prime Minister Keir Starmer hosted F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, drivers and senior team figures at a reception in 10 Downing Street ahead of the British GP.

World.title: Best Petting Zoos in Prague for Families with Kids (2026 Guide)
World.content:
Prague Zoo gets all the attention — and fair enough, it’s consistently ranked among the top zoos in the world — but the city is also full of smaller, low-key spots where kids can get hands-on with animals.

These mini farms and forest parks are perfect for a relaxed weekend outing, most are free or nearly free, and several are just a short metro ride from the centre.

Here’s our pick of the best small zoos and petting farms around Prague.

1. Milíčovský dvůr – Prague 11

Right on the edge of Milíčov forest, this outdoor farm is home to a horse, an ostrich, a fox, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits and more. Feed dispensers let kids feed the animals directly, and there’s a sandpit, a wooden playground and a small snack stand on site. Entry costs just 20 CZK. Closed Mondays.

📍 K Milíčovu 100/8, Prague 11 — nearest metro: Háje



2. Chuchle Grove Mini Zoo – Prague 5

Set on a hillside inside the Chuchle Grove nature park, this zoo run by Prague’s city forestry service cares for injured and orphaned wildlife. Expect to see mouflons, deer, wild boar, owls, lynxes and more — though petting isn’t allowed here, since the focus is conservation and education. Free entry, open 24/7, with a playground and refreshment kiosk nearby

📍 V Lázních 8, Prague 5

3. Station of Young Biologists – Prague 5

A mix of indoor and outdoor spaces near Anděl, with a tropical terrarium (crocodiles, monkeys, boas), an aviary, and outdoor pens with kangaroos, llamas, ponies and goats. Regular workshops and interactive shows run alongside the animal exhibits. General entry is free; the terrarium and greenhouses cost a small fee (20–40 CZK).

📍 Drtinova 1A, Prague 5 — near Anděl metro

4. Toulcův dvůr – Prague 10

An 8.5-hectare environmental education centre in Hostivař with cows, horses, chickens, pigs, sheep and goats, plus a cherry orchard, wetlands and a farm-to-table restaurant. Petting and feeding aren’t permitted, but it’s a beautifully kept site for a nature walk.

📍 Kubátova 1/32, Prague 10

Honourable mentions

If you’re just after a nice walk with a chance of spotting animals, these free spots are worth a detour:

Wild Garden Hostivař (Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk.

(Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk. Kunratice Forest (Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails.

(Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails. Kamýk Forest (Prague 12) — a small goat enclosure and pheasant aviary tucked next to the gamekeeper’s lodge, surrounded by walking and cycling trails.

World.title: Stromovka: A Green Paradise in the Heart of Prague
World.content:
Stromovka is one of the largest and most popular parks in Prague, drawing visitors with its beautiful nature, rich history, and numerous activities.

Let’s explore what Stromovka offers and how to get there.

Why Visit Stromovka?

Looking for a break from the city’s hustle and bustle or the perfect spot for a picnic with friends? Stromovka is your ideal choice. This vast park features green meadows, shady alleys, and ample opportunities for sports and cultural events.

What is Stromovka?

Stromovka, officially known as Královská obora, spans more than 95 hectares, making it one of Prague’s largest green spaces. Located in Prague 7, the park is a favorite among joggers, cyclists, families, and anyone looking to escape into nature without leaving the city.

It’s perfect for walks, picnics, sports, or simply relaxing on the grass.



A Brief History

Stromovka’s history dates back to the 13th century when it was established as a royal hunting ground. Over time, it evolved and expanded, becoming a public park in the 19th century. The park is home to the original Vltava Creek and several ponds, which host various water birds.

Throughout its history, Stromovka has undergone many changes, shaping it into the popular relaxation spot it is today.

Activities in Stromovka

Stromovka offers a wide range of activities for all ages. Here are some ideas:

Walking and Running: Enjoy the scenic trails.

Cycling: Explore the park on two wheels.

Picnics: Large meadows and shady spots are perfect for a picnic.

Sports: Play football, volleyball, and other sports.

Cultural Events: Attend various events hosted in the park.

How to Get to Stromovka

By Metro: The nearest metro station is Nádraží Holešovice (line C). From there, it’s just a few minutes’ walk to Stromovka.

By Tram: Trams also reach the park. The nearest stops are Výstaviště Holešovice (lines 6, 12, 17) and Planetarium Prague (line 6).

By Bike: Cycling enthusiasts can easily access Stromovka by bike. Bike-sharing stations like Rekola and Nextbike are available around the park, allowing you to ride directly into this natural haven.

World.title: August 12-31: Prague to Host Festival of New Circus Letní Letná
World.content:
The international festival of new circus and theatre, Letní Letná 2026, will take place in Prague on August 12-31.

The festival will feature over 200 performances, workshops, concerts, and various acts by circus artists from 14 countries, including a special program for children.

This year marks the 23rd edition of the festival. Letenské sady park will once again be the main venue, with tents set up to create a mini-town complete with a coffee shop and an evening bar.



Many performances will be free of charge. Additionally, the festival will offer a rich and varied daily program: children’s shows, circus, juggling and acrobat workshops, music concerts, exhibitions, lectures, creative workshops, and more.

One of this year’s highlights is Wolf by Australia’s renowned Circa ensemble. The international lineup also includes Switzerland’s Accademia Teatro Dimitri, presenting its graduate production La Grinta, and Seismic, a collaboration between French choreographer Marie Gourdain and German artist Felix Baumann, featuring Czech performers.

The Czech program includes the premiere of Vertige by AirGym Art Company, Enola by Eliška Brtnická, new productions from Losers Cirque Company, and Hey, Earth! by Cirque La Putyka.

Emerging talent will also take center stage, with performances by CZirkidz Dance Company, Teens Cirkabaret, and recent graduates of international circus schools.

Audiences will have the chance to experience works in progress, including K voknu by Michaela Stará and Filip Zahradnický, followed by discussions with the artists.

For adults, Světla a stíny by Silk&Steel explores the darker sides of human experience through aerial and ground acrobatics, while family-friendly performances include the popular (Not Only) Juggling Galashow and Orbiting Zero by Czech juggler Aleš Hrdlička.

Beyond the performances, visitors can enjoy free workshops, children’s activities, concerts, open-air events, food stalls, bars, and relaxation areas throughout the festival grounds. Babysitting is available during selected performances, and the venue is fully accessible, making Letní Letná a festival for all ages.

World.title: New Railway Tunnel to Cut Prague to Pilsen Journey to 45 Minutes
World.content:
The Czech government has approved the next phase of one of its largest railway infrastructure projects: a new tunnel connecting Prague and Beroun.

Construction is expected to begin in 2032, with completion scheduled for 2044.

The 24.7-kilometre double-track tunnel will significantly shorten travel times on one of the country’s busiest rail corridors.

Once completed, trains will travel between Prague-Smíchov station and Beroun in around 13 minutes, reducing the current journey time by more than 30 minutes.

The project will also improve connections towards western Czechia and neighbouring Germany. The journey from Prague to Pilsen is expected to take approximately 45 minutes, while international rail services to Munich and Nuremberg will become faster and more reliable.



New railway line designed for speeds of up to 200 km/h

The planned railway route will include a new high-speed section designed for trains travelling at up to 200 km/h. The tunnel will begin near Prague-Smíchov station, pass beneath the Barrandov area, and emerge near Beroun.

A separate connection on the Prague side is also planned, linking the new line with Braník Bridge and Prague-Krč. The additional infrastructure will improve connections within the capital while increasing capacity on the wider railway network.

Construction preparation underway

Preparatory work for the tunnel is already in progress. Geological surveys and technical documentation are currently being completed, with the application for a construction permit expected to be submitted between 2028 and 2029.

After the approval process, Správa železnic will launch a tender to select the construction company responsible for building the tunnel.

The Czech Railway Administration estimates the total cost of the project will continue to rise due to inflation and increasing construction expenses. However, its director general Tomáš Tóth said the estimated cost of around CZK 3 billion per kilometre remains comparable with similar railway tunnel projects abroad.

The project is expected to increase railway capacity towards western Czechia, improve timetable reliability, and strengthen connections between Prague, Pilsen, and major German cities.

World.title: Future of Prague’s Výtoň Bridge Could Be Decided by the End of This Year
World.content:
The Railway Administration (Správa železnic) is expected to decide on the future design of Prague’s Výtoň Railway Bridge by the end of this year.

If the final plan is approved, construction could begin in 2028.

The long-delayed project has become the centre of a dispute between transport authorities and heritage experts. While railway officials argue that a new three-track structure is necessary to meet future transport demands, conservationists continue to push for the preservation of the existing historic bridge.

The Railway Administration has warned that the current condition of the bridge requires a final decision soon.

Dispute over historic structure

The main proposal currently under consideration is the construction of a new three-track railway bridge. Správa železnic selected a project team last year, but the plan remains controversial due to opposition from heritage authorities and groups seeking to preserve the original structure.

The debate has also attracted international attention. UNESCO representatives are preparing a Heritage Impact Assessment (HIA), which will examine how the planned changes could affect Prague’s cultural heritage.

The Transport Association supports the construction of a new bridge, arguing that rebuilding the existing structure would be more expensive and would not provide enough additional capacity.

Construction could start in 2028

According to earlier plans from Správa železnic, work on the project was originally expected to begin sooner. A tender process was completed in 2025, with companies SUDOP Praha and TOP CON SERVIS selected for the preparation of the three-track bridge project.

The estimated cost of the entire project is around CZK 3.4 billion.

Because of the bridge’s deteriorating condition, trains currently operate on only one track and must reduce speed when crossing the structure. The construction of the additional third track alone is expected to cost approximately CZK 129 million.

World.title: Countdown: Moby takes the stage at Budapest Park this Saturday – photos
World.content:
In just a few days, on August 1, Moby will return to Budapest for the first time in fifteen years. The electronic music icon is currently in the midst of his major European tour, performing at historic venues, legendary festivals, and sold-out shows across the continent- with Budapest Park as the next stop.

Moby returns to Budapest

The tour kicked off in late June and has already travelled across Europe, combining headline concerts with appearances at some of the continent’s most renowned festivals. Headline shows have taken place in Istanbul, Luxembourg, Belgrade, and the historic Pula Arena, while festival appearances have included Release Athens, Rock Werchter, Montreux Jazz Festival, Bospop, Butterfly Dance, ICÓNICA SANTALUCÍA Sevilla Fest, Mad Cool Festival, Jazz Open Stuttgart, Jazz Open Modena, Colours of Ostrava, PhillGood Festival, and Brighton’s On The Beach Festival.

Source: DANIJEL BARTOLIĆ / NUNU MEDIA

Audience demand has been extraordinary: the Luxembourg concert sold out weeks in advance, as did the iconic Pula Arena show, followed by a sold-out performance at Brighton’s On The Beach Festival. The tour continues to gather momentum, with upcoming shows in Vilnius, Dresden, London, and Dublin already announced as sold out well ahead of their dates.

Audiences have been gathering for one reason: to experience live the songs that have shaped generations of music lovers. Classics such as Porcelain, Natural Blues, Why Does My Heart Feel So Bad?, Lift Me Up, and Extreme Ways remain as powerful as ever, while Moby’s latest album, Future Quiet, reveals a more intimate and contemplative side of his artistry.

Source: DANIJEL BARTOLIĆ / NUNU MEDIA

Nostalgia and the present

According to the artist himself, however, this tour is not about the new album. As Moby recently explained in an interview, the shows are more like a “Moby Greatest Hits Festival,” where audiences can experience energetic, rave-inspired live performances of his best-known songs in fresh new arrangements. Making the experience even more personal, Moby invited fans on Instagram to help shape the setlist by sharing which songs they would most like to hear performed live. At Budapest Park, nostalgia and the present will come together for one unforgettable evening.

Source: DANIJEL BARTOLIĆ / NUNU MEDIA

Moby’s return is about more than music. For over three decades, he has remained a passionate advocate for animal rights, environmental protection, and conscious living, while continuing to create music that resonates with millions around the world. Few artists can fill festival grounds with tens of thousands of fans while speaking with such authenticity about the causes they believe in.

The Budapest concert will be one of the highlights of the European tour, with a limited number of tickets still available.

Source: DANIJEL BARTOLIĆ / NUNU MEDIA

World.title: The end draws near for Lake Velence as Danube hits a record low in Budapest: will Hungary dry out this year?
World.content:
Never before has there been so little water in the Danube at Budapest, and the consequences are not only visible to the naked eye — for instance, you can walk down into the river’s former bed at Margaret Bridge — but could also, in some cases, cause problems for the drinking-water supply, while at the same time crippling river tourism. If the drought continues, then Lake Velence as we know it will cease to exist within days, with the once continuous expanse of water breaking up into a series of small pools, and disaster looming for wildlife.

Lake Velence as we know it may disappear by August

According to a Telex report, the Tisza government has not yet been able to decide how the situation at Lake Velence could be resolved — at considerable financial cost (though there is a plan). The lake, once famous for its beaches, rich wildlife, festivals, sporting events and high property prices, has seen tourism disappear and the lake itself is dying; plans are already under way to rescue its wildlife.

Water disappearing from Lake Velence. Photo: Facebook/Élhető Velence Egyesület

If the current drought persists — and there is no sign whatsoever to the contrary — then, according to calculations by experts at the Ministry for the Living Environment, Lake Velence as we know it, the one taught about in schools, will cease to exist by August. The water surface will split into several smaller pools, and the authorities may at most be able to ensure that these bodies of water remain linked in some form. But the problem is greater than that: with the help of the National Fishing Association, they will likely have to organise how to remove the fish from the dying lake.

No decision on water replenishment

Lake Velence is one of our shallow lakes, and one particularly affected by climate change, warming and prolonged drought. It is no surprise that it has dried up before; according to recollections, exercises were even held in its bed in the years after the change of regime. Since then, however, an entire industry has settled beside the lake, so a solution to replenishing the water must be found one way or another. Yet no decision has been made on full rehabilitation either in the newly formed ministry or in government, and “the planning and professional consultation phase is still under way”.

The ministry’s press spokesman also indicated that they simply cannot find the plan previously presented for saving Lake Velence by Zoltán Tessely, the area’s Fidesz MP. That document allegedly put the cost at 40 billion forints.

In addition, a national water inventory is under way, with the participation of the National Water Directorate and civil organisations; this could be completed around September-October. On that basis, it will then be possible to decide whether changes to agricultural production may be needed, as there may no longer be enough water available for profitable farming.

You can now casually walk through one of the biggest rivers in Hungary due to excessive drought

Another heat dome is on the way

The heat and drought causing our rivers and lakes to dry up do not appear to be easing. After June’s record heat, another heat dome — a high-pressure anticyclone — is now approaching, bringing 36-38C, perhaps even 40C, and completely rain-free weather from Wednesday. According to 24.hu, the heatwave will not be long-lasting, but it is certain to last until 5 August, that is, next Wednesday. Then a cold front will arrive, easing the heat to 29-34C, in other words, to what would count as pleasantly warm summer weather. However, meteorologist László Molnár, quoted by the paper, said that we should not expect any significant rainfall in the period that follows.

Prepare again for 40 degrees! Photo: Facebook/MÁV-csoport

Danube at record low in Budapest

The water level of the Danube in Budapest is at a record low: the gauge showed 31 centimetres on Tuesday morning, according to the morning data on the water management website of the National Water Directorate (OVF). According to the figures, the river’s lowest previous level was 33 centimetres, MTI reports.

River Danube also facing severe water shortage. Photo: Facebook/Fővárosi Vízművek

They also said the lowest recorded water level had been exceeded at several Danube gauges managed by the authority: at 8am, the level at Vác was 2cm below the previous minimum, at the Kvassay sluice in Budapest it was 10cm lower, at Tass, at the Tassi sluice, 4cm lower, and at Dunaújváros 5cm lower. At Nagymaros the water level was still 2cm above the previous low, and at Ercsi 4cm above it, but these negative records are expected to be broken there too.

They added that forecasts do not predict any significant rainfall in the catchments over the coming period; on the contrary, another warm spell is due, which will increase evaporation. The authority is continuing to use all available means to mitigate the harmful effects of water shortage, but without rain the water resources on hand are steadily diminishing.

Alarming: Almost 90% of Hungary now affected by moderate or severe drought

World.title: Shot fired after two men brawled in a car park in Budapest
World.content:
Two men brawled in the car park of a fast-food restaurant in Pesterzsébet, Budapest, on Sunday, with one allegedly firing a shot from a gas signal weapon before being arrested by police nearby, authorities said on Monday.

According to investigators, the 30-year-old man, identified as Attila G., exchanged words with another man in the car park of a hospitality venue in Pesterzsébet before the pair came to blows. During the altercation, Attila G. produced a gas signal weapon and fired one shot, prompting alarm among customers and witnesses, police said.

He fled the scene to a nearby bakery, where district officers arrested him within minutes and recovered the weapon along his route. The other participant drove away in a car before patrols arrived and is still being sought. The man was taken to the XX and XXIII District Police Headquarters in Budapest and questioned on suspicion of violent disorder committed while armed.

World.title: Large Slovak Roma families living in extreme poverty relocated to Northern Hungary with political approval? – video, updated
World.content:
In the village of Szalonna, in Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén county, two large Slovak Roma families living in deep poverty have appeared seemingly out of nowhere. According to local rumour, the mayor of Kassa (Košice) purchased houses for them in order to “be rid” of the families and proceed with demolishing a nearby slum of illegal shacks on the outskirts of the city. Several voices have already spoken out against the alleged “relocations”, but there has as yet been no response from the Hungarian government.

Large Slovak Roma families in deep poverty arriving in Hungary?

According to a report by RTL News, the Slovak Roma families—who do not speak Hungarian—have turned up without prior notice in Szalonna, a settlement already severely affected by poverty, unemployment, and social and material deprivation. Local residents have made clear they do not wish to live alongside the newcomers, a concern they have also raised with the mayor, who himself claims to have had no prior knowledge of the situation.

RTL News reports that Lenka Kovacevicova, the mayor of Kassa/Košice, recently began dismantling a shanty settlement on the outskirts of the city. She has stated that suitable “alternative housing” has been secured for those living there without heating, running water, or electricity.

According to the assurances given, the families settling in Szalonna will continue to attend school and work in Kassa/Košice, though this has been met with scepticism locally. Mihály Dancs, head of the National Roma Self-Government in Hungary, said it was clear that the mayor of Kassa/Košice was purchasing low-cost properties in Hungary in order to relocate what he described as “problematic” families. He added that a further 30 people could arrive shortly. He and Szalonna’s mayor, Zsolt Balogh, are due to travel to Kassa/Košice next Monday to seek clarification in person.

Another mayor raises alarm, urges residents not to sell

Szalonna’s mayor is not alone in voicing concern. Gergely Mikola, the young mayor of nearby Encs, took to Facebook to urge residents not to sell their properties and not to facilitate what he described as “deportations”.

The proportion of gypsy society in Hungary is increasing

Mikola claims the relocations are taking place “with Slovak political approval and funding provided by NGOs”, and that between 200 and 300 Slovak Roma could be “shifted” into Hungary, specifically into the districts of Encs, Edelény, Gönc and Szikszó.

He argues that while the scheme may appear orderly on paper, so-called voluntary departures are being incentivised through the provision of free housing, leaving the families effectively destitute regardless. Meanwhile, the receiving districts are already struggling to support residents living in hardship. The local authority therefore plans to register pre-emption rights on affected properties and is in ongoing talks with local Roma leaders to ensure a coordinated response.

The mayor also shared an image illustrating the living conditions from which these families are expected to arrive.

Update — Mayor of Szalonna: Kassa/Košice is not running a social relocation scheme

According to information received from the Košice city hall, the Slovak city is not operating any programme aimed at relocating socially disadvantaged residents to other settlements — including ones in Hungary — Zsolt Balogh, the independent mayor of the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén county village, told the Hungarian news agency on Monday evening.

In a statement, Mr Balogh said he had met in Szalonna the mayor of one district of Košice, who said that the district he leads had supported efforts to improve the living conditions of two families, for example by making their properties habitable. The two families, he added, had in any case bought property in Szalonna of their own accord, using loans and purchasing from local owners.

The statement said Mr Balogh had asked whether the municipality should expect the arrival of more families in similar circumstances, and was told by the Košice district mayor that there was no such intention, and that the support concerned only those two families.

According to MTI, Szalonna is to adopt an “identity” decree at an extraordinary council meeting, including measures intended to prevent this kind of settlement. Mr Balogh has also already discussed the matter with the lord mayor of Košice, who said the authorities wanted to resolve the problems locally, and that assistance to the two families had been the independent initiative of the district leader.

World.title: PM Péter Magyar: Tisza Party hits the road again, new campaign begins?
World.content:
The Tisza Party does not intend to distance itself from the people after its election victory and will hit the road again, travelling across the country, the prime minister said in a speech before the start of Monday’s parliamentary session.

Citing recent survey figures, Magyar said his party now has some 4.5 million active supporters, adding that no party had enjoyed such a broad base of support since the change of system 36 years ago. He added that people had placed enormous trust in Tisza, but this also entailed enormous responsibility to ensure the party did not distance itself from the people and listened to them after Tisza’s election victory.

The prime minister said the nationwide tour will take them back to the smallest settlements, markets, railway stations, squares, and streets, where they will report on their work, listen to complaints about where the state is failing, and work with the people to define the tasks ahead.

Magyar urged Tisza Island members to prepare for joint work. Referring to the party’s grassroots organisations, he said: “We started with the Tisza Islands, we won together on April 12, and building a functional and humane Hungary can only succeed with them, with those millions of Hungarian people,” he said.

Interim President Forsthoffer: Sándor Palace to reopen for visits

The presidential Sandor Palace will reopen to visitors from 1 to 8 August, the speaker of parliament, exercising the powers of the president, announced on Monday on her Facebook page. Agnes Forsthoffer wrote that the building has “not only a romantic past but also a present rooted in its historical significance”, and encouraged visitors to explore the palace’s representative rooms with a guided tour. Visitors will also hear special chapters from the palace’s 220-year history, she added.

She noted that registration for the Open Doors programme series is available on the Sándor Palace website.

Registered visitors can tour the building’s representative rooms in early classicist style and get acquainted with its history, including the mysterious Roman sarcophagus, the enigmatic death of Prime Minister Pál Teleki, the behind-the-scenes secrets of the salons, and the mystical additional meanings of the furniture and statues, according to the website.

The programme is open to individual visitors or groups of up to 20 people (or 30 on August 8). If a registered group is smaller, it may be combined with other groups or individual visitors for the same tour, it added.

Goal to build ‘truly functional, humane’ country

The government is working to complete the ruling Tisza Party’s commitments to building “a truly functional and humane Hungary” in which “the everyday security, livelihood, and dignity” of citizens are ensured, PM Magyar said ahead of the agenda in parliament on Monday.

Concerning the government’s measures, the prime minister said VAT on prescription medications will be eliminated from Sept 1, adding that “there is no household in Hungary that the move will not affect.” Some 4 million people in Hungary regularly take prescription drugs “and many have been in a situation in which they had no money to buy the prescribed product.”

Turning point in the polls: Orbán may welcome latest survey — are voters really punishing Péter Magyar?

Meanwhile, he said the government had launched a programme to assist some 400,000 children with a school-start aid of 100,000 forint (EUR 277) each. The government will also reduce VAT on firewood from 27 percent to 5 percent, because families heating their homes with wood were “left out of the previous government’s household utility price cap scheme“, the prime minister said.

“These measures are aimed at eliminating the injustice of oligarchs in the middle of Europe getting rich on the money snatched away from millions of Hungarians,” Magyar said.

World.title: Orbán government promised Chinese BYD vast subsidies and influx of thousands of guest workers
World.content:
Hungary’s previous government pledged substantial financial support for BYD’s planned investment in Szeged, a parliamentary state secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said in a video posted on Facebook on Monday.

‘Guest workers and generous subsidies’

György László Velkey stated that, according to documents held by the ministry, the Hungarian state committed more than 70 billion forints in infrastructure support for the area where BYD is set to establish operations. In addition, the government offered significant direct financial assistance to the company, although the precise sum remains a commercial secret.

Former PM Orbán with the head of the BYD, Wang Chuanfu, in Budapest. Photo: Facebook/Orbán Viktor

“I can say, however, that the scale is comparable to the funding provided for the CATL factory in Debrecen,” the state secretary noted, according to MTI.

It also emerged that BYD has been granted permission to bring in around 10,000 guest workers—almost as many as the number of jobs the investment is expected to create, he added.

Inside a BYD car. Photo: FB/Orbán

Talks with BYD leadership

Péter Stumpf, parliamentary state secretary at the Ministry for Rural and Regional Development and MP for the area, said in the same video that residents of Szeged have three key expectations regarding the project.

They expect the company to comply fully with existing legislation—particularly environmental regulations—so as not to endanger public health; to provide well-paid jobs for local residents and Hungarian workers; and to ensure that Szeged benefits from the company’s economic success.

“It appears that Péter Szijjártó, the former minister for foreign affairs and trade, and Fidesz did not represent these interests during the negotiations,” Stumpf said.

Revealed: How Russian intelligence recruits Hungarian youth – and gets away with it

Mr Velkey concluded by stressing that the current government would negotiate with the Chinese company—and with all foreign partners—solely with the interests of Szeged’s residents and the Hungarian people in mind.

Szeged Mayor László Botka at the BYD construction site in 2024. Photo: FB/László Botka

Former foreign minister joins BYD

Mr Szijjártó recently announced that he would resign his parliamentary seat and join BYD as an international executive responsible for global external relations and the development of new business divisions.

The former minister, who has been attending a world championship event in the United States, described his new contract on Facebook as “the signing of the year”. However, many—even within Fidesz—have reportedly viewed the move as a betrayal at a difficult time for the political community.

World.title: Middle Eastern airline resumes Budapest flights earlier than expected
World.content:
Flydubai is to resume its direct flights to Budapest from July 31, the airline announced on Monday in a statement to Hungary’s state news agency MTI.

The carrier said the route would restore a direct air link between Hungary and the United Arab Emirates, offering seamless access to Dubai as well as to its global network of more than 120 destinations. In June, when the company decided to cancel all flights they talked about an August restart.

Flights between Budapest and Dubai will operate three times a week — on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays — from July 31. The frequency is set to increase to a daily service from October 25, 2026.

Since its launch in 2009, flydubai has carried more than 137 million passengers. The airline currently operates a fleet of 97 Boeing 737 aircraft, the Hungarian news agency wrote.

World.title: World’s third public statue of Freddie Mercury unveiled on Lake Balaton – but it bears a striking resemblance to a Hungarian poet
World.content:
The first public statue of Queen legend Freddie Mercury in Hungary has been unveiled on the shores of Lake Balaton, in what is – somewhat surprisingly – only the third such monument in the world.

The statue was inaugurated on Saturday evening in Balatonszemes, a lakeside town that has hosted an annual Queen fan camp for the past 32 years, organised by the Queen Fan Club Cultural Association – making the choice of location a natural one. More curious, however, is the observation that the sculpture bears a remarkable likeness to a celebrated Hungarian poet.

According to a report by Blikk, the project was realised as a joint venture between the association and the local council. Among the guests at the unveiling was Peter Freestone, Mercury’s former personal assistant. The rights to Mercury’s name and legacy, currently managed by Sony Music, were also formally cleared for the statue in an official letter.

“This is my second visit to this wonderful place, where I have once again been able to meet Hungarian Queen fans in person,” said Freestone, who spent 12 years as Mercury’s assistant, close friend and confidant. He first visited Hungary for an exhibition in Budapest. He added that he appreciated the artist’s decision to depict not the flamboyant performer on stage, but a more reflective and quietly brilliant figure.

This year will mark the 33rd Queen camp in Balatonszemes, commemorating both what would have been Mercury’s 80th birthday on 5 September 2026 and Queen’s legendary 1986 concert in Budapest.

As for the Hungarian poet many believe is echoed in the statue’s features, the answer is Attila József.

One thing, however, is certain: in 1986, Freddie Mercury even sang in Hungarian – and the footage still survives.

World.title: Four bears to be transferred from Romania's Libearty Sanctuary to wildlife park in France
World.content:
Four rescued brown bears from Romania's Libearty Sanctuary in Zărnești will be relocated to a wildlife park in France as part of an international conservation partnership, Agerpres reported. The transfer, involving four young sibling bears, was described by the sanctuary's operator as an unprecedented operation for Romania.

The Millions of Friends Association (AMP), which manages the sanctuary, said the bears, named Alexandra, Anita, Chance, and Thomas, are about two and a half years old and were rescued from the wild.

They will be transported by road to Parc Animalier de Sainte-Croix after being sedated, with the journey expected to take more than a day.

“Four bears rescued from the wild and now in our care will leave Romania together for a park in France. […] It is an unprecedented transfer for AMP Libearty and a unique event for Romania," the association said.

According to AMP, as quoted by the news agency, the relocation has been planned in detail to ensure the animals' safety throughout the journey.

The organization said that the French park shares a similar vision focused on wildlife conservation and environmental education.

Parc Animalier de Sainte-Croix spans 120 hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals from 100 European wildlife species. In addition to its conservation work, the park offers visitors the opportunity to stay overnight in cabins within the park and observe the animals from close range, according to Agerpres.

World.title: Revolut opens private market funds to retail investors in Romania
World.content:
Revolut said that it launched access to private market funds for individual investors in Romania, allowing eligible customers to invest in private equity, private credit, and infrastructure assets through its app. The funds are managed by Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane, and Partners Group and are structured under the European Union’s ELTIF 2.0 framework.

Private market investments have traditionally been dominated by institutional investors, partly because minimum commitments can exceed EUR 100,000 and because products often involve complex documentation, capital calls, and long lock-up periods.

Revolut said the new offering is aimed at experienced investors with a long-term investment horizon and is intended to lower some of those entry barriers. Management and performance fees may apply.

The four asset managers included in the initial offering collectively manage or oversee more than USD 2.8 trillion in assets, according to the fintech company. Revolut said its internal fund selection team assesses each product’s strategy, performance history, operational resilience, and ability to withstand different market cycles.

“For a long time, private markets have been missing from the average investor’s portfolio, not because of a lack of interest, but because of a lack of access,” said Rolandas Juteika, Revolut’s head of wealth and trading for the European Economic Area. “By partnering with firms such as Apollo, Ares, Hamilton Lane, and Partners Group, we are changing that dynamic.”

The funds will use the ELTIF 2.0 structure, which was designed to broaden access to long-term investments across the EU. The products offered through Revolut will be evergreen funds, meaning investors can put money into an existing portfolio rather than waiting for capital to be deployed gradually.

However, the company warned that the investments remain fundamentally illiquid despite offering periodic redemption windows. Withdrawals are not guaranteed and may be limited or suspended under the terms of each fund.

“These funds are deliberately structured for long-term capital, reflecting the underlying nature of private assets,” Juteika said.

Revolut said investors should be prepared to hold the products for several years and should only allocate a small portion of their overall portfolio to an ELTIF.

World.title: Colombia to close embassy in Romania shortly after reopening it
World.content:
Colombia’s president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, announced on Sunday, July 26, that his administration, which will take office on August 7, will close at least 14 embassies, including the one in Romania, as part of a reorganization of the country’s diplomatic network.

Earlier this year, during the mandate of the current president of the South American country, Gustavo Petro, Colombia had reopened its embassy in Romania after 24 years of direct diplomatic absence between the two states.

The new president presented another course regarding the embassies. “In a first stage, I will close the embassies in Algeria, Azerbaijan, Barbados, Cuba, the Czech Republic, Ethiopia, Ghana, Haiti, Hungary, Malaysia, Nicaragua, Romania, Senegal, and South Africa,” De la Espriella said in a speech on his social media accounts in which he also announced the suspension of the opening of the mission in Palestine, according to Euronews English.

De la Espriella assured that these measures “do not mean the severing of diplomatic relations” with the affected countries, except for Cuba and Nicaragua, arguing that “there will be no link with tyrannies.”

Instead, the president-elect explained that Colombian citizens in the countries where embassies will be closed will continue to receive assistance through the concurrent representation of other diplomatic missions in the region and that the reorganization aims “to make the foreign service more efficient.”

As part of this strategy, Abelardo de la Espriella also announced the reopening of Colombia’s Embassy in Israel, which will operate in Jerusalem, a promise the new president made during the presidential campaign, and the opening of a diplomatic mission in Nigeria, to reorganize the South American country’s presence in Africa.

He also indicated that he will unify some diplomatic representations which, in his opinion, “duplicate their functions,” such as Colombia’s embassies in France and at UNESCO in Paris, as well as those in Italy and at the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in Rome, so that a single ambassador will assume both representations.

The president-elect added that within the first 100 days of his government, he will request a technical audit of the remaining diplomatic representations in order to assess their continuity and stated that the resources saved through these measures will be used to strengthen sectors such as security, health, education, and infrastructure.

World.title: Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna to perform in Romania during Imperial Christmas Gala
World.content:
The famed Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna is set to return to Bucharest and perform at the Romanian Athenaeum on December 20 for the Imperial Christmas Gala, an event that has reached its 7th edition.

The evening's repertoire will bring together famous waltzes, lively polkas and emblematic musical pages by Johann Strauss II, alongside other jewels of Viennese classical music.

“Returning to Bucharest every December is for us a gesture of continuity and artistic affection. Imperial Christmas Gala has become a symbol of the meeting between Viennese tradition and an extraordinarily receptive and cultivated audience. It is our way of saying thank you for a year that is coming to an end,” said Peter Hosek, manager of Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna, according to Eventim.

Tickets for the event start at RON 329 (EUR 63) and can go to RON 629 (EUR 120).

Founded in 1997, Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna performs concerts at the Orangery of Schönbrunn Palace, at the Vienna State Opera and at prestigious festivals in Salzburg, being constantly invited to important stages around the world: Sweden, Finland, Germany, Italy, Romania, Japan, China and the United States.

Devoted to the Viennese tradition, the orchestra performs Johann Strauss waltzes, creations by Mozart, Haydn and Schubert, as well as works dedicated to festive moments.

In recent years, Schönbrunn Palace Orchestra Vienna has consolidated its status as an ambassador of authentic Viennese style through extensive international tours and appearances on increasingly diverse stages, from Europe to Asia and overseas. The orchestra is famous for the homogeneity of its sound, stylistic precision and stage elegance.

World.title: George Enescu Philharmonic’s 2026-2027 season brings Martha Argerich, Mikhail Pletnev, Vasily Petrenko, Patricia Kopatchinskaja, Christian Tetzlaff to Bucharest
World.content:
The George Enescu Philharmonic has unveiled the program of its 2026-2027 season, with artists such as Martha Argerich, Mikhail Pletnev, Vasily Petrenko, Patricia Kopatchinskaja, and Christian Tetzlaff among the headliners.

They will be joined by Andrea Marcon, Michał Nesterowicz, Ariane Matiakh, Julian Rachlin, Javier Perianes, Maxime Pascal, Alexandre Bloch, Axel Kober, Alena Hron, Julia Hagen, Frank Dupree, and David Fray, among others.

Symphonic season opening

The symphonic season opens on October 1 and 2 with two concerts conducted by Mikhail Pletnev, featuring legendary pianist Martha Argerich, who will make her first appearance in the Philharmonic's symphonic season.

The program includes George Enescu's symphonic poem Isis, restored by Pascal Bentoiu in an expanded version featuring the Philharmonic Women's Choir. Argerich will perform Sergei Prokofiev's Piano Concerto No. 3 in C major, Op. 26, one of the signature works in her repertoire. The second part of the evening features Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Suite, presented in an arrangement by Mikhail Pletnev.

Chamber music season opening

Martha Argerich will also inaugurate the chamber music season on September 29 alongside mezzo-soprano Magdalena Kožená and pianist Iddo Bar-Shai. The first half of the program presents works by Claude Debussy and Maurice Ravel, while the second focuses on Romantic repertoire by Franz Schubert and Robert Schumann.

The 2026-2027 season will be held under the banner of the Beethoven Year, marking the 200th anniversary of the composer's death. Throughout 2027, the Philharmonic will place Beethoven's music at the center of its programming, performing the complete symphonies and concertos across the second half of the 2026-2027 season and the first half of the 2027-2028 season.

The upcoming season will see Robert Treviño start his mandate as principal conductor of the Philharmonic. He will conduct the orchestra on March 25 and March 26, 2027, in a program featuring Beethoven's Coriolan Overture, Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 3 with Alexander Gavrylyuk as soloist, and Richard Strauss's poem Ein Heldenleben. The performance of Strauss's work will be recorded for the label Ondine Records.

Before the season begins, Treviño will lead the orchestra at the 74th edition of the Ravello Festival in Italy, for an open-air concert on August 26, 2026, featuring works by Enescu and Rachmaninoff.

Guests of the 2026 – 2027 season

The Bucharest public will be able to attend performances featuring conductors Andrea Marcon, Andris Poga, Axel Kober, Asher Fisch, and Pierre Bleuse, pianists Alexandre Kantorow, Olga Kern, David Fray, and Cédric Tiberghien; violinists Christian Tetzlaff, Daishin Kashimoto, and Veronika Eberle; cellist Steven Isserlis; and vocal soloists Léo Vermot-Desroches, Julie Boulianne, Huw Montague Rendall, Jean Teitgen, Edwin Crossley-Mercer, Luigi Morassi, Theodore Platt, Stéphanie d'Oustrac, Anthea Pichanick, Nicolas Brooymans, Guillaume Andrieux, Bastien Rimondi, Marie-Eve Munger, and Pauline Sabatier.

At the same time, Mikhail Pletnev, Daniel Hope, Leonidas Kavakos, Vasily Petrenko, Christian Zacharias, Julian Rachlin and Boris Giltburg will return to the stage of the Romanian Athenaeum.

The public will be able to see Christian Zacharias, Patricia Kopatchinskaja, Frank Dupree, and Javier Perianes in a double role, as both conductors and soloists.

Among the emerging artists that will perform with the Bucharest orchestra in the upcoming season are Edgar and Raphaelle Moreau (France), Alexandre Kantorow (France), Julia Hagen (Austria), Aurélien Pascal (France), Ellinor D'Melon (Cuba), and Christian Li (Australia).

Mihaela Martin, Gabriel Bebeșelea, Tiberiu Soare, Alexandru Tomescu, Valentin Șerban, Ștefan Cazacu, Roxana Constantinescu and Florian Mitrea are among the Romanian musicians set to perform in the upcoming season.

Valentin Șerban will be the Philharmonic’s artist in residence for the 2026-2027 season.

Highlights of the program

Among the season's highlights are the Philharmonic's first modern-era performance of Hector Berlioz's oratorio L'Enfance du Christ in December 2026 and its first-ever presentation of Maurice Ravel's opera L'Enfant et les sortilèges in May 2027.

The program also includes major symphonic works such as Gustav Mahler's Symphonies Nos. 5 and 7, Richard Strauss's An Alpine Symphony and Anton Bruckner's Symphony No. 4, which will close the symphonic season.

The Philharmonic will also present a commissioned work by Romanian composer Aurelian Băcan and a work by Pascal Bentoiu, performed for the first time at the Athenaeum.

The new passes for the upcoming season will be on sale between August 3 and September 10. Pass renewals can be done by September 25. The tickets for the Symphonic Season go on sale on September 15, while those for the Chamber Music Season go on sale on August 3.

World.title: Seven in ten Romanians abroad do not plan to return home soon, study finds
World.content:
Seven in ten Romanians living abroad do not expect to return to Romania in the next 12 months, although a majority continue to invest money in the country, according to the Diaspora Sentiment 2026 study conducted by market research agency MKOR. The findings suggest that financial ties to Romania remain strong even as many expatriates see their future elsewhere.

The study found that 61% of Romanians in the diaspora have already invested in Romania, either through real estate purchases or financial support for family members, despite 70% saying they do not plan to return in the near future.

Germany recorded the highest share of diaspora members investing in Romania, at 71%, while 44% of respondents there said they regularly provide direct financial support to family members in the country.

The report also highlighted significant differences across Romanian communities abroad. Respondents in the UK had the strongest economic profile, with 29% holding management positions or running businesses, 62% having higher education degrees, and 46% reporting monthly incomes above EUR 3,000.

According to the same study, financial priorities also differ by country. Romanians in Italy tend to focus on protecting family assets, those in Germany value financial predictability, respondents in Spain are more likely to spend on products linked to nostalgia for home, while those in the UK prioritize investment returns.

The research also identified the Republic of Moldova as a potential source of young talent for Romania. Respondents there had an average age of 31, with nearly half (49%) belonging to Generation Z. At the same time, 38% were economically inactive, a figure 17 percentage points above the overall average, suggesting opportunities for recruitment, internship programs, and cross-border financial services.

“In my 13 years of entrepreneurship at MKOR, I have learned to look beyond the numbers," said Cori Cimpoca, founder of MKOR. "These people continue to invest back home even though they do not plan to return in the next 12 months. This shows a strong level of trust. Their financial connection to Romania remains active regardless of whether they intend to repatriate, and is increasingly a way of protecting family wealth rather than preparing to move back.”

The online survey was conducted in October 2025 among 2,000 Romanians aged 18 to 65 who live outside Romania for at least seven months a year. Respondents were recruited through MKOR's online panel and digital marketing campaigns.

World.title: Bucharest subway company introduces weekly subscription for Străuleşti Multimodal Terminal parking
World.content:
Metrorex, the company operating the Bucharest subway system, announced the introduction of a weekly subscription for the Străuleşti Multimodal Terminal parking facility starting August 1, 2026.

The subscription, priced at RON 100 (EUR 20), allows unlimited use of the parking facility during the 7 days of validity, representing a convenient option for commuters and all those who choose to continue their journey by subway, according to the company.

“The Străuleşti Multimodal Terminal provides the public with modern infrastructure that integrates several types of transport and facilitates urban mobility. It offers direct access to the metro network, surface public transport and suburban transport, as well as 660 parking spaces,” the cited source stated.

The same source mentioned that by using the Străuleşti parking facility, passengers can save time and costs associated with travelling by car in the congested areas of the city.

The Străuleşti Multimodal Terminal is located on Bucureştii Noi Boulevard in District 1 of Bucharest, and is part of the investment project “Subway Line 4. Section 2. Bazilescu Park – Străulești. Tunnel, gallery, stations, depot, multimodal terminal and related installations construction works.”

Metrorex closed 2025 with a turnover of RON 1.26 billion and losses of RON 312 million, representing a 72.27% increase over the losses recorded in 2014, according to the annual financial statement. The company noted that it transported 153.2 million passengers last year, roughly 13% less than the expected 176 million passengers.

World.title: Romanian Social Democrat leader says optimistic new government will be in place after mid-August
World.content:
Social Democratic Party (PSD) leader Sorin Grindeanu said he is confident Romania will have a fully empowered government after August 15, as political parties continue negotiations to end the deadlock that has left the country under an interim administration since early May. He also reiterated that PSD is seeking the prime minister's mandate as the largest party in Parliament.

“I am very optimistic that somewhere after August 15 we will have a government with full powers. That is good for Romania, and it is good for us," Grindeanu said in an interview with Antena 3 CNN on Monday evening, as reported by news agency Agerpres.

He argued that PSD had consistently sought compromises during talks hosted by president Nicușor Dan in an effort to break the political impasse.

Moreover, he also renewed PSD's claim to lead the next cabinet, saying the party's position reflects its status as the largest political force in Parliament.

“PSD is asking for the prime minister's mandate because we are the largest party in Parliament," Sorin Grindeanu said. "We made this clear during the last official consultations at Cotroceni Palace.”

Romania has been governed by a caretaker administration since the Liberal-led government of former prime minister Ilie Bolojan was dismissed in a no-confidence vote in early May. President Nicușor Dan recently said the main obstacle to forming a new coalition is not agreeing on a prime minister but finding a combination of parties capable of securing a parliamentary majority.

Sorin Grindeanu said the current Parliament is effectively divided into three major political blocs: PSD and its allies, the far-right Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) and its partners, and a bloc made up of the National Liberal Party (PNL), the Save Romania Union (USR) and, at times, the Hungarian minority party UDMR.

“You cannot form a majority without combining at least two of these forces. That is what will eventually happen," he said.

Asked whether PSD could negotiate with AUR, Grindeanu said the far-right party would first need to clarify its position if it wanted to become an acceptable partner for pro-Western parties.

“They need to clarify some things. There is a lack of credibility among some of their leaders, and I have not seen them clearly state their position, including in recent days regarding the drones that entered Romanian territory or sanctions against Russia," he said. "These are issues they must clarify if they want to become an acceptable partner, not only for PSD but for any pro-Western party.”

Sorin Grindeanu also said PSD is not afraid of the prospect of early elections, although both he and president Dan have expressed optimism that a governing majority can still be formed.

Finding a majority in Parliament to back a new government still seems rather difficult, however, as PNL and USR have repeatedly said they would not be in a government again that also includes PSD after the latter left the previous alliance and then joined far-right AUR to pass the May no-confidence motion. In their turn, the Social Democrats said they will not accept PNL leader Ilie Bolojan in the government again.

World.title: Left High and Dry: Drought Exposes Central Europe’s Water Crisis
World.content:
Water management and retention

Described as the proverbial “roof of Europe”, Czechia sees all its rivers, streams and waterways flow out of the country – a systemic and geological drainage which makes the country particularly dependent on precipitation from above.

“This is a significant disadvantage, because most of the water we manage has to be retained: in the landscape, soil, hydrogeological structures or water reservoirs,” says Adam Vizina, head of the hydrology department at the Water Management Research Institute.

Water management and retention are, therefore, key for this landlocked country, yet the authorities appear short on solutions.

“Water will always flow away, but we can reduce our vulnerability,” argues Vizina, listing measures such as slowing runoff, interconnecting water supply systems, managing water reservoirs better, or protecting the quality and quantity of groundwater.

The state reportedly spent 75 billion crowns (about 3 billion euros) in the past three years on drought adaptation, yet experts – including a report by the Supreme Audit Office published last March – have criticised the slow pace and limited scope of the measures.

The Slovak Academy of Sciences recently released its “Vision for Slovakia 2040”, an extensive 90-page framework document commissioned by the government of Robert Fico laying out the key policy challenges for the next 15 years.

Among those, the forward-looking blueprint “identifies more frequent droughts as a key consequence of climate change and argues that strengthening water management, increasing landscape water retention and improving the resilience of agriculture and ecosystems should be central priorities for Slovakia’s long-term development.”

Whether the authorities will act on the recommendations is another matter, with experts long highlighting key shortcomings in Slovakia’s water management practices, from fragmented governance between different institutions and ministries, a lack of concrete follow-through, and scattered water data hindering real-time monitoring.

Czechia and Slovakia’s subpar water-management has deep roots dating back to decades of intensive farming that followed its collectivisation in the 1950s and 1960s under Communism – with all that entailed in terms of land consolidation, water erosion and reduced soil fertility, among other environmental impacts.

On the upside, the Czech Republic continues to receive roughly the same amount of rain on average every year as it used to, according to some estimates. But the way, time and place it does are changing, as must the measures meant to retain and manage it more effectively, experts say: less rainfall in the spring but more in the fall, more intense precipitation during storms, but less frequent episodes of long-term and widespread rain.

According to Milan Vitek from the local branch of Greenpeace, Czechia might soon be faced with the choice of keeping its scarce water either in the rivers or in its fields, but won’t be able to do both. “Adaptation is something that we are decades behind when we could’ve been much further ahead,” he previously told BIRN.

Water management or retention are also recently being cited as a silver bullet to solve Hungary’s problems. Although Hungary has a renewable water reservoir of 11,833 cubic metres per person, one of the largest in Central Europe (only Slovenia and Serbia have more in the region), 95 per cent of that originates from outside and simply flows through the country.

The building of dams or hydroelectric power plants has been a politically sensitive issue since the controversial plan to build the Bos-Nagymaros dam on the Danube helped trigger popular revolt against the Communist government in 1990. Since then, proposals for new dams and hydropower projects have remained politically off-limits in Hungary.

But times are changing. Laszlo Gajdos, the new Hungarian government’s environment minister, said at the height of the extreme heat at the beginning of July that “water is one of our most valuable resources for the future”.

Gajdos said the government must do everything it can to improve water retention, even with dam construction where necessary. “We should not let water flow through Hungary; it needs to be retained somehow. Personally, I don’t like this method, but it seems inevitable building some dams,” he told RTL.hu.

The government of Peter Magyar is working on a new climate and environmental law, expected by late autumn, which is set to address water management issues.

Gajdos, who became Hungary’s first environment minister in 16 years, stressed that water retention is a regional issue requiring cooperation with neighbouring countries.

Andras Szollosi-Nagy, who used to advise international organisations including the UN on water diplomacy and is the founder member of the World Water Council, could not agree more.

“Water retention is always somehow part of national sovereignty,” Szollosi-Nagy says. “The country upstream believes all the water is theirs, but if they retain it, neighbouring countries are affected. We need integrated water management in the region.”

He says there is no silver bullet to solve all the problems: dams, reservoirs, new technologies, satellite-based monitoring and controlled flooding could all play a role.

“Hungary’s water management system has been systematically dismantled in recent decades,” he says. “Now we need to rebuild it from scratch.”

World.title: Letter from Washington: US Seeks to Score Material Goals in the Balkans
World.content:
Greetings from America, which this month celebrated 250 years of independence from the British crown under a president who has called himself a king – and is also seen that way by the many thousands of people who have joined the “No Kings” protests in the US.

Donald Trump would not even allow the kings of football, the Spanish national team who won the World Cup, to enjoy their rightful moment on the throne this month. Instead, he lingered on stage after presenting them with the trophy at the stadium in New Jersey. An awkward situation was averted by Trump’s pal, FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who pulled the US leader aside, suggesting that it was time for him to step away.

Meanwhile, beside the footballing euphoria, the US-Iran memorandum of understanding has turned out to be more of a major misunderstanding. The war has escalated, bringing new American casualties and higher fuel prices, while reopening an uncomfortable question: what is the actual endgame? If the goal is to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, to prevent further escalation in the Middle East, why is the United States simultaneously signing an agreement that would allow Saudi Arabia to develop the very same capability?

While all this has been happening, the Trump administration’s policy towards the Balkans has started to become increasingly clear. It is moving more aggressively into areas it considers important, such as energy, defence and infrastructure, while trying to push Russia, China and the European Union out of those spheres. Washington does not appear to be choosing its friends based on how developed their democracies are. Nor is it particularly troubled when someone in the Balkans talks about “ethnic cleansing”.

World.title: On Albania’s Adriatic Coast, Tourism Ambitions Put at Risk by Pollution
World.content:
Violeta was unimpressed by the rubbish blighting her summer holiday.

“It’s awful, isn’t it?” the 24-year-old said of the litter and construction waste strewn along beachfront at Golem Beach, a sandy stretch of Adriatic coast just south of the Albanian port city of Durres.

Golem is one of the most affordable holiday destinations in Albania, just 30 kilometres west of the capital, Tirana, and a relatively quick trip from neighbouring Kosovo. It is often packed with visitors, but Violeta said one week was enough.

“We’re going somewhere cleaner because of the pollution, like Ksamil,” she told BIRN, referring to a beach at the southern end of Albania. Pointing at rubbish, she said: “It bothers me because animals eat it and there are kids running around.”

World.title: What’s Driving the Real-Estate Price Surges in Eastern and South-East Europe?
World.content:
Rapidly rising real estate prices to the east and south of the Trieste-Szczecin line made existing dwelling owners happy - but potential buyers, especially younger people, less so.

According to Eurostat, in the first quarter of 2026, property prices in Bulgaria, Slovakia, and Croatia recorded price growth of 14 per cent over the first quarter of 2025. In a longer perspective of 3 and 10 years, the fortunes of individual countries have changed.

Generally, the total appreciation of housing real estate has been rapid, with Hungary in 10 years heading the list, followed by Bulgaria, Czechia, and Croatia.

However, Eurostat does not provide comparable data for countries southeast of Croatia, but Bosnia, Serbia, Montenegro, and others have followed similar paths. According to the Agency for Statistics of Bosnia, housing real estate prices increased by 20.4 per cent in the first quarter of 2026 compared to the first quarter of 2025. Nussubpekova recently reported a double-digit growth rate for Serbia.

World.title: North Macedonia Mourns Much-Loved Actor Goce Todorovski
World.content:
Goce Todorovski. Photo: Drama Theatre.

Actor Goce Todorovski has died aged 75, his family and the Drama Theatre in Skopje, where he spent most of his career, confirmed on Monday. The cause of death was not immediately announced.

Born in the western town of Kichevo in 1951, Todorovski graduated from the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Skopje before joining the Drama Theatre in 1978. He went on to perform in more than 50 theatre productions, while also building a prolific career in television, radio and cinema.

His gift for comedy made him one of the country’s most enduring and popular actors.

For many Macedonians, Todorovski will be remembered above all for his appearances in the cult television series Macedonian Folk Tales (Makedonski Narodni Prikazni), whose humorous adaptations of traditional folklore became a fixture of family viewing for decades.

He was also a familiar face to generations of children through the educational television series “Scruffy Alphabet” (Bushava Azbuka), while radio audiences knew him from the long-running satirical comedy programme Hihiriku.

His film career included memorable roles in several classics of Macedonian and former Yugoslav cinema, including Happy New ’49 (Srekna Nova ’49), Weekend of the Dead (Vikend na Mrtovci), Trieste Via Skopje (Trst via Skopje), The Red Horse (Crveniot Konj), and many others.

Beyond his screen work, Todorovski was one of the leading comic actors of the Macedonian stage, collaborating with many of the country’s best-known theatre directors and helping shape the repertoire of the Drama Theatre for nearly five decades.

“Goce Todorovski never sought the audience’s affection. He won it from the moment he stepped onto the stage,” the Drama Theatre wrote in its farewell.

“His performances possessed a rare immediacy: a precise acting rhythm that seemed entirely effortless, expressive facial gestures, a distinctive stage presence, and the roguish charm with which he could effortlessly bridge the gap between the stage and the audience,” it said.

Todorovski’s performances earned numerous awards, including the state “23 October” prize for culture and the lifetime achievement award at the Vojdan Chernodrinski Theatre Festival in 2025, as well as the Presidential Order of Merit in 2023.

News of his death prompted an outpouring of tributes from fellow actors, public figures and audiences, many recalling the humour, warmth and distinctive characters that made Todorovski one of the defining faces of North Macedonia’s acting scene.

Actress Maja Andonovska Ilijevski wrote that Macedonian theatre had lost “a great man and a great actor”. Recalling their time filming the cult TV series Macedonian Folk Tales, she said Todorovski had been not only an acting legend but also a wonderful colleague, whose humour and warmth made those days unforgettable.

Andonovska said the countless characters Todorovski brought to life will remain part of the country’s collective memory, adding that “some people never truly leave – they live on through their roles, the memories of their colleagues and the love of their audience”.

Photographer Goran Anastasovski described Todorovski as “the man who made us laugh for decades” and “a giant on stage”, adding that his legacy of bringing smiles to various generations will endure.
