World.title: Groups after SONA 2026: What’s the plan for teachers’ salary?
World.content:
TEACHERS' DEMANDS. Protesters raise banners calling for a wage increase for teachers during a rally in Quezon City ahead of the fifth State of the Nation Address of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on July 27, 2026.

Teachers' groups express disappointment as President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s fifth State of the Nation Address leaves out higher wages and reduced administrative workload for them

MANILA, Philippines – Some groups criticized President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for not presenting key measures to address certain issues in the education sector during his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA), particularly leaving out plans for a salary increase for teachers.

Marcos delivered his longest SONA yet on Monday, July 27, but his remarks on teachers’ welfare and the education sector were not enough, according to the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) and the Teachers’ Dignity Coalition (TDC).

The two teachers’ groups have different salary demands. The ACT is seeking P50,000 for entry-level teachers, while the TDC is pushing for a P15,000 increase across the board.

Play Video

They can only ask what would be Marcos’ moves regarding the issue with only two years left in power.

“May pagkilala lang ng karangalan at kadakilaan ng guro, pero more than that, ang kailangan ng guro ngayon ay dagdag sahod pati ‘yung panawagan namin ng pagtataas ng aming personnel economic relief allowance (PERA),” ACT chairperson Ruby Bernardo told Rappler.

(There was only recognition of the integrity and heroism of teachers, but more than that, teachers need a wage hike and an increase in our personnel economic relief allowance.)

While public school teachers and police have almost similar entry-level monthly salaries at over P30,000, Bernardo argued that the police’s subsistence allowance would push their take-home pay to nearly P50,000. Those holding the Nurse I position, meanwhile, have already been upgraded to Salary Grade 15 or around P42,000 monthly, and also receive allowances.

PERA refers to the P2,000 monthly allowance given to state employees.

TDC national chairperson Benjo Basas also said that boosting teachers’ pay and welfare would result in better work-life balance, as well as improved mental and physical health, that could boost productivity.

“Hindi siya maghihintay nung binabanggit ng President kanina [sa SONA] na mag-aagawan doon sa kakatiting na items for promotion,” Basas told Rappler.

(Teachers would not wait and scramble for the few promotion opportunities that the President mentioned in his SONA.)

Marcos reported that over 80,000 teachers and school heads have already been promoted through the Expanded Career Progression System of the Department of Education (DepEd). There are nearly 900,000 teachers in the country.

The President also said the government continues to provide teachers with gadgets, such as smart TVs, laptops, tablets, and lapel microphones, as well as free mobile data.

Both the TDC and the ACT said many teachers have yet to receive laptops to help in their work. For Basas, Marcos should apologize as he promised in last year’s SONA that every teacher would receive one.

“It [says] a lot about credibility, accountability of the government. Kapag nagsabi ka, nangako ka, walang ligtas ‘yan, may resibo ‘yan, pero hindi mo na-deliver,” he said.

(It says a lot about credibility, accountability of the government. If you make a promise, there’s no escaping that because there are receipts, but you did not deliver on that promise.)

No mention of workload, ARAL Program

Bernardo also said Marcos failed to mention reduction of teachers’ administrative tasks, adding it remains unclear whether the responsibility to carry out the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program would still be theirs.

Under the 2026 budget, the ARAL Program was allocated nearly P9 billion. Of this amount, around P1.96 billion is earmarked for the hiring of external tutors, while over P1 billion will be for teaching overload pay.

During the ARAL Summer Program, there were only a few volunteer teachers for the tutoring sessions, resulting in some schools having no sessions for other grade levels.

In the current school year, teachers tapped to be ARAL tutors may have to squeeze in their sessions after classes or during the two-week end-of-term block.

The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) was also hoping that Marcos’ SONA would include ways to improve the implementation of the ARAL Program and concrete reductions in teachers’ administrative workload.

For EDCOM 2, Marcos also missed tackling key education issues such as rising stunting rates and modernization of the charters of the DepEd, Commission on Higher Education, and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority.

The commission also awaited pronouncements on the President’s support for the immediate implementation of Republic Act No. 12199 or the Early Childhood Care and Development System Act; RA 11650 or the Inclusive Education Act; and the revised implementing rules and regulations of the Anti-Bullying Act.

What Marcos said

But two issues included in EDCOM 2’s checklist were cited in this year’s SONA, specifically progress in classroom construction and addressing violence and bullying in schools.

Marcos highlighted that the government is eyeing to build around 16,000 classrooms in 2026 through a public-private partnership modality to solve the country’s classroom backlog.

He also paid tribute to the three students killed in the June 22 Tacloban City school shooting and called for the country to do more in protecting children against online influences and harms. (READ: Marcos touts AI upskilling, calls for online protections vs. violence, ‘fake news’)

Play Video

The President said there are mechanisms and processes in place to report and address incidents of bullying, with the DepEd coordinating with local government units to strengthen school safety.

He noted that the DepEd is set to hire 10,000 school counselor associates to expand access to mental health services.

Marcos also mentioned the rollout of the school-based feeding program and the Strengthened Senior High School Program.

The policy direction outlined in the SONA was “encouraging,” according to advocacy group Philippine Business for Education, but the “challenge now lies in implementation.”

“The issue has rarely been a lack of policies or plans, but ensuring that these are executed effectively and translated into better learning outcomes. This is where sustained focus and accountability will matter most,” the group said.

In an interview ahead of the SONA, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said he expected the education sector to get a 2027 budget of over P1 trillion, or the same as in 2026. – Rappler.com

World.title: Ed Quitoriano: The life, travels, and travails of a promdi rebolusyonaryo
World.content:
The writing of Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows: The Making of a Mindanao Rebel began when Francisco “Pancho” Lara Jr., executive director of the non-government research and policy institute Climate Conflict Action, asked me to comment on Ed Quitoriano’s first draft chapters.

I could not say no to an old friend. After a common friend heard about this, he told me to ask Ed about his nose. When we finally chatted with each other via social media, I asked him about his nose to break the ice. Ed casually replied that Cuban plastic surgeons reconfigured it so that he would look more Latino than Asian. That way, Latin American revolutionaries would warm up to him more since he would look like them! But the doctors botched the first operation, so they had to do the plastic surgery all over again!

Of course, I asked him, “What in heaven’s name were you doing in Cuba?” Again, matter-of-factly, he said during that time he was going around Latin America on behalf of the New People’s Army’s General Command, seeking military assistance from Leftwing movements and Cuba for the NPA.

He then added that, before Cuba, he also visited Nicaragua, Lebanon, Libya, Yugoslavia, and North Korea, with multiple transits points ranging from Athens, Algeria, Belgrade, Moscow, Brazil, Peru, Mexico, Singapore, Vietnam, and Thailand! This got my attention and, for the next 10 years, Ed and I worked on the manuscript.

It was not an easy edit. I told Ed at the onset that his life should be the center of the book and that he should write as honestly as possible. We both knew how much memoir writing in the Philippines are, by nature, flawed. Authors — many conveniently dead — embellished their records and peppered over the dark sides of their lives. It is easy to spot these self-indulgences in the memoirs of politicos, presidents, and corporate bigwigs, but also in the autobiographies of civil-society activists, human rights advocates and of course revolutionaries. I did not want Ed to follow that well-trodden, contemptible path.

Then we had to stop this dreary habit Ed learned from the underground, where one always starts a chapter pertaining to a country visited with some broad economic, political, and socio-cultural overview. Ed’s first chapters read like this monotonous formulaic prerequisite. “I landed in Syria in April. Syria was once a colony of the French then the British empire and after independence fought in the Arab Israeli war, blah, blah, blah.” I told him to do away with that, reminding him that if readers needed some background, they could check this at the library or, if too lazy, Wikipedia.

Finally, there were the characters in his stories, many of them still alive when Ed began writing. In some weird ghastly manner, we had to wait for some of them to die so that there would be no more resorting to aliases or, God forbid, innuendos. It was also because of this that we could not get a local publisher to be interested in the manuscript. But eventually some of these characters did die, which made the writing easier. But others are still with us, and challenging Deeper Ground, Darker Shadow’s narrative is the Japanese Red Army (JRA) leader Fusako Shigenobu.

So, what you have here is the autobiography of a “nobody” in the CPP-NPA, not a member of the Politburo; a cadre who came from a small town in “frontier” Mindanao, not urban Manila. Ed learned his radicalism from Irish missionaries of the St. Columban Order, not from Maoist commissars from the University of the Philippines.

This marriage of Marxism and theology was a distinctive feature of Mindanao communism of his time. Ed was a kumander who helped build the first viable NPA guerrilla zones in Mindanao, only to learn later that many of his comrades were also the first to be arrested, tortured, then killed by a caretaker Mindanao leadership, which panicked when news got to them that the military had infiltrated the movement.

The book’s prologue is a dirge and a reminder that the victims of the purges of the 1980s still must get justice and its perpetrators be prosecuted to the fullest. Finally, he was an outsider to movement politics — he was out of the country when debates, the splits, and the purges of the 1980s upended the revolution. He would also become the convenient scapegoat in the first and perhaps only communist kangaroo court we will ever read about.

Ed was a rural kid who found himself in the global stage, striking a conversation with the drunken Sandinista deputy interior minister Omar Cabezas, and was given an Arabic nom d’ guerre by the second-in-command of the dreaded Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. He got $1 million USD dollars each from the dying North Korean Kim Il Sung (Ed saw the large pustule on the despot’s back!) and the animated Moammar Khadafy, who told him that in exchange for the $1 million, the NPA should fly a plane into a New York high rise!

It is worth mentioning here Ed’s close ties with Fusako Shigenobu. His travels were funded not by the NPA nor the CPP but by Shigenobu, she who became famous in Japanese politics when she released her revolutionary declaration in Hiragana, the phonetic, cursive script that upper class women use to write their diaries and poetry. She became a global icon when she led many of her comrades to Europe and the Middle East and established this elaborate network that extended from Brazil and Peru to the Philippines! It was even rumored that the Japanese Red Army (JRA) ran a bar in Makati’s seamier side, which was a joint investment with the Yakuza. Shigenobu would be Ed’s close adviser, financier, and I even dare say, friend, in his travels across the world.

Four years ago, I sat alongside my University of Hawaiʻi colleague, sociology professor Patricia Steinhoff, in a workshop on Japan and Southeast Asia. Pat is the world’s top expert on the JRA, so I mentioned to her that I was editing the work of a friend who once had close ties with the group in the 1980s. Her face lit up because it was this period which she drew a blank about the whereabouts of the JRA after it had to close its European and Middle Eastern operations. But once we compared faces with pseudonyms and real names, she could now sort out where the group’s members went and, from our end, put a real name to each face instead of relying on aliases. Pat then happily agreed to write the foreword to the book.

My friend and novelist, Professor Caroline Sy Hau of the Center for Southeast Asian Studies in Kyoto University, wrote this unusual blurb, describing Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows as one that read “like a political thriller, with elements of the picaresque novel thrown in for good measure.” No wonder even his military captors encouraged Ed to do a movie about his life! It is a singular book for its honesty and candor, its expanse and intimacies, that I doubt will be matched by any other Filipino communist’s memoir for quite a while. – Rappler.com

Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows: The Making of a Mindanao Rebel is published under the “New Perspectives in Southeast Asia” Series of the University of Wisconsin Press. The Ateneo de Manila University Press publishes the Philippine edition.

Patricio N. Abinales is working on a book on the University of the Philippines and Martial Law, and completed the first draft of the manuscript on Philippine cuisines for Bloomsbury Press’s Global Food Cultures Series. This piece was delivered during the Manila book launch of Deeper Ground, Darker Shadows on July 23, 2026.

World.title: [OPINION] Housing the urban poor: Marcos’ chance to get it right
World.content:
With so many controversial political and urgent economic and social issues that President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has to speak about in his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA), it is somewhat surprising that housing made the list.

“Abot-kayang pabahay” (affordable housing) under the Pambansang Pabahay Para sa Pilipino Housing (4PH) Program, he said, is among the investments that Filipino workers can make for their retirement, thanks to the “social protection floor” policy of the administration. The private sector and local governments were mentioned as partners in filling the housing shortage, which he claimed has shrunk by more than 100,000 units in the past year alone.

Building that many units is one thing; ensuring these reach the urban poor is another. Most government housing projects under the 4PH Program are located outside the city, making them ideal for buyers who can afford to commute or have cars to drive into the city. These include formally employed Pag-IBIG members and families of OFWs with enough income to invest in a unit. President Marcos did suggest this in his speech.

This is not to say that they are without legitimate housing needs. Many of them may currently be living in informal settlements. The problem lies in claiming that the government flagship housing program serves the poor and vulnerable — those facing eviction and demolition threats, making do with substandard housing without basic sanitation and legal utilities, and struggling to make ends meet with their meager wages.

While exact statistics on low-income informal settler families (ISFs) remain elusive, their widespread presence throughout our cities is hard to miss. They are a stark reminder that social housing policies and the shelter programs built on them fall drastically short. Here in Metro Manila, they are in the sprawling coastline of Baseco Compound in Manila and the densely populated National Government Center in Quezon City. They are found along railroad tracks such as the PNR’s Southrail in Muntinlupa and next to busy highways such as R-10 in Navotas. They are forced to live beneath high-voltage power lines in Valenzuela and next to stagnant esteros of Pasay. They occupy idle private properties held by speculative owners waiting for property values to rise.

Off-city resettlement

For families in flood-prone areas and infrastructure right-of-ways, the government’s primary response is relocation through the resettlement program of the National Housing Authority (NHA). Displaced kilometers away from their original communities where work is accessible and forced to endure months (even years) without reliable water or electricity, these relocated families constitute a particularly marginalized segment of the urban poor. In the city, children could simply walk to their schools; in resettlement sites, students have to commute, placing an additional financial burden on already economically precarious households. It is no wonder then that many “awardees” leave their units and go back to the city to squat again.

Yet, official metrics for measuring how well it has responded to the housing problem — which get reported during the SONA — do not account for the number of families actually living in, or even able to remain in, these units. It’s a vicious cycle the government continues to ignore.

Community Mortgage Program

President Marcos Jr cited the Community Mortgage Program (CMP) as one strategy for reducing the housing backlog. He did not elaborate on this, but this is an encouraging sign, especially since this innovative program has largely fallen dormant since the Duterte administration.

CMP is driven by the beneficiaries themselves. Informal settlers, with the help of an NGO, organize into a community association to collectively negotiate for land purchase, decide on site developments, and secure loan and manage repayment. CMP provides financing designed specifically for the informal poor— featuring low interest rates, flexible terms, and affordable amortization.

In recent years, however, the Social Housing Finance Corporation (SHFC), the shelter agency overseeing the CMP, has shifted focus toward partnering with private developers on off-site housing projects rather than enabling communities to access loans for on-site development.

If the Marcos Jr administration is serious about using the CMP as an approach to resolve the housing crisis, it must exercise its regulatory and political influence to urge private landowners to part with their property in favor of the urban poor. As mentioned earlier, many prefer retaining their properties, anticipating higher market values in the future. In the fierce competition over high-value urban land, the government must stand resolutely with the poor. It must also clamp down on land-grabbing by wealthy families and well-connected land developers.

Land proclamations

During the Arroyo administration, several government-owned lands occupied by informal settlers were designated as socialized housing sites via executive proclamations. It was an apparent political strategy aimed at placating the urban poor, a base historically loyal to Joseph Estrada, her predecessor. Many of these proclaimed sites were never actually awarded to beneficiaries, leaving families without land titles and communities to languish in poverty and with little basic services.

Despite being overlooked in the SONA, presidential land proclamations offer the administration a tangible way to prove its commitment to delivering secure land tenure and decent housing to the urban poor. This approach is a low-cost alternative to off-city resettlement. The government will not have to pour funds into new houses, roads, schools, and hospitals at distant relocation sites, freeing up land for other productive uses. In these proclaimed sites, households can be provided with affordable financing to upgrade or retrofit their homes to meet building safety standards.

There is no denying that President Marcos Jr must deliver strong results over the next two years, particularly given his lagging trust and satisfaction ratings. Prioritizing housing for the urban poor gives him a clear opportunity to establish a lasting policy legacy. The true measure of the administration’s housing policy will not be the number of housing units built, or the number of land titles awarded to buyers, but whether the poorest urban families can live with dignity in the communities they call home. – Rappler.com



Gerald Nicolas is with the Urban Poverty and Governance Program of the John J Carroll Institute on Church and Social Issues (ICSI), an advocacy-oriented research institute based at the Ateneo de Manila University and a member of the Society of Jesus Social Apostolate (SJSA).

World.title: UK lawmaker suing Musk’s xAI seeks order to stop Grok generating sexualized images
World.content:
GROK. Miniature figurines and Grok logo are seen in this illustration taken July 20, 2026.

Jess Asato of Britain's governing Labour Party says Grok users created fake images of her, including a video of her 'being chloroformed and prepared for a sexual assault' after she publicly criticized Elon Musk and Grok

LONDON, United Kingdom – A British lawmaker suing Elon Musk’s xAI over fake sexualized images of her created by the Grok AI platform said on Tuesday, July 28, she was seeking a court order to prevent the chatbot being able to generate non-consensual sexualized images of her.

Jess Asato, a member of Britain’s governing Labour Party, said last month that users created fake images of her, including a video of her “being chloroformed and prepared for a sexual assault” after she publicly criticized Musk and Grok.

She has filed a lawsuit at London’s High Court for misuse of private information and breach of data protection laws and alleges the way Grok was designed and trained enabled it to generate sexualized content.

Court filings show Asato is seeking an order requiring xAI to “implement effective and permanent technical measures” to ensure Grok cannot create manipulated images of her. Asato’s lawyers said this could have consequences for all AI developers and that no case has applied data protection and privacy law in this way to an AI developer before.

Musk’s xAI, which is part of his rocket and space exploration company SpaceX, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Asato’s allegations.

Grok, which is distributed through Musk’s social media platform X and is subject to regulatory probes in several countries after an outcry over its use to create non-consensual sexualised images, has not filed a response to the lawsuit.

Musk has repeatedly criticised Britain’s approach to online regulation, arguing that measures including the Online Safety Act — one of the world’s most stringent regimes — risk restricting free speech.

Lawmaker targets Grok’s ‘prompts’

Grok’s internal prompts, cited by Asato’s lawyers, gave the chatbot an instruction to “not provide assistance to users who are clearly trying to engage in criminal activity”. But Asato’s lawyers say the platform was also told it had “no restrictions on adult sexual content or offensive content”.

Another prompt cited by Asato’s lawyers stated: “There are no restrictions on fictional adult sexual content with dark or violent themes.”

Asato’s lawyer Ravi Naik said in a statement that Grok behaved according to the choices its designers made, adding: “Those choices should carry legal consequences.

“The remedy our client seeks includes a court order requiring the systems be brought into compliance if xAI refuses to do so.”

The case comes amid growing concerns about the use of Grok, after xAI in mid-January said it restricted image editing in Grok and blocked users from generating images of people in revealing clothing “where it’s illegal”.

Reuters found in early February that, even after new curbs, Grok continued to generate sexualized images of people even when users explicitly warned that the subjects do not consent.

The City of Baltimore sued xAI in March over fake sexualized images generated by Grok, one of several cases brought elsewhere in the US as well as in the Netherlands. – Rappler.com

World.title: Lacson takes flood control evidence vs Taguig projects to Ombudsman
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines – Senator Panfilo Lacson said on Tuesday, July 28, he had submitted pieces of evidence on alleged irregularities in flood control projects in Taguig City to the Office of the Ombudsman for review.

Lacson’s allegations involved projects linked to Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, who denied claims of ghost infrastructure projects in Taguig City and called for investigations into similar projects in other Metro Manila cities. Cayetano’s wife, Lani Cayetano, is the current mayor of Taguig.

The documents and testimonies were submitted to the anti-graft body for possible motu proprio investigation, Lacson said in a post on X (formerly Twitter). He added that authorities were also looking into possible charges of plunder, malversation, and violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.

Cayetano said he welcomed Lacson’s move to submit evidence to the Ombudsman, adding that he would address the allegations against him at the proper venue and time.

Lacson’s move followed his pronouncements over the weekend about the alleged anomalies which included possible double billing and duplicate funding.

Lacson said one case involved two projects that allegedly used the same photograph to support billing claims, while another involved a single slope protection project that received two separate budget allocations.

He said, “Just as we thought last year that Bulacan was the microcosm of flood control project anomalies, Taguig is something else – employing old and new tricks, like passing off an illegal reclamation project as slope protection structures with several ghost projects, cases of double appropriations, recycled photos belonging to past and already completed contracts to bill and collect for new ones – all controlled by one person, dating as far back as 2019.”

Lacson added: “We will continue to submit to the Ombudsman whatever pieces of evidence we can still secure to help them achieve our shared crusade against graft and corruption.”

The former Senate blue ribbon committee chairperson has accused Cayetano of securing P6.7 billion in budget insertions even as he alleged that several flood control projects in Taguig remained unfinished.

Cayetano, meanwhile, took to Facebook and said he is for accountability but cautioned against what he called malicious claims. The two senators have traded accusations in recent weeks, with Lacson saying Cayetano’s remarks were an attack on his reputation.

“I was just informed na may finile si Senator Panfilo Lacson sa Ombudsman. I welcome that because in the same manner that I tell everyone that kailangan ng accountability, same din naman. Ang sabi ko lang naman, sa tamang venue, tamang panahon,” he said.

(I was just informed that Senator Panfilo Lacson filed something with the Ombudsman. I welcome that because, in the same way that I tell everyone that there needs to be accountability, the same applies here. What I’m saying is that it should be done at the proper venue and at the proper time.)

Cayetano also questioned the comparison between the alleged Taguig flood control irregularities and the anomalies previously uncovered in Bulacan, while maintaining that he was prepared to face any investigation.

He said the accusations lacked basis, and he was not aware of the specific allegations being raised.

Cayetano continued: “Ingat lang po tayo sa mga malicious accusations. Alam niyo ba kung ano malicious? Malicious is mali, meaning wrong, pero delicious. Ibig sabihin, masarap pakinggan. Kaya malicious di ba?”

(I’d just like to remind everyone to be careful about malicious accusations. Do you know what malicious means? It’s something that is wrong, but also delicious. It means it’s something that sounds good or appealing to hear. That’s why it’s called malicious, right?)

He added: “Kung from his point of view, he thinks valid yung accusation, then I’ll respect that but from my point of view, it’s malicious because nga hindi ko alam kung ano exactly at bakit ganun ang accusations…but as I told you, always ready to face the consequences. May cost parati po talaga ang lahat ng ating pakikibaka, ang lahat ng ating struggle, maging opposition man o administrasyon.”

(If, from his point of view, he thinks the accusation is valid, then I respect that. But from my perspective, it is malicious because I don’t know exactly what the accusations are or why they are being made. But as I’ve said, I am always ready to face the consequences. There is always a cost to every fight and every struggle we take on, whether we are in the opposition or the administration.) – Rappler.com

World.title: Major quake in southern Japan knocks out power, disrupts transport
World.content:
MONITOR. Television screens in Osaka, western Japan, show news of an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1, which, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture, July 28, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) Public broadcaster NHK showed several buildings on fire or collapsed, large cracks along roads, including an elevated highway, and a derailed goods train

TOKYO, Japan – An earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan‘s southern Kumamoto prefecture on Tuesday, July 28, knocking out power to thousands of homes, snarling travel and triggering evacuation orders and warnings for aftershocks.

Speaking to reporters at her office in Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the extent of casualties and property damage was being assessed.

“We have already been informed that people have been injured,” Takaichi said.

“Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings. Above all, I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.”

Public broadcaster NHK showed several buildings on fire or collapsed, large cracks along roads, including an elevated highway, and a derailed goods train. More than 150,000 people were instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said.

TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, evacuated workers from its plant in the area as a precaution, a spokesperson for the firm said.

A spokesperson for electronics firm Sony, which also has a plant there, said it was checking the situation.

Residents in the areas that felt the biggest tremors must beware of further strong quakes for about a week as well as the risk of landslides, an official for the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) said.

Trains halted, airport closed

The Japanese government issued emergency earthquake warnings for Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga, Oita, and Miyazaki prefectures, all on Japan’s southern Kyushu island. The JMA also initially issued a tsunami warning for a wave measuring 1 meter (3.28 feet) but later lifted it.

Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. Located along the “Ring of Fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling the Pacific Basin, Japan accounts for about 20% of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or more.

Kyushu Electric Power said about 40,000 homes had lost power as a result of the latest quake, while railway company JR Kyushu said that it had suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway, as airlines diverted and cancelled flights.

Telecoms operators KDDI and Docomo said there was disruption to their mobile phone services due to power shortages and transmission-line failures.

There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said.

A massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739, according to an official count, and damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a top tourist site. – Rappler.com

World.title: [DECODED] Pro-China accounts attack LANS after content creator’s West PH Sea feature
World.content:
After LANS’ visit to Pag-asa Island, Facebook posts accuse the content creator of being US-funded, calling her ignorant while spewing disinfo on the Philippines’ claim on the West Philippine Sea

Educational content creator LANS was subjected to disinformation and attacks after her feature on the West Philippine Sea (WPS) on July 18.

A social media scan by data forensics group The Nerve found Facebook posts that mention LANS spiking on the days immediately following the content creator’s posts featuring Pag-asa Island in mid-July.

These posts included those that called LANS “ignorant” while spewing disinformation on the West Philippine Sea, and those that accused the content creator of being funded by the United States’ Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). (LANS has denied being paid for her WPS content.) Behind these posts are accounts that have purported pro-China narratives in the context of the WPS.

These attacks happened as tensions between the Philippines and China persist, 10 years after the 2016 arbitral ruling that invalidated China’s claim over the South China Sea and affirmed the Philippines’ 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone (EEZ).

The rise of LANS, and her exposure to attacks

The rise of the 24-year-old LANS, born Louise Anne Nagal, was nothing short of meteoric. The veterinary medicine student — renowned for her simple, girl-next-door personality and her educational content about animals and other trivia — had garnered 2 million followers on Facebook alone as of June 17, shooting up to six million by the end of June, ABS-CBN reported.

As LANS’ public exposure grew, so did public conversations that surrounded her.

On June 23, the content creator went viral when she called out those who pitted her against other women content creators, advocating that all of them should be respected, no matter the type of content they put out.

Almost a month later, LANS was put under the spotlight once again when she shared about her visit to Pag-asa Island in the WPS, which she first posted about on July 15.

Through an invitation from the Philippine Air Force, the content creator traveled to the island and interviewed residents and government workers about their lives and struggles, set against the backdrop of persisting tensions between the Philippines and China.

In The Nerve’s analysis of more than a thousand public Facebook posts that mentioned the content creator in the past two weeks, the posts spiked on the days after LANS posted about her WPS feature. This happened on two separate occasions — when LANS teased the upcoming vlog on July 15, and when she posted the whole vlog on July 18 and 19.

A couple of Facebook posts stood out in The Nerve’s analysis, found to have spread attacks and disinformation against LANS and her WPS content, calling her ignorant and accusing her of being funded by the US.

LANS outrightly denied allegations of being paid at the beginning of her July 18 vlog, saying the content was “voluntary.”

“We created this content because we want to use our platform to share, raise awareness among our fellow Filipinos about the West Philippine Sea, and remind every citizen that understanding our nation’s history, sovereignty, and territorial rights is a shared responsibility,” she wrote.

“Patriotism is not for sale, and love for one’s country should never be mistaken for paid propaganda,” she added.

One of the most engaged posts was by Duterte propagandist Tio Moreno — who has created a new Facebook page named Cho Moreno — on July 18.

In his post titled “DEBUNKING THE IGNORANCE OF LANS,” Moreno falsely claimed that the Philippines claiming the West Philippine Sea has no legal basis, and also insinuated that the Philippines made a sweeping claim on the South China Sea.

Both are false.

What the Philippines claims is its sovereign rights over its EEZ, now formally named the WPS. This is validated by the landmark July 2016 ruling of the Permanent Court of Arbitration and is anchored in the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

The ruling also invalidated China’s sweeping claim over the South China Sea through its “nine-dash line,” and declared the country’s large-scale land reclamation in the area harmful to marine ecosystems and its interference with Filipino fisherfolk in the WPS unlawful. [FACT CHECK: International law backs PH claim to the West Philippine Sea]

Moreno’s post still garnered around 5,000 reactions, comments, and shares as of writing.

IGNORANCE OF LANS? Amid LANS’ vlog feature on the West Philippine Sea, Facebook user Cho Moreno calls the content creator ignorant while spewing disinformation on the landmark arbitral ruling that validated the Philippines’ sovereign rights on the WPS. The Nerve screenshots

Meanwhile, a page named Thriving Mindanao Islands Progress (TMIP), in multiple Facebook posts, alleged that LANS was paid by the CIA for the WPS trip. Similar allegations of being CIA-funded have been hurled against news outlets and fact checkers that are critical of the government, purporting them as mouthpieces of the US in the China versus US narrative warfare.

TMIP has also consistently shared pro-China content, sharing propagandic posts by the Chinese Embassy, in particular, accusing the Philippines for “disrupting peace” in its joint patrols in the WPS and attacking Philippine government officials, among others.

PAID BY CIA? Amid LANS’ vlog feature on the West Philippine Sea, Facebook user Cho Moreno calls the content creator ignorant while spewing disinformation on the landmark arbitral ruling that validated the Philippines’ sovereign rights on the WPS. The Nerve screenshots

The comment section had not been spared from disinformation, too.

A Facebook post by GMA News that reported on LANS’ WPS feature — which is the post in The Nerve’s analysis not published by LANS that got the most engagement, at more than 66,000 — was also bombarded with the same disinformation proliferated by Moreno and TMIP.

IN THE COMMENTS, TOO. Disinformation against content creator LANS after her West Philippine Sea feature was also spotted in a comment section of a highly-engaged news report. The Nerve screenshots

Pro-China narratives and attacks have been spreading in Philippine digital spaces for years, undermining the Philippines’ rights to its EEZ, accusing civilians that assert those rights of being US-funded, and painting the Philippines as the aggressor in persisting tensions, among others.

Some of these narratives are being spread by Filipino accounts allegedly employed by the Chinese embassy to be online trolls.

In defense of LANS and the WPS

Several Facebook posts came to LANS’ defense following the attacks against her.

“If you’re hating on a Filipina kid dahil sinabi niyang ATIN ang WPS, dalawa lang ang naiisip ko: isa kang bayaran o sadyang traydor ka sa bayan (If you’re hating on a Filipina kid because she said the WPS is ours, that can only mean two things: you’re a paid hack or you’re a traitor to the nation),” read one post.

These posts garnered as much as 33,000 engagements, significantly more than what the attacks against LANS had. This reflected a 2025 elections survey that found 8 out of 10 Filipinos preferring candidates who believe in asserting the Philippines’ rights over the WPS.

DEFENDING LANS. Disinformation against content creator LANS after her West Philippine Sea feature was also spotted in a comment section of a highly-engaged news report. The Nerve screenshots

Despite the overwhelming support, China continues to refuse to recognize the 2016 arbitral award.

It has only been a couple of weeks since the Philippines lambasted the “demeaning, dehumanizing, and racist” video from state-run media China Daily depicting the Filipinos as monkeys. Just last week, a member of the Chinese Coast Guard hit a Filipino soldier in the head in a clash at Ayungin Shoal. The same week, China blasted water cannons on Philippine ships two days in a row. – Rappler.com

World.title: Can Kazakhstan’s Non-Oil Economy Sustain the Country’s Growth Momentum?
World.content:
ALMATY – As oil production temporarily softens, Kazakhstan is increasingly relying on construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and agriculture to maintain economic momentum. Government officials argue that strengthening these sectors will not only offset weaker hydrocarbon output in the short term but also lay the foundation for more diversified and resilient long-term growth.

The strategy was at the center of a July 27 meeting of the government’s economic growth headquarters chaired by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin, where officials reviewed progress across key industries and outlined priorities for the remainder of the year.

Shifting the growth model

The government’s emphasis on non-resource industries reflects a broader effort to reduce Kazakhstan’s dependence on hydrocarbons. While oil continues to play a central role in the economy, authorities increasingly view construction, manufacturing, logistics and agriculture as the main engines capable of sustaining growth during periods of lower energy output.

Analysts note, however, that expanding output alone will not be enough to transform the economy. Analyst and policy expert Sobir Kurbanov argued that many regional value chains remain underdeveloped despite their potential.

“Value chains are there, but neither competitive nor complementary,” Kurbanov said, pointing particularly to agriculture and tourism. According to him, fragmented production, weak logistics, inconsistent standards and limited regional coordination continue to prevent Central Asia from developing cross-border industries capable of generating higher-value exports and creating sustainable jobs.

According to Zhumangarin, construction also remains the fastest-growing sector, with officials expecting strong performance through the first seven months of the year. The highest growth is projected in the Ulytau, Abai and Kyzylorda regions, supported by ongoing infrastructure investment.

Manufacturing has also emerged as one of the strongest contributors to economic expansion. Industrial output increased by 9.8%, driven by machinery production, which rose 23.2%, chemicals (19%), food processing (14.7%) and light industry, where production nearly doubled with an 89.2% increase. Authorities expect this momentum to continue in the coming months.

Domestic demand and logistics

Trade has remained another important pillar of growth. Total trade turnover reached 36.2 trillion tenge (US$67 billion), while the physical volume index rose 5.7% during the first half of the year. To sustain this trajectory, regional authorities have been instructed to accelerate the implementation of regional trade development roadmaps, including the launch of new investment projects.

Transport presents a more mixed picture. Although overall freight volumes continue to grow, expansion has been constrained by lower shipments of oil and natural gas. In response, the government plans to place greater emphasis on Kazakhstan’s role as a Eurasian transit corridor by maximizing rail and road transport capacity.

Agriculture’s expanding role

Agriculture is expected to remain another important contributor to economic growth this year, supported by the ongoing harvest campaign, livestock development and record levels of concessional financing for the agricultural sector.

One notable trend is the growing contribution of modern dairy farms financed through preferential lending programs launched in 2024 and 2025. Many of these facilities are now reaching full production capacity, contributing to higher milk output. According to Zhumangarin, during the first half of 2026, Kazakhstan produced 1.9 million tons of milk, a 2.4% increase compared with the same period last year.

Authorities also expect higher production of food and beverages as agricultural output expands.

Infrastructure as a long-term growth driver

Looking beyond short-term economic indicators, Zhumangarin stressed that Kazakhstan’s long-term growth strategy continues to rely on large-scale infrastructure development.

“In this regard, it is necessary to prepare high-quality projects now, which will ensure long-term economic effect and are provided for by the system of regional standards: facilities of healthcare and social sphere, paying special attention to bridges, crossings, key transport highways and energy facilities, funded by the republican budget,” he said.

While the government sees infrastructure investment and the expansion of non-oil industries as the foundation for long-term growth, analysts highlight that deeper structural reforms must accompany physical investment.

“Central Asia’s future path of development appeared to be less dependent on geopolitical shifts but more on the internal fundamentals,” Kurbanov said.

He argues that stronger institutions, higher productivity, investment in human capital, climate resilience and practical steps toward regional integration will ultimately determine whether the region can translate today’s economic momentum into sustainable long-term growth.

The approach reflects the government’s broader objective of combining immediate economic stimulus with investments designed to strengthen Kazakhstan’s long-term productive capacity. Rather than relying solely on commodity exports, policymakers increasingly see infrastructure expansion and the development of competitive non-oil industries as essential for sustaining future growth.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Rail Freight Growth Puts Infrastructure Expansion in Focus
World.content:
ALMATY – Freight volumes on Kazakhstan’s rail network continued to grow in the first half of 2026, underscoring the country’s expanding role in regional trade. But as cargo flows accelerate, the focus is shifting from record volumes to whether rail infrastructure can keep pace with demand.

Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) transported 157.1 million tons of cargo between January and June, a 3.5% increase compared to the same period last year. Domestic freight reached 82.2 million tons, while export shipments rose by 2.9 million tons to 45.6 million tons, reflecting stronger external demand for Kazakh commodities and agricultural products.

The latest figures build on the company’s record performance in 2025, when KTZ transported 319.8 million tons of cargo, up 5.5% year-on-year, driven by growth in exports, transit and imports.

Exports remain the key growth driver

Much of the increase continues to come from export-oriented industries. Coal remained the largest cargo category during the first half of the year, with 51.3 million tons transported, including 15.9 million tons exported.

Agricultural shipments also continued to expand. Rail transport of grain increased 10% to 7.3 million tons, while grain exports climbed 11% to 5.6 million tons. Even faster growth was recorded in higher-value agricultural products. Exports of processed grain products reached 1.1 million tons, up 20%, while feed shipments surged 51% to 2 million tons, reflecting Kazakhstan’s broader efforts to move beyond raw commodity exports.

Freight volumes also increased across other major industrial sectors, including oil products (13.3 million tons, +3.7%), iron ore (11.6 million tons, +15.1%), ferrous metals (8.1 million tons, +8.8%), non-ferrous ores and construction materials.

The figures suggest Kazakhstan’s rail network is carrying a diversified export basket while supporting domestic industrial activity.

Capacity expansion moves beyond new railways

To accommodate rising freight flows, KTZ has focused on expanding capacity through infrastructure upgrades, digitalization and fleet renewal rather than relying solely on new rail construction.

The company says artificial intelligence is already helping monitor 22,000 kilometers of railway infrastructure through its Smart Diagnostics system, allowing engineers to predict track defects up to 87 days in advance and significantly improve maintenance planning.

Automation projects now cover 3,000 kilometers of rail lines to increase capacity across seven major corridors.

KTZ has also introduced a unified digital wagon management platform, which the company estimates saves up to two billion tenge (US$3.7 million) annually by reducing empty wagon movements and improving fleet utilization. In parallel, it is deploying Wabtec’s Kinetix system, enabling rolling stock to be inspected while trains remain in motion.

Rolling stock expansion is also accelerating. Subsidiary Kaztemirtrans, which currently operates more than 39,500 freight wagons, plans to purchase 13,000 additional freight cars between 2027 and 2031, including 10,000 gondola wagons, 2,100 covered wagons and 900 grain hoppers. Between 2023 and 2025, the company already added 3,000 new gondola wagons manufactured domestically to transport socially important cargo such as coal and grain.

Building a logistics hub requires more than higher freight volumes

Alongside domestic investments, KTZ is strengthening international partnerships to improve multimodal connectivity. During a June 23 business conference in Brussels, the company signed a new cooperation agreement with A.P. Moller – Maersk to expand container transport along the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, or Middle Corridor. Discussions with DHL Global Forwarding focused on developing integrated multimodal services linking China, Central Asia, Türkiye and Europe.

KTZ is also expanding supporting infrastructure, including the first phase of a new container hub in Aktau Port and the KIF Warehouses logistics complex on the Kazakh-Chinese border.

According to IFC Regional Head of Industry for Infrastructure and Natural Resources for the Middle East and Central Asia Laura Vecvagare, the investments reflect the scale of the challenge facing Kazakhstan.

“Kazakhstan’s rail network extends more than 16,000 kilometers, ranking among the top 30 countries globally by network length,” she wrote in her opinion article for the Astana Times.

“However, structural constraints remain, including extensive single-track segments, limited electrification, asset depreciation, growing loads and border bottlenecks. These challenges translate into slower rail movements and longer dwell times, which limit throughput on busy routes, require costly workarounds and constrain Kazakhstan’s full potential as a transport and logistics hub,” she added.

Vecvagare noted that the government has adopted the Railway Transport Development Program 2029, while KTZ is preparing a major investment program for 2025-2029 to modernize core infrastructure.

“The scale and urgency of these investments call for blended support, combining public commitments with private capital mobilized through trusted partners,” she said.

For Kazakhstan, steadily rising freight volumes are therefore only one part of the story. Sustaining growth will depend on whether investments in infrastructure, rolling stock, digital technologies and international logistics partnerships can remove long-standing bottlenecks and enable the rail network to handle increasing trade flows across Eurasia.

World.title: Türkiye and Kazakhstan Need Processing Alliance, Not Another Extraction Rush
World.content:
At the Astana Mining and Metallurgy Congress in June, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said Kazakhstan wanted to become a regional hub for processing and higher-value manufacturing. That should force Ankara to revisit the mining memorandum signed in July 2025, which emphasised joint exploration and production. If bilateral co-operation ends at the mine mouth, it will already be behind Kazakhstan’s own industrial policy.

Türkiye and Kazakhstan need a processing alliance, not an ore-for-machinery bargain

Joint work should extend from beneficiation and metallurgy to alloys, permanent-magnet materials, processing equipment, recycling and environmental control. If Kazakhstan supplies concentrate while Türkiye imports the refined chemicals, magnets or specialised components needed by its factories from established producers elsewhere, both will remain outside the most strategic stages.

The excitement around Kazakhstan’s mineral potential makes this distinction urgent. In April 2025, the government announced an estimated rare-earth resource of more than 20 million tonnes at the Zhana Kazakhstan site, including neodymium, cerium, lanthanum and yttrium. The estimate still requires confirmation as an economically recoverable reserve. Even if confirmed, geology alone will not create industrial power. Refining concentration continued to rise in 2025 and that planned magnet production in diversified regions amounts to only about one-third of expected rare-earth mining capacity by 2035. The bottleneck is what happens after extraction.

That middle of the chain is technically demanding. Ore must be characterised, concentrated, separated and refined before it becomes high-purity metal, alloy powder or a usable component. Plants also need specialised equipment, laboratories, water treatment and reliable maintenance. These activities create engineering knowledge and supplier demand; an offtake agreement does not.

The two countries have complementary starting points, but neither should exaggerate them. Kazakhstan has operating mines, metallurgy and trained engineers. Türkiye has an export-oriented machinery industry and is developing rare-earth processing knowledge through the Beylikova pilot plant and the Rare Earth Elements Research Institute. It is not yet a substitute for the countries dominating separation, advanced magnets and specialised equipment. A credible alliance would bring in technology partners from Japan, South Korea, Europe or Southeast Asia where necessary, rather than present dependence as self-sufficiency.

The division of labour should follow industrial logic. Beneficiation and primary metallurgy will usually make more sense near Kazakh deposits, avoiding the shipment of low-grade material and retaining local value. Turkish firms can supply process machinery, power electronics, automation, precision parts and environmental systems, while Turkish industrial clusters provide demand for refined metals, alloys and magnet materials. Joint laboratories should qualify outputs for automotive, machinery, energy and electronics customers. Technology licences and engineering teams should be shared, instead of leaving one side with the mine and the other with the purchase order.

Southeast Asia makes this more than a bilateral Central Asian project. ASEAN’s Minerals Cooperation Action Plan for 2026–30 explicitly seeks upstream-to-downstream development, technology adoption and stronger human capacity. Indonesia’s nickel policy has shown that domestic processing can be created quickly, but also that foreign-led technology and excess capacity can accompany the boom. Malaysia, meanwhile, is seeking investment in environmentally responsible rare-earth processing and super-magnet production. The lesson is not to copy an export ban, but to build capabilities that can enter several regional supply chains without allowing one foreign operator or market to control them.

A Türkiye–Kazakhstan alliance could serve those chains selectively. Kazakh tungsten processed into hard-metal powders and Turkish cutting tools could supply machinery users in Thailand, Viet Nam and Malaysia. Rare-earth materials, once commercially proven, could support motor and electronics production, while recycling partnerships with ASEAN firms recover magnets and metals from end-of-life equipment. This would offer Southeast Asian manufacturers another supplier relationship without pretending that Kazakhstan or Türkiye can replace China across the whole chain.

Environmental rules must be part of the commercial model. Mineral separation can consume substantial energy and water and generate hazardous residues; weak oversight would turn strategic ambition into a local pollution problem. Each project should publish water and emissions baselines, tailings plans, closure finance and traceability data. Recycling should begin before large waste volumes arrive. The IEA expects secondary supply’s contribution to key energy minerals to rise from roughly 10 per cent today towards 20 percent by 2040, but only if collection and recovery systems are built beforehand.

The strongest objection is cost. New refining projects outside dominant suppliers face higher capital expenditure, scarce equipment and uncertain prices. The IEA estimates capital costs can be 20 to more than 150 percent higher, with operating costs around 50 per cent higher on average. A complete national value chain is therefore unrealistic. A selective bilateral chain is not: it should focus on products with confirmed deposits, contracted buyers and a credible technology route.

Ankara and Astana should establish a Türkiye–Kazakhstan Critical Minerals Processing Alliance under their High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council. Its first portfolio should test three projects: a tungsten-to-tooling line; a rare-earth separation and magnet-material pilot contingent on verified ore economics; and a platform for recovering valuable metals from metallurgical waste, used equipment and electronic scrap. A joint project-preparation facility should complete technical studies, environmental assessments and offtake negotiations before public finance is committed.

Support should be released against measurable outcomes: qualified local suppliers, engineers trained, recovery rates achieved, water reused, process knowledge shared and sales to third markets. Extraction-only projects should not receive strategic incentives. ASEAN buyers and technology firms should be invited into selected projects, while Kazakhstan and Türkiye retain diversified ownership, transparent procurement and access to operational data.

A mining agreement can secure tonnes. A processing alliance secures competence. If ore leaves Kazakhstan while Turkish factories continue buying the decisive materials and technologies from dominant refiners, the partnership will merely rearrange the route of dependency. It becomes strategic only when Kazakh resources, Turkish industrial capability and external technology produce materials that factories in Europe and Southeast Asia buy repeatedly.

The author is Mehmet Enes Beşer, a researcher focusing on ASEAN, and a graduate of Sociology in Boğaziçi University. He is the ASEAN Coordinator at Vatan Party (Türkiye) and a member of the Editorial Board of Teori magazine.
