World.title: Two powerful earthquakes hit Japan within an hour
World.content:
Japan's south-western Kyushu island has been struck by two strong earthquakes within an hour, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).

An initial magnitude-7.1 quake hit the Kumamoto south-western prefecture at 4:35pm local time (5:35pm AEST) on Tuesday.

The prefecture was then struck by 26 additional aftershocks ranging in magnitude between 3.3 and 4.5, before a magnitude-6.1 tremor was recorded at 5:12pm (6:12pm AEST).

Loading...

The quakes hit just south of the town of Uki, near the prefecture's capital city, local authorities reported.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said.

"Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed."

One hospital had reported more than 50 injuries, according to Japan's public broadcaster NHK.

NHK is also reporting people have been trapped inside a shopping mall damaged in the earthquake.

Police earlier said they had received reports of what sounded like an explosion at the Aeon Mall outlet in Kumamoto, with no information on damage or any casualties.

Seismology authorities from Geoscience Australia and the United States Geological Survey reported the initial quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometres below the sea's surface.

A tsunami warning for a wave measuring 1 metre was issued after the earthquake, the JMA said.

The warning was lifted about two hours later.

Japan's south-western Kumamoto prefecture has been hit by a magnitude-7.1 earthquake, followed by a magnitude-6.1 tremor less than an hour later. (Reuters)

Urgent government response

The Japanese government also issued emergency earthquake warnings for Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga, Oita, and Miyazaki prefectures, all on Japan's southern Kyushu island.

The tremor caused power outages for at least 48,000 households in the Kumamoto prefecture and fires broke out in several locations, Japan's state broadcaster NHK reported.

Ms Takaichi also confirmed a meeting of the country's Emergency Assembly Team was called in the Countermeasures Room to assess the quake.

She said local fire stations were responding to the incidents and urged all people to stay away from the coast.

"The investigation team was dispatched from the government cabinet office and human and physical casualties have been investigated," Ms Takaichi told the media.

"There are places where power outages are taking place. I urge people to take shelter and evacuate to safe places."

The extent of damage to the area is being assessed. (Supplied: Nippon Hoso Kyokai )

Local media outlet NHK reported that police are seeking the whereabouts of nine people.

NHK also reported a train was derailed during the earthquake.

Ms Takaichi released a statement on X that urged local government ministries and emergency response agencies to immediately assess damage and to prioritise any necessary rescue of residents.

Japan is one of the world's most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes.

Japanese authorities warned of a tsunami risk in at least two south-western prefectures moments after the quake struck. (Supplied: JMA)

Earthquake prone area

Located along the "Ring of Fire" of volcanoes and oceanic trenches partly encircling ⁠the Pacific Basin, ‌Japan accounts for about 20 per cent ‌of the world's earthquakes of magnitude-6 or more.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

Kyushu Electric Power said there were no ‌reports of irregularities at ⁠its Sendai and Genkai nuclear power stations after the earthquake.

Japan's Nuclear Regulation Authority said no abnormalities were found at three nearby nuclear power plants.

Train operator JR Kyushu said it had suspended ⁠services, including its high-speed Shinkansen trains following the quake.

AP/Reuters

World.title: With a forceful declaration, Ben Carroll halted Jacinta Allan's agenda
World.content:
With a forceful declaration, Ben Carroll brought the Allan government's agenda to a skidding halt.

"Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews, I am not Jacinta Allan," the new Victorian premier said.

This was a clear distinction offered up by the new premier in his maiden speech to journalists and the public. It was deliberate.

With this statement he's given himself less than four months to convince Victorians that their lives and the state will be different under his leadership.

It's a big ask.

Allan's critics often complained she had failed to differentiate herself from Andrews's dominant reign.

Already, Carroll has put integrity front and centre of his new regime, committing to a royal commission into the construction sector and a special prosecutor to probe corruption.

This is designed to cauterise the allegations of criminality on government building sites that dogged Allan and ultimately triggered the first knifing of a Victorian Labor premier this century.

While he was all smiles after he won the ballot, Carroll needs to show Victorians he is serious about poor behaviour.

Ben Carroll was smiling as he left the chaotic meeting where he was eventually elected as leader. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Allan's refusal to act has meant some voters now believe the government has something to hide.

It may mean difficult hearings for Labor supporters with the record of Jacinta Allan and her predecessors potentially coming under the microscope.

But this is all part of Carroll's message.

"It is clear that Victorians want change," he said.

" That change starts today. "

Labor desperate for clear air

Carroll is also pledging to be more pro-business and tougher on crime.

It sounds a bit like a Coalition pitch, but one he'll try to steer to middle and working class Victorians: the communities that polls show have deserted Labor.

It's also a pitch to return Labor to the type of centrist, Labor right faction-leaning government championed by past premiers Steve Bracks and John Brumby from 1999–2010.

Carroll, like Bracks, is from Labor's right faction, while Allan and Andrews were from the left.

Bracks says Carroll's immediate commitments on integrity will give him "clear air" to promote his own agenda.

"Essentially he's really saying, 'I am my own man, judge me on what I will do,'" Bracks told ABC's Afternoon Briefing.

"He didn't say he's not Steve Bracks," he quipped.

The other spectre that looms is the $34.5 billion Suburban Rail Loop — Allan's signature project.

Will Carroll pause the project that is eating up billions of dollars? At his first press conference he said he had no announcements to make.

That's not a no.

Ben Carroll appears at his first press conference as Victorian premier, alongside Gabrielle Williams, who will serve as his deputy. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Carroll is biting off a lot in just four months. And there's only three more sitting weeks before Victorians head to the polls in November.

But Labor is desperate. That's why they've acted.

To use Carroll's own words: "Circumstances have changed."

Carroll's ScoMo moment

Ben Carroll will also have to convince Victorians he can be trusted.

There's a transactional cost of a coup, especially when he famously looked his former boss in the eye at a June press conference and said he supported her because he wanted his daughter to be proud he backed her.

It was his ScoMo moment.

Scott Morrison famously hugged then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull, saying he was "ambitious" for his leader before replacing him a few days later.

He went on to win the 2019 election.

Carroll will also have to rebuild trust with a caucus who have been battered and bruised by their first hostile leadership takeover since 1999.

Jacinta Allan walks into Labor caucus meeting flanked by her loyal minister Sonya Kilkenny, who went on to make a chaotic, failed bid for leadership. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

As Victorians waited to hear the outcome of the Labor leadership ballot, those of us waiting outside could actually hear the yelling from inside the caucus room.

I've stood outside that party room many times before and I've never heard yelling like that.

The messages coming out from MPs were this room is a mess. This is chaos. This is diabolical.

From here, Labor and Carroll have just four months to keep it together.

Ben Carroll pictured after he was unanimously elected as state Labor leader following the resignation of premier Jacinta Allan. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

This isn't necessarily about winning the election.

It's about stopping the bleeding and ensuring the party doesn't get decimated on election day. It's a possibility many feared.

Allan's appalling personal approval ratings were a drag on the vote, and it meant voters weren't even willing to consider Labor.

Carroll is trying to change that by at least being part of the conversation.

The public has shown at the last two elections that it's sceptical on the Liberal Party's credentials to govern.

This change may let Labor re-enter the discussion, especially with One Nation's resurgence.

One Nation's influence complicates the electoral calculus, with Labor figures believing the Coalition will not be able to win a majority but will instead have to rely on One Nation.

So if Labor can save some of the furniture and be a strong opposition it could find itself back in power in four years.

Ben Carroll is setting himself up to do much more. The clock is ticking.

World.title: Hanson reveals who paid for Italy trip with Gina Rinehart
World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has confirmed mining magnate Gina Rinehart paid for her flights from London to Sicily, via Rome, and for her to attend a high-end fashion parade on the luxurious Italian island.

Senator Hanson updated her parliamentary register of interests on Tuesday and also confirmed she personally paid for her accommodation, meals and other daily expenses during the trip from July 11 to 16.

The trip made headlines when the pair were spotted seaside in Sicily, but until now she had not revealed how the travel was funded, other than to insist taxpayers did not pay "one cent".

Ms Hanson has previously declared a series of gifts from Mrs Rinehart and Hancock Prospecting in her register, including interstate flights, hospitality and a "bloody big orange bulldozer" that was gifted by the billionaire on stage at a regional summit while she made bulldozer sounds.

The disclosure log reveals Pauline Hanson, right, attended two Dolce & Gabbana fashion shows in Italy earlier this month. (Instagram: @beatyesterday_art)

The updated disclosure does not include reference to how her flights from Australia to London were funded, although if she personally footed the bill, she would not have to declare that.

The ABC has asked Ms Hanson's office how these flights were paid for.

Senator Hanson last week posted an apparent pitch from producers for Seven's Spotlight, which filmed part of her London visit, suggesting the program might cover some of her UK travel costs.

In the document, a senior producer said Spotlight wanted Senator Hanson to meet UK Reform leader Nigel Farage in Britain, but this fell through after he resigned from parliament around the time the pair were due to meet.

Instead, Senator Hanson took part in a podcast interview hosted by UK far-right activist Tommy Robinson, who has an extensive criminal record and has served prison sentences for offences including assault, fraud and contempt of court.

Hanson defends Europe trip, anti-immigration comments In her first appearance since returning to Australia, Pauline Hanson fields questions about her trip to Europe with billionaire Gina Rinehart.

She also participated in a street walk with Mr Robinson, whose real name is Stephen-Yaxley Lennon, in his hometown of Luton.

A Seven spokesperson later said the program only paid for "incidentals" related to the interactions with Mr Robinson, "including a vehicle used in the production process and a hotel room used for filming purposes as well as security to protect Seven staff while recording on UK streets".

Mrs Rinehart and Senator Hanson have appeared to grow increasingly close over recent months, as the senator's popularity in published opinion polls has soared.

In April, the Queensland senator also accepted a new $1 million Cirrus G7 plane from Mrs Rinehart, which she described as "sexy" and "fast".

World.title: Ocean search for missing baby boy suspended because of rough weather
World.content:
The search for a three-month-old baby boy still missing after the bodies of his mother and sister were recovered from waters off SA's South East has been suspended because of weather conditions, police say.

Police said it was too dangerous to continue the search off Port MacDonnell, and it was halted about 3:30pm on Tuesday but that it would resume tomorrow morning.

Superintendent Trent Cox, officer in charge of the Limestone Coast Region, said while police held grave concerns, they would leave "no stone unturned".

"The information we have from survivability experts is that it is very, very unlikely the missing baby has survived," he said.

"[But] we will continue to search until the expert advice tells us that there is no prospect of finding the child alive."

Emergency services have searched the area for a second day. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

The girl who died was 23 months old, while their mother was a 36-year-old from Compton, near Mount Gambier.

Their bodies were recovered on Monday.

"We are keeping a very open mind as to the circumstances that led to the mother and daughter being in the water, and the other child being missing," Superintendent Cox said.

"There are a number of scenarios we're investigating."

Police said today's weather conditions had been challenging, and that high winds had meant the search was confined to land.

"[Conditions] did not enable us to get water assets on the water," Superintendent Cox said.

Earlier, authorities said the missing boy was "about" two months old, and Superintendent Cox later described him as a three-month-old.

Police investigating 'number of theories'

The tragedy first came to light about 11:15am on Monday, when emergency services were called to Cape Northumberland, a headland near Port MacDonnell distinguished by rugged cliffs.

Police said the woman's car — a white Isuzu MU-X, with South Australian registration S592 BJR — was found "abandoned with its engine running".

They said there was "no information to suggest" anyone else was involved in the incident.

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas today sounded a note of caution, warning that there was a need to be "careful not to jump to conclusions".

"It's very difficult at this point in time to understand exactly what transpired here," Mr Malinauskas said.

"There are a number of theories that the police are actively investigating."

The area is characterised by its rough conditions. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

Police have asked anyone with information about the woman's car, or with dash cam footage that could assist, to contact them.

The search and investigation has involved SES volunteers, SA Police's Water Operations Unit, Major Crime investigators, the Forensic Response Section and other maritime agencies.

Superintendent Cox said weather conditions were expected to be more favourable on Wednesday.

"The forecast is that it's not as extreme as today — still challenging. It's an exposed area," he said.

"We'll be out there at first light again, we'll hold a briefing for our emergency services personnel and volunteers who are assisting, as well as the police."

The search was expected to resume about 8am.

World.title: Cairns man jailed for fatally stabbing housemate in fight
World.content:
A Cairns man has been sentenced to seven years' jail for stabbing his housemate to death in a fight.

Steven Edward Anderson, 69, pleaded guilty to manslaughter at the Supreme Court in Cairns this afternoon.

The court heard Anderson was on parole for drug offences when, in the early hours of May 10, 2023, he wrestled a knife from Darren "Lenny" Smith, 57, and stabbed him three times.

The fight occurred at a home in the suburb of White Rock, where Anderson and Mr Smith each rented a bedroom.

Mr Smith had been living there for about two years, the court heard.

Anderson, a long-term friend of live-in home owner Angela Tanner, had moved in about three months before the fatal fight.

Loud music and a fight

The court heard Mr Smith had been drinking and listening to music throughout the evening that led up to the confrontation.

Anderson needed to get up early the next morning and, at one point, yelled at Mr Smith to "turn the f***ing music down" before going for a drive to "cool off".

The fatal fight happened at a share house in the suburb of White Rock. (ABC Far North: Kristy Sexton-McGrath)

Ms Tanner took a speaker from a drunk Mr Smith, told him to go to bed, and warned him that if he could not get along with Anderson, one of the men would have to leave.

But about 1:20am, Ms Tanner woke to Mr Smith yelling, "Come out and fight" and, "I've got more right to be here than you," the court heard.

Mr Smith had used a permanent marker to write threatening messages on a fridge he and Anderson shared.

Crown prosecutor Nicole Friedewald said it was "not known with any certainty" who introduced the knife to the fight, but it was accepted Mr Smith may have taken it from the kitchen.

"During that fight, wrestle, as it was described by the defendant himself — he stabbed Mr Smith three times to the chest," Ms Friedewald said.

One of the wounds damaged Mr Smith's left lung and heart, the court heard.

Crown prosecutor Nicole Friedewald told the court Anderson continued the fight after disarming Mr Smith. (ABC Far North: Brendan Mounter)

Anderson called Triple Zero (000) and tried to resuscitate Mr Smith until emergency services arrived.

Mr Smith died at the scene after emergency surgery failed to suture lacerations to his heart, Ms Friedewald said.

Father-of-two's death left 'terrible void'

Ms Friedewald read a statement to the court on behalf of Mr Smith's former wife Aya Eto, describing how his death had greatly affected her and their two teenage sons.

"Darren's guidance, love and presence are forever gone, leaving a terrible void that is impossible to fill," she said.

"Bringing up boys in a foreign country has always been challenging since my first baby was born but it became much harder since Darren died.

"It has been very painful to watch the boys going through their grief."

Steven Edward Anderson was initially charged with murder but pleaded guilty to manslaughter. (ABC News: Mark Rigby)

Mr Smith's brother, Michael, also made a statement describing Mr Smith as a "knowledgeable man" and well-respected architect who moved to Cairns "looking for a challenge to fuel the need to excel".

He said months before his brother's death, a "distressed" Mr Smith had called him saying he wanted to move home to Victoria.

"Mum often says she is the one in jail; she is the one serving time for her son," his statement said.

" We are always thinking about how this tragedy could have been prevented. "

Two men had 'history'

Anderson was initially charged with murder.

Defence barrister Brydie Bilic said there was a "broader history" between the two men, stemming from an incident where Anderson invited some friends to the home and a fire broke out.

Anderson had since been diagnosed with "incurable" prostate cancer while in custody, the court heard.

In sentencing, Justice James Henry said Mr Smith's behaviour on the night was "irritating" and "provocative" but Anderson "elected to continue on [the fight] while armed, rather than resist and retreat".

With time served, Anderson is eligible to apply for parole immediately.

World.title: Country footy player charged after 'ugly' scenes in southern WA
World.content:
A country football player has been charged with assault and choking after clashes during a game in southern Western Australia.

The man was allegedly involved in two incidents during Sunday's Lower South West Football League clash in Kojonup between the hometown Cougars and the Bridgetown Bulldogs.

Footage of two incidents during the game prompted public outcry and a police investigation.

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed Kojonup Police, with assistance from Busselton detectives, charged the man, from Cowaramup, with assault occasioning bodily harm and "impeding another person's breathing or blood circulation by applying pressure to the neck".

The Cowaramup man is accused of choking an opposing player. (Supplied)

On Tuesday WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch said violence on the football field was "not on".

"You are not immune on the sporting field," he said.

"We understand there are normal contacts in the spirit of play, but if it is outside of play and a deliberate targeted attack, then it is an assault."

Loading...

Game 'turned ugly'

Kojonup Football Club vice-president Matt Marinoni said the top-of-the-table clash was a "tense and fiery" game that "turned ugly".

He said the umpires did not see the off-ball incident.

"Then there was a lot of noise in the crowd," Mr Marinoni said.

"From there there was a bit of a wrestle and melee because we saw one of our teammates was on the ground, unconscious."

That player is in good spirits and recovering from his facial injuries and concussion, but is "shaken", according to the club.

A spokesperson from the Lower South West Football League told the ABC it was aware of the incident.

"The matter has been referred to the Country Football WA tribunal process and will be dealt with in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures," the spokesperson said.

The league declined to comment further, in order to "preserve the integrity and fairness of the tribunal process".

The Bridgetown Football Club said the matter was being dealt with by Country Football WA.

"[We] do not condone the behaviour shown during Sunday's game," the club said in a statement.

"This has no place in football and does not reflect the true values of our club."

The 23-year-old is due to face the Katanning Magistrates Court in August.

World.title: Prison worker stands trial accused of raping inmate
World.content:
A prison worker is standing trial in South Australia's District Court charged with the alleged rape of a female prisoner at an Adelaide prison facility.

Enio Screpanti has pleaded not guilty to the aggravated indecent assault and rape of the woman on separate occasions in the early 2020s.

Opening the trial on Tuesday, prosecutor Christine Hanna told the jury that both alleged incidents had occurred when Mr Screpanti and the victim had been alone together.

"On one occasion … the accused asked [the alleged victim] to accompany him to the gym," Ms Hanna said.

"And while they were together alone in the gym the accused asked [the alleged victim] to walk on the treadmill while it was in use so that he could check it."

Ms Hanna said it was alleged Mr Screpanti had then sexually assaulted the woman.

She told the jury the alleged victim was again alone with Mr Screpanti several months later and, on that occasion, he "asked [her] to come to a shed as they had a job to do".

Ms Hanna said it was alleged the now 67-year-old then raped her.

Enio Screpanti has pleaded not guilty to the charges. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The prosecutor told the jury two prisoners would be called to give evidence about interactions between the alleged victim and Mr Screpanti.

"There were physical incidents which are not the subject of charges," Ms Hanna said.

"[Prisoner] Angie Walsh saw an incident where the accused pinned [the alleged victim] by her arms against a pantry."

Ms Hanna told the jury another prisoner, Nicole McGuinness, had seen Mr Screpanti exiting the bathroom where the alleged victim was taking a shower.

"On the prosecution case that evidence still has a part to play in your (the jury) consideration and deliberations on the charged acts," Ms Hanna said.

"That evidence is not introduced into this trial to simply paint the accused in a bad light," she said.

"It is introduced to you for a particular reason … it is evidence, the prosecution say, about the way the accused related to [the alleged victim].

"It might for example assist you to understand how [the alleged victim] responded to the alleged charged acts.

"It might also help you to understand that the alleged charged acts did not come out of the blue."

Enio Screpanti was working at an Adelaide prison facility at the time of the alleged offences. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Screpanti's defence lawyer Gilbert Aitken urged the jury to carefully scrutinise the evidence of witnesses.

"I ask you to keep in mind what a witness actually saw as distinct from what may have been assumed," he said.

"Some witnesses, namely prisoners or ex-prisoners may have reason for things like resentment, hostility or indeed self-interest.

"This, as you've heard, is a prison case. The defence says that context matters."

Mr Aitken said the jury would also be told about "the loss of CCTV evidence that is no longer available".

The trial is continuing.

World.title: Commonwealth Games LIVE: Aths program to heat up with 100m finals, Peter Bol to hit the track

Australia’s Torrie Lewis. Eddie Jim

World.title: Health boss grilled over lack of Indigenous directors on three hospital boards
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandPublic service Health boss grilled over lack of Indigenous directors on three hospital boards Matt Dennien July 28, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren has claimed the lack of legally required First Nations members on three hospital service boards is the result of “unscheduled vacancies”, despite the departures being forced or known in advance of a recent major overhaul. The comments, made during the state budget estimates hearing of a parliamentary committee, came amid accusations the Crisafulli LNP has sought to unpick Indigenous representation and policies in a push dubbed “Project Invisibility”. After reports from the ABC last month highlighting the lack of First Nations directors in the state’s largest hospital and health services – Metro North and Metro South, the latter of which also caters to the greatest Indigenous population – Rosengren faced questions on Tuesday. Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren at Tuesday’s estimates hearing. Queensland parliament Quizzed by Labor’s opposition health spokesperson, Mark Bailey, Rosengren confirmed the Sunshine Coast hospital board was also lacking a First Nations director, which is a requirement under legislation governing the 16 bodies running public health services.



“Very recently, the process to undertake a scheduled recruitment across all of the hospital and health boards was completed, and with the appointment of a substantive number of new board members in April of this year,” Rosengren said. “Subsequent to that process, there are three boards where they’ve experienced resignations of board members that are identified First Nations, and there is an active recruitment campaign that is nearing an end to identify appropriate replacements for those unscheduled vacancies that exist on the board structure. “But the other 13 of the HHS’s all have an identified First Nations board director, including three of our hospital and health boards where their chair is an identified First Nations [person], and that is a nation-leading framework for our boards in Queensland.” After changing the law to allow the sacking of health board directors without reason, on March 27 Health Minister Tim Nicholls announced 50 new additions to the boards – including three former LNP figures – after a months-long two-yearly appointment round overhaul.





Queensland Health was yet to provide a response before publication to questions seeking clarification of Rosengren’s comments. Editor's pick Public service LNP-sponsor data centre firm taps ex-premier to join major meetings Former truth-telling inquiry chair Joshua Creamer suggested last month the Crisafulli government had a deliberate strategy, dubbed “Project Invisibility”, to wind back First Nations representation and policies. The government has said its focus has been on “redirecting funds into practical, locally led projects which deliver tangible outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander discrete communities through our Closing the Gap Priorities Fund”. World.title: This Lion has no fears after two concussions. But there’s a deeper issue
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 This Lion has no fears after two concussions. But there’s a deeper issue Nick Wright Updated July 28, 2026 — 8:12pm ,first published 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Even after suffering two concussions within three weeks, Noah Answerth insists the thought of premature retirement has never crossed his mind. “Not really, no. Concussion is going to happen in our game, I guess, and you can’t really help it – I signed up to play,” he said. “I got concussed when I was a young kid playing, and I just love the game, so concussion isn’t really going to stop me from getting my chance to play AFL.” The Lions’ Noah Answerth suffered back-to-back concussions this year. Getty Images After copping a knee to the head in round three against St Kilda and missing two weeks under concussion protocols, Answerth suffered another blow upon his comeback against Melbourne, leading teammate Harris Andrews to voice his concern for the 26-year-old’s wellbeing.



The Lions were diligent in his recovery – sidelining him for five weeks – and he has returned to become a pillar of Brisbane’s top-four charge. Related Article AFL 2026 Bailey-Ashcroft double act powers Lions to seventh straight win Having averaged six touches and 1.6 rebound 50s in his first five games of the season, his past six have yielded 14.17 disposals, 2.5 rebound 50s, and 2.5 tackles an outing. Ahead of his 100th AFL appearance on Saturday, against Carlton, Answerth revealed it was other injuries – a ruptured Achilles suffered at Marvel Stadium last year, and a back concern from his teenage days – that had left him fearing this milestone would be unattainable. “When I was 17, I fractured my L1 vertebrae. I thought about not playing ever again after that, but just the confidence [my coaches] had in me to keep going, and obviously Brisbane to take a chance … I’m lucky enough to still be here,” Answerth said.



“The club looked after me really well [during the concussions]. Coming back from my Achilles as well, it gave me a bit more time to prepare and play at the level I wanted to. “I think coming back, you’re a bit hampered from the Achilles, and a bit slower, and it probably affects you a little bit, so having that time actually allowed me to probably improve. Noah Answerth in action against Port Adelaide. Getty Images “I haven’t had any effects. I’m happy and love playing footy and working and studying. If anything, it’s probably put myself more into focus.” Concern for the long-term impacts of head trauma is at an all-time high, with young Lions defender Ty Gallop drawing the ire of pundits after he tackled Port Adelaide rival Mitch Georgiades.



Georgiades had just returned from a concussion lay-off, and the sight of Gallop appearing to slam him back down, with his head hitting the turf, garnered a serious misconduct charge. Gallop faced the AFL Tribunal on Tuesday night and copped a three-game suspension, pleading guilty to what he insisted was retaliation after believing the Power star had grabbed at his broken thumb. “For Ty, it’s a competitive game, and we all try and be competitive. Sometimes you may have a brain fade like that, which is always hard, but you don’t mean it in that way – sometimes you’re playing the game and things happen,” Answerth said. Loading “I think he’s a gentle giant really, he’s doing a lot of work with Harris – I actually sort of see him as that Harris Andrews-type of character.



“I daresay he’ll be a very good leader for us in the future … [the incident] was very out of character.” According to the AFL Players’ Association’s Insights and Impacts Report, 82 per cent of players had a “high level of concern” for the long-term implications of concussion. Related Article AFL 2026 Fagan factor: Will coach’s future keep dynamic duo at Lions? While 86 per cent reported their concussions, a fifth still “somewhat, or completely, downplayed the severity of their symptoms”, with concerns about losing their spot on the team the overwhelming reason. With each instance of concussion, according to UQ’s Queensland Brain Institute expert Professor Fatima Nasrallah, the likelihood of further concussions increases. That is why she has a greater fear for those playing at the grassroots, where there is less attention and medical support.



Nasrallah is nearing the end of a three-year study into adolescent concussions to find a more concrete biomarker assessment of a head trauma, but said a cultural stigma hindering concussion reporting made recruiting participants a challenge. She appealed for greater funding to be injected into schools and junior clubs to ensure they are better equipped to protect and inform athletes. “You’ll go to a game which has under-12s – if it’s soccer, they’re heading the ball; if it’s rugby, they’re going full force – and there is no mandate for them to actually follow guidelines,” Nasrallah said. “We know the developing brain is a lot more vulnerable to change. A lot more effort has to go into the children to change the culture – it’s peer pressure, it’s wanting to have a career in the space. “People are reluctant to be involved in research studies because the moment they label themselves as having a concussion, they can’t go back to play. Parents don’t want to know about it – the children are influenced by the parents – and there has to be a change in culture from an early age.



“If you look at a broader scale, particularly in regional and remote areas, you’ll find that number is much higher in terms of the under-reporting.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘It’s a very bad look’: Premiership Lion hit with three-match ban, apologises for incident
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Ty Gallop admits his retaliation against Mitch Georgiades “wasn’t fair”.

James Hird is among the candidates to advance to the next round of the Essendon coaching search.

Collingwood spiritual leader Brayden Maynard is set for surgery on his leg. Brisbane defender Ty Gallop has been suspended for three games for a serious misconduct act he admits is a “very bad look” for the AFL. Gallop pleaded guilty at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday for what he described as retaliation on Mitch Georgiades after the Port Adelaide forward grabbed his broken thumb. The 20-year-old had tackled Georgiades to the ground during Sunday’s clash in Brisbane and, after the ball left the area, shoved the Port attacker face-first into the turf. The moment that had Ty Gallop in hot water. Fox Footy



Gallop played the match with strapping on a broken right thumb. “Mitch has grabbed my thumb as I have gone to stand up,” Gallop said, adding Georgiades’ action was intentional. But Gallop expressed remorse for retaliating, saying he had phoned Georgiades to apologise. “Looking back now and watching the footage, I understand that the retaliation to what happened wasn’t fair,” he said. Mitch Georgiades clashes with Gallop at the Gabba. AFL Photos



“I have gone out of my way to push him down, which I am sorry for and I do regret. I’d like to have that time over again. “It’s a very bad look and there’s no room for it in footy.” Gallop said his retaliation was an “immediate reaction”. “I have grabbed the back of his jersey and pushed him back into the ground,” he said. “I think I play a hard brand of footy, but I play a very fair brand of footy as well ... it was purely out of retaliation.”



Under questioning from the AFL’s counsel Nick Pane KC, Gallop agreed his act was totally unreasonable and unacceptable. Pane asked the tribunal for a three-game suspension. “Georgiades’ head made forceful contact with the ground,” Pane said. “The action had significant potential to cause serious injury.” The Port spearhead wasn’t hurt in the incident.

- AAP Bombers narrow down shortlist, ex-Socceroos and Victory hard man to help choose their next coach



Peter Ryan Essendon have settled on four candidates, including club legend James Hird, to move into the second phase of the selection process to fill their vacant senior coaching position. Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis have already met with club president Andrew Welsh, CEO Tim Roberts and board member Ted Richards as part of the initial coffee chat. James Hird is a panellist on Footy Classified and the coaching director of VFL club Port Melbourne. Nine Two competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the four candidates will now move to the next phase of the process, which will include interviews by Melbourne Victory great and former coach Kevin Muscat, and long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop.



That pair has been invited to be part of the process to complement the current selection panel of Welsh, Roberts, Richards, club vice president and ex-Victory chairman Anthony Di Pietro and the Essendon’s general manager of people and culture, Caroline Monzon. The Bombers were keen to include coaching experts in the selection process as they sort through the candidates. Mark McVeigh during his time as interim coach of the Giants. AFL Photos Muscat coached the Victory in the A-League from 2013 to 2019 and has also had stints coaching in Belgium, Japan and China. Wardrop was a key figure during Mick Malthouse’s time as West Coast coach and then in his early years at Collingwood. He then joined Hawthorn, where he worked as opposition analyst during their premiership run, before returning to the Eagles to work alongside Adam Simpson as they won the 2018 flag. Hird declared his desire to be included in the process as a candidate immediately after Brad Scott was sacked. Hird supporters have campaigned for him to get the role however Welsh has been adamant a proper process would occur to select the best coach for Essendon.



Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘Horse’ has bolted: Why Longmire won’t coach the Bombers or the Blues Hird, a premiership captain at the Bombers, has been director of coaching at Port Melbourne for two seasons and had a short stint as an assistant at GWS since he finished up as Essendon coach in 2015 following the fallout from the drugs saga that occurred when he was coach. Hird is one of Essendon’s greatest ever players, winning two flags, a Brownlow Medal, a Norm Smith Medal and five club best and fairests. McVeigh, Hird’s friend and former teammate at Essendon, is an assistant coach at Sydney after a long stint with the Giants. He was interim coach for 13 matches at the Giants in 2022 and played 232 matches for the Bombers. It was during McVeigh’s time as Giants interim coach that Hird and another of their former Essendon teammates, current Bombers caretaker coach Dean Solomon, served as two of his assistants. Davis was an assistant coach at the Brisbane Lions for 13 years, helping to transform them from cellar dwellers to a premiership winning powerhouse under Chris Fagan. He joined Adelaide as director of coaching in 2025 where has supported Matthew Nicks as the Crows have taken the step up to top-four and premiership contention. Before that, he coached the NT Thunder to a NEAFL premiership in 2011. Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham in 2026. Getty



Graham played for West Coast before joining St Kilda in 2012 as a development coach. He then worked at West Coast until 2021 as they reached two grand finals and won a flag. The Crows poached Murray Davis from the Brisbane Lions to support coach Matthew Nicks. AFL Photos He coached West Perth in the WAFL and even stepped in for one game for one win as Eagles coach when Adam Simpson was unavailable. Graham then joined Fremantle in 2022 and helped the ladder leaders become a premiership contender. He made a strong impression when he pitched for the vacant Collingwood job in 2021 and is also expected to be in the final group of candidates for the Carlton job. Solomon is expected to declare whether he wants to be part of the process soon. Essendon have won one game under Solomon and sit 17th on the ladder with two wins for the season.

- Peter Ryan



Finals blow for Magpies as star defender is sent for surgery Jon Pierik Collingwood’s bid to play finals this season has taken a major hit with star defender Brayden Maynard sent for surgery. Maynard will have a procedure on the tendon above his left knee and will miss up to a month, meaning he could be touch and go even if the eighth-placed Magpies, currently 10 points clear of 10th-placed St Kilda, take part in the new wildcard round. Out of action: Collingwood defender Brayden Maynard. AFL Photos





Collingwood have won six matches straight but are dealing with soreness and illness heading into Thursday night’s blockbuster against Geelong at the MCG. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 So much for being too old and too slow. Here’s how the Pies can make the top four Jordan De Goey (virus) missed training, while ruckman Darcy Cameron and rebounding half-back Josh Daicos were barely sighted. However, Lachie Schultz trained well and is pushing for a return. A key focus of this week’s clash will be the expected tagging role shutdown specialist Oisin Mullin has on Nick Daicos. The Magpies were thumped by 54 points when the teams last met in round nine, Daicos having 29 disposals but not his typical influence in Scott Pendlebury’s record-equalling 432nd game. McRae and Daicos, the Brownlow Medal favourite, met on Tuesday afternoon to discuss plans.



“The great thing with Nick, and what we have done over a number of years now, is he’s not a target that stands still. If you’re a target that stands still, then you can take things away,” McRae said. “It’s hard to take everything away from Nick because he can play everywhere, and we’ll work our way through what that looks like.” McRae said Daicos’ teammates had become better at aiding the playmaker when opponents attempted to stymie him. “His running capability is like nothing I have seen, and so that’s a challenge for the opposition,” McRae said. The ninth-placed Cats are also dealing with injury issues for a contest with plenty riding on the result. A win could elevate the winner into the top six, however briefly, while the loser will remain firmly mired in the battle for the wildcard round.



Meanwhile, McRae said he would be “honoured” if given the chance to coach his home state of South Australia in next year’s State of Origin clash against Western Australia. McRae was a wingman for the Croweaters when they last played Victoria at the MCG in 1999. He said he grew up a passionate supporter, and remembers Stephen Kernahan booting 10 goals against Victoria at Football Park in 1984. “All those memories are really vivid for me, and something I aspired to do as a player and was lucky enough to do that, and if I was asked to do it [as coach], I’d go,” he said.



The Magpies and 2023 Norm Smith medallist Bobby Hill continue to work towards a financial parting of ways, with Hill expected to be paid his salary for this season, but not the remaining four years. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Why one of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned school photos
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Why one of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned school photos Emily Kowal July 28, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned class photos, citing child safety concerns, leaving photography businesses scrambling and disappointed parents without the treasured keepsakes. Across the country, childcare centres are in a state of upheaval after a string of abuse incidents led to sweeping reforms banning staff from carrying mobile phones, smartwatches, tablets or any device capable of taking or transmitting images of children. It also created new rules on where photos and videos of children could be stored. Queensland mum Carrie said she was saddened when her children’s childcare stopped photos. For Goodstart Early Learning, which has more than 660 centres across Australia, the risk of photographs beyond its control being manipulated is too high at present. “Until we can be certain that every photography session is conducted by a photographer who has strict controls on the storage and security of photographs of children, we won’t be allowing commercial photography in our centres,” it said.



The phasing-out of traditional class photos comes at a time of growing debates and concern about the safety of children’s images. Schools have been warned it is no longer safe to share student’s images online as artificial intelligence becomes weaponised. Australian crime professor Michael Salter, an internationally recognised child sexual exploitation expert, said commercial photographers and childcare centres needed to change their practices. “The fact is that images of children, especially high-quality resolution images of children, now have an additional currency and valence they didn’t use to have,” Salter said. “It’s incumbent on parents to be very aware of the importance of preserving the privacy of their children. We are simply in an era where images and video is being scraped at scale. Internet service providers have not yet responded to the threat of this kind of data harvesting. “I think the photography industry and the education sector need to be alive to the risks and what minimum standards mean in this new environment.”



Related Article Exclusive

Education ‘No risk-free way’: Schools warned to stop posting student photos online While regulations do not prohibit commercial photography, many centres have come to the realisation that once the images are taken, they hand over control to photographers to store and process images safely. Queensland mum Carrie, who asked for her surname to be withheld, treasures the preschool photos of her children. But when she flicks to her son’s album, the pictures suddenly stop. “It came out of nowhere,” said Carrie. “Maybe in the big scheme of things, it is just a photo, but it is nostalgic to look back on. It’s almost a rite of passage,” she said. The decision shocked early childhood photographers, some of whom had been snapping photos at the centres for decades, and triggered a “mass wave of disruption and panic in the photography industry”, said Queensland photographer Liz Teece.



While current laws and regulations do not ban third-party school photos, they do not explicitly outline a standard policy or procedure. “Everyone is interpreting the Australian Children’s Education & Care Quality Authority regulations differently,” said Teece. “We have had mass revolt from parents who just want their child’s photo. It’s been incredibly tough to say to families we are sorry, but we just can’t.” Sydney photographer Clayton Walker has spent more than $50,000 updating his systems, having cybersecurity experts examine the software and training his staff in mandatory child protection issues. Families can log in and delete their own child’s photos at any time, even if the centre wants them active longer, and they do not keep images forever. Goodstart said it hoped to be able to reintroduce class photography in the future. “We are always exploring ways to improve our systems and practices and will be happy to reintroduce commercial class photography when we can assure ourselves that it is as safe as possible and meets the requirements of the national model code.”



“A lot of centres are making some pretty strong changes about their data and privacy policies and who they are allowing into the centre. It’s just created change, and there’s no particular one way that companies are doing it,” said Walker. He wishes the laws were clearer, as do other photographers, who have since formed an alliance, calling for official standards of consent, data security, child safety and professional conduct. Greens MLC Abigail Boyd, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into Australia’s besieged childcare, sector said those in charge “still haven’t learnt the lesson”. “The teachers and educators I speak to are exasperated at failures in leadership in this sector. Not a single one of them has identified to me concerns about professional photographers taking photos with prudent and standard privacy and safety conditions.”



Mum Carrie said the decision was confusing, given many centres used apps to share photos of their children throughout the day. She worries that too will soon disappear. “I hate that I have to work and send my kids to day care, so it is nice to get those little updates,” said Carrie. World.title: The hatred of Jacinta Allan was unfair. But it had become visceral
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election The hatred of Jacinta Allan was unfair. But it had become visceral Chip Le Grand July 28, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Labor MP this week relayed her exasperation at knocking on doors in their electorate, trying to talk to constituents. Throughout what used to be safe Labor streets, one door was slammed after the next. “They hate her,” she said flatly. This has been the experience of government MPs for months. Jacinta Allan’s unpopularity had made her leadership untenable. Jason South A visceral loathing of Jacinta Allan had seeped into the state, making it impossible for her caucus colleagues to have door-step and train-station conversations about cost-of-living relief and schools and local transport.



Some of this was unfair. Some of it odious and misogynistic. Some of it was hand-me-down hatred inherited from Daniel Andrews. For government MPs, the rights and wrongs mattered less than the need to find a way to connect with people who, in four months, will decide whether they keep their jobs. Put simply, Allan’s unpopularity had become a dead weight on her government’s re-election prospects. This is the reason, more than any other, that a majority of Labor MPs were convinced the time had come to dump Allan and install a new leader. That the new leader is Ben Carroll matters less than he is not Jacinta Allan or her equally loathed predecessor. Carroll made this much clear in his first public comments as premier: “Let me make one thing clear: I am not Daniel Andrews. I am not Jacinta Allan.”



Related Article Inside story

Political leadership After an icy meeting, the premier still had a glimmer of hope. Then came a second knock at the door This is also the reason why the elevation of Carroll and his deputy, Gabrielle Williams, while not a panacea to the government’s electoral ills, will encourage some voters to look at Labor again. To people outside politics, these may seem like harsh things to write about a woman who served for 27 years in parliament, all but four in government, and led this state. People inside politics know these observations are more based in electoral science than sentiment. There is a reason that all respected pollsters play close attention to the relative popularity of party leaders. Jim Reed, the founder of the Resolve Political Monitor surveys published by this masthead, says that when it comes to determining how someone will vote, attitude towards a party leader counts for more than whatever they think about any given policy. “Our vote driver analyses consistently point to the leader being by far the biggest factor in people’s estimation of the party options, way beyond any single achievement, policy offering or candidate,” he explains.



“That’s particularly true at a state level where the leader is really the party personified. Many voters struggle to name a minister or a shadow.” Allan’s approval rating according the most recent Resolve survey, published earlier this month, was wallowing at minus 36. This is the kind of number that former prime minister Scott Morrison dragged into the 2022 federal election. In the final stages of that campaign, his effect on undecided voters had become so toxic he was kept in a plane for as many hours as possible, criss-crossing the nation to seats the Coalition had already lost or could never win. The best that can be said about Carroll is that, according to a Resolve survey published in April, only one out of five voters know enough about him to have formed a view one way or another.



This may seem like faint praise, but it gives Labor a faint chance in November. Photo: Matt Golding Some say you are better to stick with the devil you know but when you are a third-term government plagued by building industry corruption and laden with debt, it is time to pull in your horns. World.title: Health boss grilled over lack of Indigenous directors on three hospital boards
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandPublic service Health boss grilled over lack of Indigenous directors on three hospital boards Matt Dennien July 28, 2026 — 8:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren has claimed the lack of legally required First Nations members on three hospital service boards is the result of “unscheduled vacancies”, despite the departures being forced or known in advance of a recent major overhaul. The comments, made during the state budget estimates hearing of a parliamentary committee, came amid accusations the Crisafulli LNP has sought to unpick Indigenous representation and policies in a push dubbed “Project Invisibility”. After reports from the ABC last month highlighting the lack of First Nations directors in the state’s largest hospital and health services – Metro North and Metro South, the latter of which also caters to the greatest Indigenous population – Rosengren faced questions on Tuesday. Queensland Health director-general David Rosengren at Tuesday’s estimates hearing. Queensland parliament Quizzed by Labor’s opposition health spokesperson, Mark Bailey, Rosengren confirmed the Sunshine Coast hospital board was also lacking a First Nations director, which is a requirement under legislation governing the 16 bodies running public health services.



“Very recently, the process to undertake a scheduled recruitment across all of the hospital and health boards was completed, and with the appointment of a substantive number of new board members in April of this year,” Rosengren said. “Subsequent to that process, there are three boards where they’ve experienced resignations of board members that are identified First Nations, and there is an active recruitment campaign that is nearing an end to identify appropriate replacements for those unscheduled vacancies that exist on the board structure. “But the other 13 of the HHS’s all have an identified First Nations board director, including three of our hospital and health boards where their chair is an identified First Nations [person], and that is a nation-leading framework for our boards in Queensland.” After changing the law to allow the sacking of health board directors without reason, on March 27 Health Minister Tim Nicholls announced 50 new additions to the boards – including three former LNP figures – after a months-long two-yearly appointment round overhaul.





Queensland Health was yet to provide a response before publication to questions seeking clarification of Rosengren’s comments. Editor's pick Public service LNP-sponsor data centre firm taps ex-premier to join major meetings Former truth-telling inquiry chair Joshua Creamer suggested last month the Crisafulli government had a deliberate strategy, dubbed “Project Invisibility”, to wind back First Nations representation and policies. The government has said its focus has been on “redirecting funds into practical, locally led projects which deliver tangible outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander discrete communities through our Closing the Gap Priorities Fund”.
