World.title: This Lion has no fears after two concussions. But there’s a deeper issue
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 This Lion has no fears after two concussions. But there’s a deeper issue Nick Wright Updated July 28, 2026 — 8:12pm ,first published 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Even after suffering two concussions within three weeks, Noah Answerth insists the thought of premature retirement has never crossed his mind. “Not really, no. Concussion is going to happen in our game, I guess, and you can’t really help it – I signed up to play,” he said. “I got concussed when I was a young kid playing, and I just love the game, so concussion isn’t really going to stop me from getting my chance to play AFL.” The Lions’ Noah Answerth suffered back-to-back concussions this year. Getty Images After copping a knee to the head in round three against St Kilda and missing two weeks under concussion protocols, Answerth suffered another blow upon his comeback against Melbourne, leading teammate Harris Andrews to voice his concern for the 26-year-old’s wellbeing.



The Lions were diligent in his recovery – sidelining him for five weeks – and he has returned to become a pillar of Brisbane’s top-four charge. Related Article AFL 2026 Bailey-Ashcroft double act powers Lions to seventh straight win Having averaged six touches and 1.6 rebound 50s in his first five games of the season, his past six have yielded 14.17 disposals, 2.5 rebound 50s, and 2.5 tackles an outing. Ahead of his 100th AFL appearance on Saturday, against Carlton, Answerth revealed it was other injuries – a ruptured Achilles suffered at Marvel Stadium last year, and a back concern from his teenage days – that had left him fearing this milestone would be unattainable. “When I was 17, I fractured my L1 vertebrae. I thought about not playing ever again after that, but just the confidence [my coaches] had in me to keep going, and obviously Brisbane to take a chance … I’m lucky enough to still be here,” Answerth said.



“The club looked after me really well [during the concussions]. Coming back from my Achilles as well, it gave me a bit more time to prepare and play at the level I wanted to. “I think coming back, you’re a bit hampered from the Achilles, and a bit slower, and it probably affects you a little bit, so having that time actually allowed me to probably improve. Noah Answerth in action against Port Adelaide. Getty Images “I haven’t had any effects. I’m happy and love playing footy and working and studying. If anything, it’s probably put myself more into focus.” Concern for the long-term impacts of head trauma is at an all-time high, with young Lions defender Ty Gallop drawing the ire of pundits after he tackled Port Adelaide rival Mitch Georgiades.



Georgiades had just returned from a concussion lay-off, and the sight of Gallop appearing to slam him back down, with his head hitting the turf, garnered a serious misconduct charge. Gallop faced the AFL Tribunal on Tuesday night and copped a three-game suspension, pleading guilty to what he insisted was retaliation after believing the Power star had grabbed at his broken thumb. “For Ty, it’s a competitive game, and we all try and be competitive. Sometimes you may have a brain fade like that, which is always hard, but you don’t mean it in that way – sometimes you’re playing the game and things happen,” Answerth said. Loading “I think he’s a gentle giant really, he’s doing a lot of work with Harris – I actually sort of see him as that Harris Andrews-type of character.



“I daresay he’ll be a very good leader for us in the future … [the incident] was very out of character.” According to the AFL Players’ Association’s Insights and Impacts Report, 82 per cent of players had a “high level of concern” for the long-term implications of concussion. Related Article AFL 2026 Fagan factor: Will coach’s future keep dynamic duo at Lions? While 86 per cent reported their concussions, a fifth still “somewhat, or completely, downplayed the severity of their symptoms”, with concerns about losing their spot on the team the overwhelming reason. With each instance of concussion, according to UQ’s Queensland Brain Institute expert Professor Fatima Nasrallah, the likelihood of further concussions increases. That is why she has a greater fear for those playing at the grassroots, where there is less attention and medical support.



Nasrallah is nearing the end of a three-year study into adolescent concussions to find a more concrete biomarker assessment of a head trauma, but said a cultural stigma hindering concussion reporting made recruiting participants a challenge. She appealed for greater funding to be injected into schools and junior clubs to ensure they are better equipped to protect and inform athletes. “You’ll go to a game which has under-12s – if it’s soccer, they’re heading the ball; if it’s rugby, they’re going full force – and there is no mandate for them to actually follow guidelines,” Nasrallah said. “We know the developing brain is a lot more vulnerable to change. A lot more effort has to go into the children to change the culture – it’s peer pressure, it’s wanting to have a career in the space. “People are reluctant to be involved in research studies because the moment they label themselves as having a concussion, they can’t go back to play. Parents don’t want to know about it – the children are influenced by the parents – and there has to be a change in culture from an early age.



“If you look at a broader scale, particularly in regional and remote areas, you’ll find that number is much higher in terms of the under-reporting.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: New broom must sweep clean and courageously
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters New broom must sweep clean and courageously July 28, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. VICTORIA This new Labor “broom” must sweep clean, quickly and courageously.

A royal commission into alleged corruption in the Big Build is a given. The Outdoor Recreation Victoria Bill 2026 - currently before parliament to use taxpayer funds for a new huntin’, shootin’, fishin’, 4WD drivin’ masculine monolith merging the Game Management Authority and Victorian Fisheries Authority, must be withdrawn.

At every turn, former premier Jacinta Allan kowtowed to shooters and the pro-gun construction unions. The new premier must defy these vested interests and be prepared to wear the predictable flack. Voters admire strength of character.

Allan leaves a plethora of problems: unaffordable SRL; explosions of crime and potholes; overturning police advice on gun limits; unpopular housing policies (demolitions of old towers, impositions of new towers); teacher rebellion; WFH meddling; and abject neglect of animal welfare and wildlife policy.

Voters don’t expect instant miracles. They do expect a dramatic re-set.

Joan Reilly, Surrey Hills Deference to leader comes at cost

Tone deafness, arrogance and a selfish drive to place herself above her party assured that any good work Jacinta Allan initiated as premier would be forever tainted by the allegations of corruption in the Bid Build which she refused to acknowledge.

Her resignation may not be enough to protect the Labor Party, who will find out in November just how much their deference to her leadership has cost it. It would be unforgivable if it has eroded their traditional supporter base to the point where it will benefit One Nation.

Pete Dunne, Highett



Allan’s decency under duress

I am sorry to see Jacinta go. I have appreciated her unflappable communication style as well as her warmth and genuine rapport, especially with women and refugees. She has displayed leadership qualities I admire.

Thank you, Jacinta - your decency under duress has been admirable.

Susan Mahar, Fitzroy North Shopping list of problems to fix

New Labor leader, Ben Carroll should now project confidence. Following from his announcement of a royal commission, he must produce a plan to reduce debt, come up with a sensible not-lock-everyone-up plan for law and order, conduct an audit into our Big Build program and, while he is at it, address Jess Wilson’s signature policy of eliminating potholes on our roads.

Jennifer Quigley, Balwyn It is time to go

The ALP state governments under former premiers Dan Andrews and Jacinta Allan took Victoria so far into the red, that it just has to go. Sadly, other parties seem worse. One Nation has neither candidates nor policies: moaning is no solution.

Meanwhile, the Coalition has yet to clearly articulate credible solutions, beyond a royal commission into the CFMEU.

The current crisis is actually much more wholistic: the entire management of public infrastructure projects, including basic maintenance and upgrades of roads, transport, schools, hospitals. Not to mention delivery of education, child/aged care and NDIS services falling between federal and state stools.

I am laying hope in community independents and minor parties dedicated to political integrity and transparency holding the balance of power, and negotiating productively to see us through this crisis in our democracy.

Caroline Leslie, Hawthorn Leadership issues

Jacinta’s Allan’s inability to act on allegations of corruption and her strong defence of the union movement while Dan Andrews pivoted from the socialist left to become a private advisor to billionaires tells you all you need to know about Victorian Labor.

Anton Whitehead, Portsea SRL is to blame

As Jacinta Allan was readying for her resignation broadcast (28/7), I listened to the desperation of a woman on the wireless pleading for funding to address domestic violence. She rammed home the fear, deaths and kids without mothers.

All I could think of was $50 billion (realistically) for the Eastern Suburban Rail Loop (SRL) which few need.

A nearby pothole (affectionately) known as ″⁣Gabrielle″⁣ (named for the transport infrastructure minister) has been ″⁣repaired″⁣ but already subsides a bit. A cheap election fix while billions go to the SRL.

And underfunded hospitals, medical staff training, schools, teachers, police, ambos, firies and environmental preservation? Add your own SRL related deficiency.

Let’s hope that One Nation doesn’t offer SRL cancellation - an irresistible temptation that could trigger a landslide.

Ronald Elliott, Sandringham



Thank you for your service

I would like to thank Jacinta Allan for her service to the state. Whilst the Big Build had many problems, it is true that Allan’s has overseen a major upgrade in Victoria’s public transport network.

Without that major investment, Victoria would have become mired in total transport gridlock by now.

David Fry, Windsor City-centric ALP

I believe Labor will lose the November election because it has become a city-centric party that tried to implement massively expensive inner-city transport programs that placed huge demand on its budget and ignored outer city transport needs. These massive investments in city central infrastructure have also seen accusations of corrupt business practices between the government and the CFMEU which have never been properly investigated or clarified.

Changing leadership so close to an election will not help as fault doesn’t rest with the premier alone. The party needs new leadership and broad-based policies that appeal to a broader voting public base. A time spent in opposition will give them time to rethink and build anew.

John Blackwell, Hastings Go independent

Michael Bachelard asks ″⁣Victorian politics is a mess. Who on earth can you vote for″⁣, 28/7). The answer is simple – vote for an independent and encourage one in your electorate to stand. The ‘Voices for...’ organisations are promoting candidates in a large number of state electorates for the upcoming November election.

The effectiveness of independents has clearly been demonstrated in the federal sphere despite the underhand tactics of the two major parties and One Nation which has not disclosed donation sources.

We need more people who are not bound by party constraints, who listen to the concerns of their communities before voting on issues and developing policies that reflect those concerns. People who can work constructively with others not just bleat negativity.

Jenny Callaghan, Hawthorn Mosaic of members

Re Michael Bachelard’s article (28/7). There are alternatives to the major parties in Victoria and they come with the advantage that they have not been corroded by the desperate need to cling to power at all costs.

A coalition formed by minor parties and independents might lack experience, but experience can be gained more readily than integrity can be restored.

David Rose, Montrose One Nation unknowns

It will be interesting to see who One Nation selects for candidates in the Victoria election. They don’t have local branches, so to select them, they request applications like job vacancies. They have a terrible history in selecting candidates with many exposed for outrageous social media history prior to the election.

They have policies devised for federal elections, but they will need to develop specific policies for state elections. The really interesting thing will be to see who of their candidates is elected as parliamentary leader, and will each elected candidate follow the party line.

My bet is that many elected candidates will be anarchists and drop-outs who won’t listen to anyone else, including Pauline, and will become independents.

John Rome, Mt Lawley, WA



THE FORUM Trump’s influence

Re Paul Sakkal’s article “Libs still split over deal with One Nation” 28/7.

Andrew Bragg says the Liberal Party must acknowledge that if neither Coalition or One Nation held a majority but could combine to form government, then “of course, we would be pragmatic.”

Bragg then went on to state: “The number one priority is to beat the communist Labor government”. This is straight out of the Trump playbook. Voters beware, there are those amongst the Coalition who openly admire and appear to wish to follow the Trump playbook. I cannot believe the Coalition’s lack of decent policies and moral fibre.

Margaret McMullan, Box Hill Embrace dignity

I can only applaud the lucid explanation by Andrew Denton on ABC TV’s 7.30 (27/8) as to why and how the use of telehealth for Voluntary Assisted Dying (VAD) is not just appropriate, but is necessary to benefit those facing the end of their life. Often, in intense pain and suffering, travel is not possible for these people, but dignity certainly is. To politicians of every ilk, let’s get it done.

Greg Cooper, Mount Martha Climate catastrophy

High temperatures and unreliable rain across Europe have contributed to record wildfires, this time in France, Spain and even Scotland (“Fears for Bordeaux as ‘unprecedented’ wildfire reaches the city’s outskirts”, 28/7).

Global warming is an obvious culprit, contributing to the destruction of farmland, homes and infrastructure. Hundreds of thousands of people have had to flee.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calls it a climate emergency. Of course, it is. Any individual fire can have multiple contributing causes, but the evidence is clear that global warming is a major factor overall.

Droughts and bushfires, storms and floods are getting worse all over the world. The expense of robust climate action is high, but the long-term cost of inaction is far worse.

John Hughes, Mentone Keep city height limit

Norman Day, Rob Adams and others in The Age have recently highlighted the inappropriateness of the scale of development proposed on the vacant metro construction site opposite Flinders Street station. The most recent proposal is well in excess of the 40 metre height limit which has been held for 40 years.

The Cain government came to power with the policy of implementing the stalled Melbourne City Strategy Plan. The vision for the plan was to protect the low central core and reinforce the taller towers to the east and west on the flanking hills to the east of the central Hoddle grid.

Evan Walker, an architect, as minister for planning was responsible for setting up a Central City Task Force to implement the Strategy Plan. The task force was formed including planners and urban designers to prepare plans and guidelines to realise the vision of the Strategy Plan. I was one of the urban designers on this Task Force.

The urban design objective was to maintain the central core of human scaled buildings and laneways so loved by Melburnians and tourists alike. To achieve this, a 40 metre height limit was included in the planning scheme either side of Swanston Street and stretching up to Parliament House either side of Bourke Street and including Chinatown.

I ask that the present minister for planning and the City of Melbourne respect the foresight of the Cain Labor Government and maintain the 40 metre height limit on the site opposite Flinders Street Station.

John Curtis, North Melbourne



Car memories

Like other correspondents, we had a Mini Moke in the ’70s which was a great little vehicle. We could go do the banking, come back to the Moke, throw the change bag and deposit book on the seat and walk off.

Bill our guard, a large Alsatian dog, made sure no one touched it as it had no windows or roof. n the early ’60s my uncle had a Goggomobil; another great car with attitude especially driving amongst Melbourne truck traffic. Great memories of real cars.

Jill French, Hervey Bay, Qld AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding State government

Congratulations to Jacinta Allan who managed to push Hanson (to page 12) and Trump (to page 22) of The Age (28/7) before they got a mention. So good.

Margaret Raffle, Keilor East Labor with its union snouts in troughs and the Libs with its corporate snouts in troughs, thank god we’ve got Pauline – oh, wait ...

Joan Kerr, Geelong



Oh Carroll! At least you know what’s in the poisoned chalice.

Paul Custance, Highett It is now plain that Labor does not deserve to be returned to government. Disunity is death.

Stephen Yolland, Doncaster Blowing the place up is an extraordinary strategy from the planning minister!

Pauline Brown, Woodend Ben Carroll? No thanks! Many will be opting for another woman: the very positive Jess Wilson.

Paul Murchison, Kingsbury Emergency call

I didn’t receive the national emergency signal. The advice from the minister for emergency management was not to be alarmed. Go figure!

Kay Moulton, Surrey Hills



When my phone received a “presidential alert” message Monday afternoon, I feared that a Trump invasion was imminent.

David Johnston, Healesville I felt that the alarm was not really an alarming sound. This modern world is filled with electronic sounds. Something like a fire engine or police vehicle sound might be more appropriate. Public input should be sought.

John Kirkby, Mornington Furthermore

US tariffs on Australia for slavery and forced labour sounds right. We’re ever more forced by Labor to be slaves to the US.

Mark Freeman, Macleod When an ″⁣Aussie sheila″⁣ wins a medal at Glasgow’s Commonwealth Games, she is a ″⁣braw lassie″⁣, indeed.

Tris Raouf, Hadfield The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: ‘It’s a very bad look’: Premiership Lion hit with three-match ban, apologises for incident
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Ty Gallop admits his retaliation against Mitch Georgiades “wasn’t fair”.

James Hird is among the candidates to advance to the next round of the Essendon coaching search.

Collingwood spiritual leader Brayden Maynard is set for surgery on his leg. Brisbane defender Ty Gallop has been suspended for three games for a serious misconduct act he admits is a “very bad look” for the AFL. Gallop pleaded guilty at the AFL tribunal on Tuesday for what he described as retaliation on Mitch Georgiades after the Port Adelaide forward grabbed his broken thumb. The 20-year-old had tackled Georgiades to the ground during Sunday’s clash in Brisbane and, after the ball left the area, shoved the Port attacker face-first into the turf. The moment that had Ty Gallop in hot water. Fox Footy



Gallop played the match with strapping on a broken right thumb. “Mitch has grabbed my thumb as I have gone to stand up,” Gallop said, adding Georgiades’ action was intentional. But Gallop expressed remorse for retaliating, saying he had phoned Georgiades to apologise. “Looking back now and watching the footage, I understand that the retaliation to what happened wasn’t fair,” he said. Mitch Georgiades clashes with Gallop at the Gabba. AFL Photos



“I have gone out of my way to push him down, which I am sorry for and I do regret. I’d like to have that time over again. “It’s a very bad look and there’s no room for it in footy.” Gallop said his retaliation was an “immediate reaction”. “I have grabbed the back of his jersey and pushed him back into the ground,” he said. “I think I play a hard brand of footy, but I play a very fair brand of footy as well ... it was purely out of retaliation.”



Under questioning from the AFL’s counsel Nick Pane KC, Gallop agreed his act was totally unreasonable and unacceptable. Pane asked the tribunal for a three-game suspension. “Georgiades’ head made forceful contact with the ground,” Pane said. “The action had significant potential to cause serious injury.” The Port spearhead wasn’t hurt in the incident.

- AAP Bombers narrow down shortlist, ex-Socceroos and Victory hard man to help choose their next coach



Peter Ryan Essendon have settled on four candidates, including club legend James Hird, to move into the second phase of the selection process to fill their vacant senior coaching position. Hird, Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham, Sydney assistant and former Bomber Mark McVeigh and Adelaide director of coaching Murray Davis have already met with club president Andrew Welsh, CEO Tim Roberts and board member Ted Richards as part of the initial coffee chat. James Hird is a panellist on Footy Classified and the coaching director of VFL club Port Melbourne. Nine Two competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed the four candidates will now move to the next phase of the process, which will include interviews by Melbourne Victory great and former coach Kevin Muscat, and long-time opposition analyst at Collingwood and Hawthorn John Wardrop.



That pair has been invited to be part of the process to complement the current selection panel of Welsh, Roberts, Richards, club vice president and ex-Victory chairman Anthony Di Pietro and the Essendon’s general manager of people and culture, Caroline Monzon. The Bombers were keen to include coaching experts in the selection process as they sort through the candidates. Mark McVeigh during his time as interim coach of the Giants. AFL Photos Muscat coached the Victory in the A-League from 2013 to 2019 and has also had stints coaching in Belgium, Japan and China. Wardrop was a key figure during Mick Malthouse’s time as West Coast coach and then in his early years at Collingwood. He then joined Hawthorn, where he worked as opposition analyst during their premiership run, before returning to the Eagles to work alongside Adam Simpson as they won the 2018 flag. Hird declared his desire to be included in the process as a candidate immediately after Brad Scott was sacked. Hird supporters have campaigned for him to get the role however Welsh has been adamant a proper process would occur to select the best coach for Essendon.



Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘Horse’ has bolted: Why Longmire won’t coach the Bombers or the Blues Hird, a premiership captain at the Bombers, has been director of coaching at Port Melbourne for two seasons and had a short stint as an assistant at GWS since he finished up as Essendon coach in 2015 following the fallout from the drugs saga that occurred when he was coach. Hird is one of Essendon’s greatest ever players, winning two flags, a Brownlow Medal, a Norm Smith Medal and five club best and fairests. McVeigh, Hird’s friend and former teammate at Essendon, is an assistant coach at Sydney after a long stint with the Giants. He was interim coach for 13 matches at the Giants in 2022 and played 232 matches for the Bombers. It was during McVeigh’s time as Giants interim coach that Hird and another of their former Essendon teammates, current Bombers caretaker coach Dean Solomon, served as two of his assistants. Davis was an assistant coach at the Brisbane Lions for 13 years, helping to transform them from cellar dwellers to a premiership winning powerhouse under Chris Fagan. He joined Adelaide as director of coaching in 2025 where has supported Matthew Nicks as the Crows have taken the step up to top-four and premiership contention. Before that, he coached the NT Thunder to a NEAFL premiership in 2011. Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham in 2026. Getty



Graham played for West Coast before joining St Kilda in 2012 as a development coach. He then worked at West Coast until 2021 as they reached two grand finals and won a flag. The Crows poached Murray Davis from the Brisbane Lions to support coach Matthew Nicks. AFL Photos He coached West Perth in the WAFL and even stepped in for one game for one win as Eagles coach when Adam Simpson was unavailable. Graham then joined Fremantle in 2022 and helped the ladder leaders become a premiership contender. He made a strong impression when he pitched for the vacant Collingwood job in 2021 and is also expected to be in the final group of candidates for the Carlton job. Solomon is expected to declare whether he wants to be part of the process soon. Essendon have won one game under Solomon and sit 17th on the ladder with two wins for the season.

- Peter Ryan



Finals blow for Magpies as star defender is sent for surgery Jon Pierik Collingwood’s bid to play finals this season has taken a major hit with star defender Brayden Maynard sent for surgery. Maynard will have a procedure on the tendon above his left knee and will miss up to a month, meaning he could be touch and go even if the eighth-placed Magpies, currently 10 points clear of 10th-placed St Kilda, take part in the new wildcard round. Out of action: Collingwood defender Brayden Maynard. AFL Photos





Collingwood have won six matches straight but are dealing with soreness and illness heading into Thursday night’s blockbuster against Geelong at the MCG. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 So much for being too old and too slow. Here’s how the Pies can make the top four Jordan De Goey (virus) missed training, while ruckman Darcy Cameron and rebounding half-back Josh Daicos were barely sighted. However, Lachie Schultz trained well and is pushing for a return. A key focus of this week’s clash will be the expected tagging role shutdown specialist Oisin Mullin has on Nick Daicos. The Magpies were thumped by 54 points when the teams last met in round nine, Daicos having 29 disposals but not his typical influence in Scott Pendlebury’s record-equalling 432nd game. McRae and Daicos, the Brownlow Medal favourite, met on Tuesday afternoon to discuss plans.



“The great thing with Nick, and what we have done over a number of years now, is he’s not a target that stands still. If you’re a target that stands still, then you can take things away,” McRae said. “It’s hard to take everything away from Nick because he can play everywhere, and we’ll work our way through what that looks like.” McRae said Daicos’ teammates had become better at aiding the playmaker when opponents attempted to stymie him. “His running capability is like nothing I have seen, and so that’s a challenge for the opposition,” McRae said. The ninth-placed Cats are also dealing with injury issues for a contest with plenty riding on the result. A win could elevate the winner into the top six, however briefly, while the loser will remain firmly mired in the battle for the wildcard round.



Meanwhile, McRae said he would be “honoured” if given the chance to coach his home state of South Australia in next year’s State of Origin clash against Western Australia. McRae was a wingman for the Croweaters when they last played Victoria at the MCG in 1999. He said he grew up a passionate supporter, and remembers Stephen Kernahan booting 10 goals against Victoria at Football Park in 1984. “All those memories are really vivid for me, and something I aspired to do as a player and was lucky enough to do that, and if I was asked to do it [as coach], I’d go,” he said.



The Magpies and 2023 Norm Smith medallist Bobby Hill continue to work towards a financial parting of ways, with Hill expected to be paid his salary for this season, but not the remaining four years. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Why one of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned school photos
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation Why one of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned school photos Emily Kowal July 28, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Australia’s largest childcare providers has banned class photos, citing child safety concerns, leaving photography businesses scrambling and disappointed parents without the treasured keepsakes. Across the country, childcare centres are in a state of upheaval after a string of abuse incidents led to sweeping reforms banning staff from carrying mobile phones, smartwatches, tablets or any device capable of taking or transmitting images of children. It also created new rules on where photos and videos of children could be stored. Queensland mum Carrie said she was saddened when her children’s childcare stopped photos. For Goodstart Early Learning, which has more than 660 centres across Australia, the risk of photographs beyond its control being manipulated is too high at present. “Until we can be certain that every photography session is conducted by a photographer who has strict controls on the storage and security of photographs of children, we won’t be allowing commercial photography in our centres,” it said.



The phasing-out of traditional class photos comes at a time of growing debates and concern about the safety of children’s images. Schools have been warned it is no longer safe to share student’s images online as artificial intelligence becomes weaponised. Australian crime professor Michael Salter, an internationally recognised child sexual exploitation expert, said commercial photographers and childcare centres needed to change their practices. “The fact is that images of children, especially high-quality resolution images of children, now have an additional currency and valence they didn’t use to have,” Salter said. “It’s incumbent on parents to be very aware of the importance of preserving the privacy of their children. We are simply in an era where images and video is being scraped at scale. Internet service providers have not yet responded to the threat of this kind of data harvesting. “I think the photography industry and the education sector need to be alive to the risks and what minimum standards mean in this new environment.”



Related Article Exclusive

Education ‘No risk-free way’: Schools warned to stop posting student photos online While regulations do not prohibit commercial photography, many centres have come to the realisation that once the images are taken, they hand over control to photographers to store and process images safely. Queensland mum Carrie, who asked for her surname to be withheld, treasures the preschool photos of her children. But when she flicks to her son’s album, the pictures suddenly stop. “It came out of nowhere,” said Carrie. “Maybe in the big scheme of things, it is just a photo, but it is nostalgic to look back on. It’s almost a rite of passage,” she said. The decision shocked early childhood photographers, some of whom had been snapping photos at the centres for decades, and triggered a “mass wave of disruption and panic in the photography industry”, said Queensland photographer Liz Teece.



While current laws and regulations do not ban third-party school photos, they do not explicitly outline a standard policy or procedure. “Everyone is interpreting the Australian Children’s Education & Care Quality Authority regulations differently,” said Teece. “We have had mass revolt from parents who just want their child’s photo. It’s been incredibly tough to say to families we are sorry, but we just can’t.” Sydney photographer Clayton Walker has spent more than $50,000 updating his systems, having cybersecurity experts examine the software and training his staff in mandatory child protection issues. Families can log in and delete their own child’s photos at any time, even if the centre wants them active longer, and they do not keep images forever. Goodstart said it hoped to be able to reintroduce class photography in the future. “We are always exploring ways to improve our systems and practices and will be happy to reintroduce commercial class photography when we can assure ourselves that it is as safe as possible and meets the requirements of the national model code.”



“A lot of centres are making some pretty strong changes about their data and privacy policies and who they are allowing into the centre. It’s just created change, and there’s no particular one way that companies are doing it,” said Walker. He wishes the laws were clearer, as do other photographers, who have since formed an alliance, calling for official standards of consent, data security, child safety and professional conduct. Greens MLC Abigail Boyd, who chaired a parliamentary inquiry into Australia’s besieged childcare, sector said those in charge “still haven’t learnt the lesson”. “The teachers and educators I speak to are exasperated at failures in leadership in this sector. Not a single one of them has identified to me concerns about professional photographers taking photos with prudent and standard privacy and safety conditions.”



Mum Carrie said the decision was confusing, given many centres used apps to share photos of their children throughout the day. She worries that too will soon disappear. “I hate that I have to work and send my kids to day care, so it is nice to get those little updates,” said Carrie. World.title: The week in Parliament : A new watcher of judges and a free-for-all debate on petitions
World.content:
Highlights for the coming week in Parliament include a new judge watcher, a large group of visiting female Pacifica MPs, a Privileges Committee hearing into MBIE staff, and a free-for-all debate on petitions. Also, a briefing on bird flu and, of course, a bevy of bills up for debate.

A Privileges hearing into MBIE immigration

On Tuesday evening Parliament's Privileges Committee begins hearings into whether MBIE's Immigration leadership misled a Select Committee over the status and success of a failed IT upgrade project.

When Parliament's rights and responsibilities (i.e. Privileges) may have been contravened, complaints are first made to the sitting Speaker. If the Speaker believes there is a potential 'matter of privilege' it is referred to the Privileges Committee, a cross-party committee of senior MPs who hold hearings and make a recommendation to the House.

The hearing is from 5-6pm this evening.

A new watcher for the judges

Early business from MPs on Tuesday was a short debate on a motion that the House recommend that the Governor General appoint Paul Norman Collins as Judicial Conduct Commissioner for a term of 5 years, under section 7(2) of the Judicial Conduct Commissioner and Judicial Conduct Panel Act 2004.

The Attorney General noted that The Chief Justice had been consulted as required. Only National, Labour and Green MPs spoke on the motion and all agreed.

Parliament has sovereignty among the three branches of government (the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary), but a key constitutional principle in the relationship that the Executive and Legislature have with the judiciary is "comity". A mutual respect and restraint, recognising one another's independence. This is why it is very poor form for an MP or minister to criticise a judge or judicial decision.

To maintain judicial independence there is an independent overseer of judicial conduct. The role does not review decisions. This helps to keep politicians from muddying comity's limpid waters.

Female MPs in the Fale

Pacifica women MPs are visiting New Zealand's Parliament this week as part of the Tai a Kiwa: Stronger Pacific Parliament's programme. This week's programme includes female MPs from across the Pacific and will discuss issues of common interest; including Leading Effectively in Male-dominated Environments, featuring General Rose King (New Zealand's Chief of Army) and Cushla Tangaere-Manuel (MP for Ikaroa-Rāwhiti, Labour; and former chief executive of the Ngāti Porou East Coast Rugby Union).

Depressingly, another session covers Online Harm & Gender-Based Harassment and features Nicola Grigg (Minister for Women's Affairs), Carmel Sepuloni (Deputy Leader of Labour), Tamatha Paul (Green MP for Wellington Central), and Hana-Rāwhiti Maipi-Clarke (MP for Hauraki-Waikato, Te Pāti Māori).

A petition free-for-all

At noon on Wednesday MPs will spend an hour debating everything any Kiwi has complained about. Well, almost. This doesn't include complaints over a beer at the pub. It is a debate about anything that has been raised in a formal petition to Parliament. But that is still a lot of things. This Tuesday alone Parliament received the following five petitions:

Petition of Hannah McKeich requesting that the House make childcare screening mandatory for parents before scheduled surgery or in cases of emergency hospitalisation.

Petition of Pegasus Residents Group requesting that the House urge the Government to ensure that the proposal to redevelop the Pegasus Golf Course is not progressed through the fast-track approvals process.

Petition of Andreas Fox requesting that the House amend the definition of rape in the Crimes Act 1961 so that rape does not require the perpetrator to have a penis.

Petition of Sheryl Tristram requesting that the House suspend the provisions of section 23(4) of the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990, where these relate to persons charged with offences against children.

Petition of Tracey McLeod requesting that the House investigate funding for the Rotorua Lakes sewerage schemes and the Rotorua Te Arawa Lakes strategy.

A bird flu briefing

Often when a new biosecurity threat arrives in New Zealand there is a ministerial briefing to the House on the issue, outlining the response that is planned. Thus far, the recent detection of H5N1 has not provoked a briefing.

For those wanting an update on what could be an avian catastrophe in a country where many bird species are threatened (without even touching on commercial bird raising for eggs or meat).

A briefing is scheduled to the Primary Industry Committee at 10am on Thursday morning. The briefing is coming from biosecurity staff from both the Department of Conservation and the Ministry for Primary Industries.

Four laws up for finalising

Among the bills being debated in the House this week, the government is hoping to finalize four that the House also spent time on last week.

The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill is written to ease the use of Special Purpose Vehicles, entities created to fund and build infrastructure at a remove from a Local Council's balance sheets; and to repay their financing by charging levies to those benefited by the infrastructure, for up to 50 years. The ongoing liability for levies would be added to a property's LIM. This bill has now passed its third and final reading leaving only final confirmations and assent from the Crown.

The Employment Leave Bill would replace the Holidays Act 2003, which has long caused confusion. There is wide agreement that it could be improved, but less agreement over whether this bill will fix the issue. This is a tough area to get right when it must cover full time, part-time, variable hours, shifts, contracts, and casual workers. The plan is for a Committee stage on Tuesday and third reading on Wednesday.

The English Language Bill is, at its core, just eight words long. It doesn't change anything, but confirms that "English is an official language of New Zealand." Legal scholars will tell you that this is already the case - otherwise it would be a problem that this bill is written in English.

The Arms Bill slightly alters a few aspects of weapon regulation. Major changes include removing the arms regulator role from the Police, introducing new licence types for museum employees, and new rules for who can use restricted types of weapons for pest control.

Other bills slated for debate this week are the Crimes Amendment Bill, the Oranga Tamariki (Responding to Serious Youth Offending) Amendment Bill, the Building and Construction (Strengthening Occupational Licensing Regimes) Amendment Bill, and the Commerce (Promoting Competition and Other Matters) Amendment Bill.

World.title: MBIE chief denies attempt to mislead Parliament over failed $35m project
World.content:
The chief executive of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment has accepted the ministry got things wrong when it did not disclose information to MPs about a cancelled IT project earlier this year.

But he denies the ministry deliberately attempted to mislead Parliament.

In March, MBIE failed to tell Parliament's Education and Workforce Committee that the $35 million Biometric Capability Update (BCU) project had been axed, telling MPs there was no public review about its progress.

In reality, the project was already dead.

In June, Speaker Gerry Brownlee referred the matter to the Privileges Committee, after Labour's Phil Twyford and the Education and Workforce Committee both raised it as a matter of privilege.

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley appearing before the Privileges Committee. Giles Dexter / RNZ

Appearing before the Privileges Committee on Tuesday evening, MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley said the ministry had a "genuinely held belief" that there were Budget and commercial sensitivities limiting what it could say in a public forum.

"In hindsight, we should have taken a different approach."

Committee chair Chris Bishop asked why, when asked in March about the key risks and milestones in the project's implementation, Blakeley could not simply say it had been terminated.

"I agree. We got it wrong. I accept that and we should have said differently," Blakeley said.

He added MBIE was still in negotiations over a final payment to Japanese tech company NEC over the project at the time, and so it was concerned that talking about it publicly would make it difficult to conclude those negotiations.

He also accepted MBIE could have gone into a "secret hearing" with the public removed from the committee room.

The decision not to talk about it was not an active decision, he insisted, but more an understanding between himself and Immigration New Zealand's then-boss Alison McDonald that there were sensitivities that limited what they could say.

Blakeley acknowledged that too was a failing.

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley, and the now retired head of INZ Alison McDonald, at select committee in March 2026. Screenshot / New Zealand Parliament

National's Scott Simpson said given Twyford had been asking questions and filing Official Information Act requests before the meeting, it should have been a sufficient flag.

"I agree with you," Blakeley replied.

"It's surprising, in hindsight, that there's no written material on BCU that shows that we weren't well enough prepared, and I accept that."

ACT's Parmjeet Parmar asked Blakeley whether he was happy with the information the ministry had provided.

"At the time, I didn't think I was doing anything wrong. I thought I was answering the questions as best I could, given the limitations that we had."

Parmar also questioned whether there were discussions after the hearing in March about what was said.

"We felt that we'd raised the questions as best we could, given the limitations we were under," Blakeley replied.

National's Chris Bishop. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

An audibly and visibly frustrated Bishop said the entire situation "beggars belief".

"The project was a disaster. The fact that no-one bothered to prepare to explain why it was a disaster, that's both terrible and good for you, bad for the public service," Bishop told Blakeley.

Blakeley would not answer questions from media following the hearing, saying he would wait for the Committee's findings.

Appearing via Zoom from the United Kingdom, the now-retired McDonald said in her mind, the programme had not stopped.

"It hadn't stopped. It had carried on going. The IT project was one element of the identity programme and we had done a lot of preparation around our future services, which is the big IT overhaul piece, if you like, for Immigration New Zealand.

"The biometric capability IT project wasn't managed by me or Immigration New Zealand. It was managed by another part of MBIE."

Bishop asked why McDonald was fronting on it if Immigration New Zealand had nothing to do with it.

McDonald explained the deputy secretary responsible had just resigned and Blakeley had only just started in an acting capacity.

"I honestly thought I was trying to help the committee understand that we were moving in a different direction. On reflection, that was the wrong thing to do."

She accepted that when Tywford was asking about milestones, she should have "paused a bit" and realised he was asking about the IT project specifically, rather than the wider work programme.

"I had no intention whatsoever to mislead the select committee and I find the suggestion that I might have acted deliberately to mislead Parliament extremely distressing," she said.

Education Minister Erica Stanford. RNZ / Louis Dunham

Immigration minister Erica Stanford has accused the ministry of deliberately witholding information from her and the previous Labour government about the project.

On Tuesday morning, Stanford would not presuppose what happened in the hearing.

World.title: Man accused of threatening to carry out attacks on two Auckland schools
World.content:
A man accused of threatening to carry out attacks on two Auckland schools and destroy public buildings allegedly said that he wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist.

Tiedan Huo is on trial in the Manukau District Court, facing a raft of charges relating to a manifesto he allegedly distributed threatening to kill people at Waiuku and Rutherford colleges. He also allegedly threatened to destroy or damage two police stations and buildings at Parliament.

The man has also been charged with unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of explosives and possession of objectionable material.

Huo denies all the charges.

In his opening address to the jury, Crown prosecutor Gareth Kayes said that on 12 March last year, staff at Waiuku College woke to a chilling email that had been sent at 1:42am.

"It was titled 'Important: Don't come to school tomorrow'. And it started with the words 'This is my manifesto'."

Man accused of threatening to attack two Auckland schools Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

The email spoke of being bullied and humiliated by teachers at the school, being unfairly treated by police and being made to feel like a second-class citizen for being Chinese.

"I am going to do something about this now. I have began [sic] preparing for doing something about this since February this year and have finished now."

The email went on to set out in some detail the preparations the sender said they'd made to carry out attacks on Waiuku and Rutherford colleges, as well as damaging the Pukekohe and Te Atatu police stations and buildings at Parliament.

That included making firearms using a 3D printer and creating bullets and explosives to be used in an attack.

The sender said they wanted to kill more people than the Christchurch mosque terrorist, who murdered 51 innocent people on March 15, 2019.

"Do not assume that my guns will not work or are fake because they are 3D printed, that will be very bad."

The email was purportedly sent by a female former Waiuku College student, but after she allowed police to examine her electronic devices, officers established this was not the case, and their inquiries led them to Huo.

The threatening email was sent via an encrypted service but police found a screenshot on Huo's laptop captured just minutes after it was sent, showing the same username as the email.

"There were also a hundred used shotgun shells and a large knife," Kayes told the jury.

"Mr Huo's mother had a second address where Mr Huo would also stay ... In Mr Huo's bedroom at that address police found a loaded pump-action shotgun."

DNA analysis of the firearm found it was 90 billion times more likely to have come from Huo than anyone else.

His mother held a valid firearms licence and a second shotgun was found locked up in a gun safe at her home. Huo has not been charged in relation to that weapon.

Kayes said police found numerous manifestos and videos from mass shooters and terrorists, including the video taken by the Christchurch terrorist.

"These are all what's called, legally, 'objectionable publications'," Kayes told the jury.

"You might be relieved to hear you won't need to view them as part of this trial. That's because they've already all been classified as objectionable by the New Zealand Classifications Office."

What the jury would have to determine, the prosecutor said, was whether Huo did have the publications in his possession. It was the same question they must ask regarding the firearms and explosives charges, he said.

"I suggest that once you have heard all the evidence you will be left in no doubt that it was Mr Huo who sent the manifesto."

The Crown's first witness, Waiuku College principal Stuart Kelly, was asked about the process of putting the school into lockdown after the email was received.

He said the school had taken the threat "very, very seriously".

World.title: A delayed flu season could be on the way as winter ills and chills hit
World.content:
Dr Mamaeroa David on protecting against winter illness Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Winter ills and chills are upon us, but while there are plenty of viruses going around, a health modeller says the flu season is yet to peak.

University of Canterbury mathematical modeller, Professor Michael Plank, said we were in the middle of the winter respiratory season, which was about normal for the time of year, but rates of influenza remained low.

It seemed there was either a small flu season this year, or a late one, Plank said, with the possibility of more illness yet to come.

In 2025, New Zealand had an extended, late flu season, Plank said with cases going through to December due to a new variant of influenza, which prolonged the season.

Michael Plank. (File photo)

"It could mean we see a delayed flu season or smaller flu season this winter. There's a similar pattern in Australia as well.

"Influenza rates there have increased noticeably in the last couple of weeks and there are signs it might be starting to uptick here as well."

Plank said the start of the flu season could be soon, with a peak to come in the next month.

Cases of Covid-19 were also relatively low at present, Plank said, noting it was less seasonal than other viruses and could be a "little all over the place".

"Covid is at very low levels really, looking at the wastewater data, and hospital admissions [for Covid-19] were also very low at the moment."

RSV, Respiratory syncytial virus, was probably at its peak, Plank said, and there were various other viruses around causing similar cough and cold symptoms.

His advice was anyone who was ill should stay at home and keep up to date with vaccinations.

It was certainly not too late to get a flu vaccination, Plank said, as if a late flu season did begin, anyone newly vaccinated would gave high levels of immunity.

He also urged people to stay up to date with Covid boosters.

Senior Māori Medical Advisor with the Immunisation Advisory and Auckland GP, Dr Mamaeroa David, told Morning Report cold viruses were chugging along as well as RSV.

"I feel like we're getting one illness, getting knocked back, going back to kindy or work and getting the next bout of germs," she said.

She said if people could afford it, RAT testing for Covid, influenza and RSV could be useful to let people know what they had - especially since most GPs had a two to three week wait for appointments.

Covid-19 RAT tests. (File photo) AFP

"If you know what you've got, you may not need to see a GP."

Flu vaccination rates were lagging, she said, but as flu season hadn't fully kicked in yet, she agreed there was still time to be immunised.

"Flu vaccination is funded for over 65s and people with other co-morbidities, but if it's not funded for you, most places, like Chemist Warehouse can give you the vaccine for about $24.

"The flu hasn't hit yet but it is coming."

Auckland school feeling the strain

At Glenbrook School in rural South Auckland, principal Lysandra Stuart said winter illnesses were having a large impact on learning with high levels of absenteeism from students and staff.

"We're probably seeing a little bit more than we would typically see at this time of year. If you're a parent and a staff memver you get the double whammy of your students and your children getting sick."

Classes were being impacted by sickness. (File photo) Unsplash

Last week, the first week back of term, Stuart said she had three staff off and and this week she already had to drop tools and get into the classroom to cover classes.

She said one day she had five classes in the school hall with her.

"We're seeing it with our working parents too... kids come back with a sniff or cough too early."

Stuart believe that could be down to pressures around attendance.

She said there were days where 50 to 60 percent of a class were away.

Brining in relievers could be "horrendously costly", she said, so her school often looked at splitting or doubling classes when teachers were away.

In a worst case scenario, Stuart said parents were asked to help out.

Her advice to parents was the "usual stuff", she said, including having a good routine around sleep, eating well if possible and looking after hygiene.

"If you need to stay home please do, because we don't want others getting sick."

The Ministry of Education's Helen Hurst, said the ministry was not aware of any widespread national staffing disruption across schools.

"Just like in the wider population, schools typically experience higher levels of illness during the winter months, and some schools may face temporary challenges managing staff and student absences."

She said schools had well established processes for managing illness and infectious diseases including accessing relief staff, adjusting operational arrangements and working with Health NZ and public health officials.

"We continue to encourage schools and families to follow health guidance on when children should stay home and when they are well enough to attend school."

Advice for businesses

The Employers and Manufacturers Association's (EMA) head of advocacy Alan McDonald said he hadn't heard of any major disruption to workplaces due to illness this winter.

He said sickness at work hit each business differently, and the answer could sometimes be getting in a contractor to help or having to rely on other people doing a little bit extra.

"Generally employers are much more... they recognise sickness in the workplace as something they need to manage well. The days of 'oh I've got a head cold, I feel a bit miserable, but I'll come into the office', that's over.

"If Covid taught us anything it's that if people are sick in the workplace you don't want them coming in, you don't want them infecting other people, so generally the best management is to tell them to stay home."

McDonald said this is what the EMA told its employees.
